Suleyman has long championed the belief that AI cannot truly be sentient, even though it may seem like it to humans, and has argued that the pursuit of “conscious” AI is dangerous. “Just as we should produce AI that prioritizes engagement with humans and real-world interactions in our physical and human world, we should build AI that only ever presents itself as an AI, that maximizes utility while minimizing markers of consciousness,” Suleyman wrote in a blog post last year. “We must build AI for people, not to be a digital person.” If AI is eventually considered a conscious being, it could “shake the foundations of our society,” Suleyman argues in the latest essay, because a being’s experience of consciousness is the cornerstone of all political, legal, and ethical frameworks. “This issue needs urgent public debate. We need to develop collective norms around how training documentation is drafted and deployed,” Suleyman writes.

item.title: This little-known Android setting makes public Wi-Fi less risky
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 6.27
Public Wi-Fi is convenient, but it can expose more of your browsing than you'd expect. Android has a built-in feature called Private DNS that quietly encrypts one of the most revealing parts of your connection. Here's what it does, how to turn it on, and what else helps. What's a private DNS? Encrypting the lookups your phone makes behind the scenes As you may or may not know, every time you tap a link or open an app, your phone has to figure out where that website or service actually lives. It does this through the Domain Name System, or DNS, which translates names like google.com into the numerical IP addresses computers use to reach each other. DNS is one of the oldest parts of the internet, and it wasn't designed with privacy in mind. Traditional DNS requests travel unencrypted, so anyone between you and the DNS server can read them. On your home network, of course, that usually means your internet provider. On public Wi-Fi at an airport, café, or hotel, more people could be watching. The network operator can see every domain your phone looks up, and a malicious hotspot can go further by tampering with those responses, quietly sending you to a fake login page instead of the real one. This is called DNS spoofing, and unencrypted lookups make it easier to pull off. A private DNS is how you solve that problem. Google added support for it in Android 9 Pie, and it has been part of every version since. In the case of Android, it uses a protocol called DNS-over-TLS, which wraps your lookups in the same kind of encryption that protects HTTPS websites. Instead of sending requests in plain text, your phone opens a secure connection to a trusted resolver, checks that it's talking to the right server, and sends its queries through that connection. Neat. As a result, a nosy network can no longer read or alter your DNS traffic. Private DNS does have limits, though. It doesn't hide your IP address, and a determined observer can still infer some things about the servers you connect to. It isn't a VPN. What it does is close a common gap that's easy to exploit, and it works at the operating-system level, so it covers every app on your phone without extra software. How do you set it up? Choosing a trusted provider takes less than a minute For what it's worth, setting up Private DNS takes less than a minute, and you don't need to install anything. The exact path depends on who made your phone. On Pixels and most phones running near-stock Android, open Settings, tap Network & internet, and look for Private DNS. On some models, it sits under an Advanced menu. Samsung puts it somewhere else: go to Settings, then Connections, then More connection settings, and you'll find Private DNS there. If you can't find it, searching for "Private DNS" in the Settings search bar is usually the fastest route. Once you open it, you'll see three options: Off, Automatic, and Private DNS provider hostname. Automatic is often the default. It tries to encrypt your lookups using your network's own DNS server if that server supports encryption. If it doesn't, your phone falls back to regular, unencrypted DNS without telling you, which is exactly what you'd get on a sketchy public hotspot. For real protection, choose the provider hostname option. This makes your phone use a specific encrypted resolver on every network. You'll need to enter a hostname rather than an IP address because Android confirms the server's identity as part of the encrypted handshake. Popular free choices include dns.google for Google Public DNS and one.one.one.one for Cloudflare. Personally, I use Cloudflare myself, since I've found it to be the fastest and most reliable. There's also dns.quad9.net for Quad9, which blocks known malicious domains, and dns.adguard-dns.com for AdGuard, which also filters many ads and trackers. Type it in, tap Save, and you're done. There's one quirk to know about. Some public networks, including certain hotel and corporate Wi-Fi setups, block the port that DNS-over-TLS relies on. If that happens, Android will warn you that the Private DNS server can't be accessed, and pages won't load. Switching to Automatic for a while will get you online, but you should treat that network with extra caution. Other stuff you can do Stacking simple habits for safer public Wi-Fi Private DNS is a smart baseline, but it only fixes one of the things that make public Wi-Fi risky. If you often connect at airports, coffee shops, or hotels, a few other habits make a real difference. The most effective upgrade is a reputable VPN. Private DNS encrypts only your lookups, while a VPN encrypts all of your traffic between your phone and the VPN server, hiding which sites and services you use from the local network. Most VPN apps send DNS through their own encrypted connection and override your Private DNS setting while connected, so the two don't conflict. Choose carefully, though. A free VPN with a vague privacy policy can end up seeing more of your data than the café network ever would. You can also be stricter about how your phone joins networks. Android can remember open networks you've used before and reconnect to them automatically. That makes it easier for an attacker to set up a fake hotspot with a familiar name. Forget public networks when you're done, and turn off any setting that connects to open Wi-Fi automatically. When you don't need Wi-Fi, switching it off further reduces your exposure. Pay attention to what you do while connected. Almost every major website now uses HTTPS, but check for it before entering passwords or payment details, and never click past a browser warning about an invalid certificate. For sensitive tasks like banking, your mobile data connection is generally safer than shared Wi-Fi. If you need to get a laptop online, your phone's hotspot works too. Finally, keep your phone updated. Android security patches and Google Play system updates regularly fix vulnerabilities in the networking stack and elsewhere, but they only help if you install them. Private DNS is a small step with real benefits Private DNS won't turn public Wi-Fi into a secure network, but it closes an easy gap attackers love to exploit. Set a trusted hostname, pair it with a VPN and sensible habits, and your Android phone becomes far harder to snoop on.

item.title: You don't need a powerful PC for these 8 surprisingly useful Linux projects
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.81
An old PC with a few CPU cores, several GBs of RAM, and a working network connection can still be useful long after it stops being suitable for demanding tasks, but Linux can turn that hardware into something that quietly handles useful jobs around your home or small office. I have left out some of the obvious ways to keep using an old PC and focused on projects that can add something practical to a home network. Some are services you can access every day, while others can quietly handle background tasks for weeks without needing much attention: PXE boot server Turn an old PC into a network boot server A PXE boot server lets computers start operating system installers or complete environments directly from the network. Instead of keeping a USB drive for every Linux distribution you want to install, you can keep the required boot files on one machine and make them available to other systems on your LAN. Your old PC can run DHCP and TFTP, or work alongside an existing DHCP server, depending on how your network is configured. You can also use HTTP for transferring larger installation files, which makes the server more practical for repeated installations. Keep Fedora, Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and other installers on the server, then select the required environment when a machine starts. You can also use network booting for rescue environments and diagnostic tools. The workload is modest because the machine primarily serves files across the network. An old desktop with a conventional hard drive can handle this role easily, especially when several computers are not booting simultaneously. Ebooks server Build your own ebook library An old PC can become a dedicated ebook server for your collection. Software such as Calibre-Web can provide a browser-based interface to organize books, search your library, manage metadata, and read or download books on other devices. The server does not need a powerful processor because most of the work involves serving "relatively" small files. This works particularly well for technical books and documentation because the server can hold a large collection without requiring much attention once it is configured. A browser-based library also lets you access the same collection from a laptop, tablet, or phone instead of copying files between devices. If you already have a NAS, you can store the actual books there and run the application on the old PC. That separates the application from the storage and lets you expand the library without replacing the server. Self-hosted password manager Keep your passwords on your own hardware A password manager is another service that can run on modest hardware. Vaultwarden is a lightweight Bitwarden-compatible server that can synchronize passwords and other vault data with supported clients. The computational requirements are small because the server mainly handles authentication, synchronization, and database operations. Even an older computer can manage the workload for a household. You can run it using the container image and place it behind a reverse proxy such as Caddy or Nginx. For a home-only deployment, keeping the service on your LAN avoids exposing it directly to the public internet. If you need access while traveling, WireGuard provides another option. The important work here is configuration rather than processing power. Use strong authentication, keep the server updated, protect the database with regular backups, and make sure you have a recovery method if the machine fails. This also gives the old PC a role that benefits from continuous availability. Your phone and desktop can synchronize with the same server while the password database remains under your control. Local package mirror Create a local software package archive If you maintain several Linux machines, an old PC can save network bandwidth and reduce the time required to install or update software by keeping commonly used packages locally. A package caching or mirroring system can store packages downloaded by your machines. Fedora systems can use tools such as Pulp for more sophisticated repository management, while simpler caching approaches can serve smaller environments. The value becomes clearer when you regularly reinstall machines or operate several systems running the same distribution. Instead of every computer downloading identical packages from an external repository, the local server can provide packages from inside your network. You can also maintain a repository containing software your machines depend on. That gives you a controlled archive of particular package versions and makes rebuilding systems more predictable. Storage requirements depend on how many repositories and versions you retain. CPU requirements remain relatively small because the machine spends most of its time storing files and serving them over the network. Central SSH bastion host Use an old PC as your SSH gateway Managing several servers becomes easier when SSH access goes through a single gateway. An old Linux PC can act as a bastion host, giving you one controlled entry point into the rest of your network. OpenSSH already provides the necessary functionality. From your workstation, ProxyJump can send an SSH connection through the bastion to an internal server: ssh -J bastion internal-server The internal machines can then remain inaccessible from outside the network. The gateway handles the external connection while the target server only needs to accept SSH traffic from the appropriate internal network. For a larger homelab, this approach gives you a consistent route to virtual machines, physical servers, NAS systems, and other infrastructure. n8n / Hermes Turn it into a personal automation machine with n8n Once the old PC is already running continuously, it can handle jobs that would otherwise depend on your desktop being switched on. n8n provides a visual workflow system for connecting APIs, webhooks, schedules, databases, and notification services. For example, a n8n workflow can periodically fetch RSS feeds, check a website, process incoming files, call an API, and send the result to Telegram or email. You can also use it to trigger scripts on your local network. Hermes can serve a similar purpose if you want to build more personal automation around a Linux machine. The main resource requirement depends on what your workflows actually do. Large data-processing jobs can require more RAM and CPU, while simple API-based workflows can run comfortably on older hardware. This makes an old PC a useful small, always-on automation platform. Once it is connected to your network and configured to start its services automatically, it can handle background jobs without occupying your workstation. Automated backup restoration tester Make an old PC test whether your backups actually work A backup job completing successfully does not prove that you can recover your data. An old PC can periodically restore backups and verify that the resulting files or services actually work. For file backups, you can use a script to restore a sample dataset to a temporary directory and compare checksums or expected files. For virtual machines, the test server can restore an image and boot it under KVM or QEMU. Tools such as Borg, Restic, rsync, ZFS snapshots, and Proxmox Backup Server each provide different building blocks for this kind of setup. A simple shell or Python script can orchestrate the actual test and report the result. You can then connect the result to a notification system. If a scheduled restoration fails, the server can send an alert instead of leaving you to discover the problem when you urgently need the backup. The same machine can test different backup sources over time, making it a dedicated recovery-validation system rather than another general-purpose server. Internet dead man’s switch Build a kill switch A Linux PC can also watch for regular signals from another device. If those signals stop arriving for a specified period, the server can trigger a predefined notification or workflow. You need to account for ordinary failures such as an internet outage or power loss. A single missed request should not trigger anything important, and you can also use longer timeouts and multiple checks to reduce false alarms. A simple implementation can use Uptime Kuma, a small HTTP endpoint, or a custom systemd service. Your phone or another computer periodically contacts the server. The server records the last successful heartbeat and acts if the expected check-ins stop. You can also design the project around a specific purpose. Instead of giving the machine permission to perform an irreversible action, have it notify a trusted person or trigger a reversible workflow. Give that old PC a job An aging computer does not have to run a demanding desktop environment to remain useful. Linux can turn it into infrastructure that handles a specific task continuously and reliably. Some of these projects also work well together. The same machine can host several lightweight services, or you can dedicate separate old PCs to the jobs where isolation and reliability matter more. Either way, the useful part of the hardware is no longer its ability to run a demanding desktop. It's that it can stay on, stay connected, and quietly do the job.

item.title: I found the weirdest thing interfering with my Wi-Fi, and the fix took 5 seconds
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.62
Wi-Fi problems are a tricky thing, because they can be traced back to almost anything, and no amount of router tricks will help sometimes. Sometimes, Wi-Fi is just wonky, period. As I tried to (mostly fruitlessly) investigate where my Wi-Fi problems were coming from, I recently found the strangest culprit. Chances are that it's messing up your connection, too. USB 3.0 can really be a nuisance to your Wi-Fi 2.4GHz in particular Out of all the things that could be messing up your Wi-Fi, could you ever suspect that USB 3.0 is the culprit? I know, it doesn't make a whole lot of sense. I get something like dead zones, sure, but USB? How's that related to a router that doesn't even connect via USB by itself? Alas, it absolutely can. The problem lies in radio frequency noise. USB 3.0 moves data at high speeds, and it doesn't need to be to or from your router to cause trouble, as the electrical activity itself can generate broadband interference around the 2.4GHz range. Unfortunately, that's exactly where the 2.4GHz band operates, and it also happens to be the most congested band on most networks. A badly placed USB device, cable, hub, or port can effectively raise the noise floor around your wireless gear and make a perfectly decent signal harder to hear. That's also why the 2.4GHz band is usually more affected than the 5GHz or the 6GHz; it's not that the USB device is somehow biting into your overall Wi-Fi bandwidth, but rather that it's producing so much unwanted RF noise in the wrong part of the spectrum that nearby Wi-Fi receivers start having a bad time. This is especially true if the signal wasn't much to write home about to start with. Long story short, a tiny USB 3.0 device could be messing up your entire home network, and no amount of rebooting the router will fix this particular issue. It can make perfectly good Wi-Fi look borderline broken Slow speeds aren't the only giveaway Annoyingly, figuring this out will probably take you on a merry journey through various router settings, Ethernet cable testing, and whatever else you'll find in a typical network troubleshooting toolkit. That's because the symptoms don't immediately scream "it's the USB gear." You'll see this problem behave as bad Wi-Fi tends to do. Slower speeds, spiking latency, inconsistent performance, disconnects. It also shows up as the 2.4GHz band being utterly disappointing and unreliable. What this doesn't do is mess with your actual router, so the device itself will seem to be fine; everything else won't. One clue to look out for is when the problem seems unusually localized. Maybe the laptop that sits next to a USB hub is struggling, but your phone (far away from the USB troublemakers) is thriving. Or maybe the connection gets worse when you use your external SSD. Those signs don't immediately mean that it has to be USB 3.0, but if you know that you have such devices connected close to the router or the end device, it's worth investigating. The easiest way to prove it is to make the problem disappear Change one thing and see whether it fixes it I'm sure this will elicit a "well, duh" type of response, but the easiest way to fix this is to simply unplug those USB 3.0 devices and see if that helps. Yes, it is that simple. Leave everything else exactly as it was with zero other changes, then rerun the same Wi-Fi test from the same exact spots. Don't make any other changes, such as changing channels or rebooting the router, as we're trying to isolate the problem. If the only thing that changes is the removal of USB 3.0 devices, then congrats, you've isolated the problem. To make sure it's not a one-off, repeat the test a few times. Then, plug the device back in and go over all the tests again. If the performance drops, you've found your culprit. You probably don't need to give up USB 3.0 A little distance can make a surprisingly big difference While getting rid of those USB 3.0 devices is a logical fix, it's hard to just choose to live without any of your USB gadgets. Let's talk about workarounds. The easiest fix is usually not to remove them entirely, but to put some distance between them and the router (or whatever is using Wi-Fi and struggling). Move the hub, drive, or cable farther away and re-run all the tests. Chances are it'll help. ...It didn't help? Inspect the cable itself. A better-shielded USB 3.0 cable or an extension cable can help you keep noisy hardware farther away, preserving your connection. The only downside is that introducing an extension cable may affect charging or data transfer speeds, so it's a trade-off you need to think about. The weirdest Wi-Fi problems aren't always Wi-Fi problems When I finally figured this out, I was pretty baffled. This kind of problem is often the last thing you'll think of when investigating Wi-Fi issues, but it's also one of the easiest things to check. If you're feeling stumped, unplug a few USB 3.0 devices and try your luck.

item.title: These 4 built-in Windows tools helped me build a self-healing PC
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.49
Windows doesn't need third-party utilities to take care of itself. With the right built-in tools and a bit of setup, a PC can check its own health, repair corrupted files, and even recover from a failed boot without much help from you. Task Scheduler The quiet automation engine behind every repair routine Task Scheduler is the piece that ties everything else together. On its own, it doesn't fix anything, but it runs other tools at set times or in response to specific events, so repairs happen without anyone having to remember them. You can open it by searching for Task Scheduler in the Start menu or by running taskschd.msc, and the Create Task option gives you far more control than the simplified Create Basic Task wizard. Triggers are where the tool gets interesting. A task can run on a fixed schedule, at startup, at logon, when the computer goes idle, or when a particular entry appears in the Event Viewer. That last option lets a maintenance script run in response to a logged error, such as an unexpected shutdown, instead of waiting for the next scheduled window. For system maintenance, a few settings matter more than the rest. Repair commands need administrator rights, so set the task to run with the highest privileges and allow it to run whether a user is signed in or not. Running it under the SYSTEM account avoids storing a password and keeps it independent of any single user profile. On a laptop, the Conditions tab can restrict the task to times when the machine is plugged in, which prevents a long scan from draining the battery. The Settings tab also lets you run a task as soon as possible after a scheduled start is missed. That's useful for a PC that isn't always powered on at the chosen hour, since a skipped weekly check simply happens the next time the machine is available. The practical result is a single scheduled task that launches a script containing the repair commands covered below. Once configured, it runs in the background, and its history tab shows when each run happened and whether it finished successfully. DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) Fixing the source Windows uses to repair itself DISM is a command-line tool originally built to prepare and service Windows images, but it has become one of the most useful repair utilities on a running system. Its value comes from what it repairs: the component store, a folder of reference files located in C:\Windows\WinSxS that Windows relies on when installing updates and restoring damaged system files. If that store is corrupted, other repair tools have nothing reliable to work from. DISM offers three levels of inspection, all run from an elevated Command Prompt or Terminal. The command DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth quickly checks whether corruption has already been flagged. The /ScanHealth option runs a deeper and slower scan of the component store. Finally, /RestoreHealth scans for problems and repairs whatever it finds, which is the command most people end up using. By default, RestoreHealth downloads replacement files from Windows Update, so the PC needs an internet connection for the repair to succeed. When that isn't possible, or when Windows Update itself is part of the problem, the /Source parameter can point DISM to a mounted Windows installation image instead. The image should match the installed version of Windows; otherwise, the repair may fail. A full RestoreHealth run can take anywhere from several minutes to much longer, and the progress indicator has a habit of pausing at certain percentages. That pause is normal, and interrupting the process is a worse idea than waiting. DISM writes a detailed record of each operation to C:\Windows\Logs\DISM\dism.log, which is the first place to look if a repair reports an error. In an automated maintenance routine, DISM should run first. Because the System File Checker pulls its replacement files from the component store, repairing that store beforehand gives the next step a healthy foundation. It also means that a problem DISM can't fix shows up clearly in the logs before anything else runs. SFC (System File Checker) Scanning protected system files for silent corruption System File Checker has been part of Windows for decades, and it remains the simplest way to verify that core operating system files haven't been damaged or replaced. It works through Windows Resource Protection, which guards critical files, folders, and registry keys. When SFC finds a protected file that doesn't match its expected version, it replaces it with a clean copy from the component store. The standard command is sfc /scannow, run from an elevated prompt. The scan checks every protected file and repairs what it can, reporting one of a handful of outcomes when it finishes. The best result is a message stating that no integrity violations were found. Other messages indicate that it found and repaired corrupt files, or that some files couldn't be fixed. For a scan that only reports problems without changing anything, the /verifyonly switch is available. SFC's biggest limitation is its dependence on the component store. If the reference copies are damaged, SFC can't restore healthy files, which is exactly why running DISM first is the recommended order. When both are chained together in a script, DISM repairs the source, and SFC then uses that source to fix the live system files. Every scan is recorded in C:\Windows\Logs\CBS\CBS.log. That file is long and noisy, but filtering it for lines tagged with [SR] isolates the entries created by SFC, making it much easier to see which files were affected. SFC can also work when Windows won't start normally. From the Windows Recovery Environment, the /offbootdir and /offwindir parameters point the scan at the offline Windows installation, so files can be repaired without booting into the desktop. There are trade-offs to scheduling it. A scan uses noticeable disk and processor resources, so running it daily is unnecessary for most people. A weekly run during idle hours catches problems early without getting in the way. Quick Machine Recovery (QMR) Letting Windows fix boot failures through the cloud The tools above can only help when Windows starts. Quick Machine Recovery covers the scenario they can't: a PC that fails to boot at all. It's a Windows 11 feature that Microsoft built on top of the older Startup Repair tool, and it became available to Home and Pro users starting with the August 2025 security update for version 24H2 and later. When Windows detects repeated boot failures, the PC enters the Windows Recovery Environment instead of looping endlessly. QMR then connects to the internet over Ethernet or Wi-Fi and checks Windows Update for a remediation that addresses the problem. If a fix exists, it downloads and applies it, then restarts the machine. If the repair doesn't work, the device returns to the recovery environment with the usual troubleshooting options. The feature is enabled by default on unmanaged Windows 11 Home and Pro machines, and its toggle lives under Settings, System, Recovery. Devices managed by an organization have it turned off by default, leaving the decision to administrators. An additional setting enables automatic remediation, which makes the PC keep checking for a solution at set intervals rather than stopping after a single attempt. When QMR is switched off, Windows falls back to the local Startup Repair process. It's important to understand what QMR is designed for. Microsoft positions it as a response to widespread boot problems, such as a faulty update or driver affecting many devices at once, where the company can identify the issue and push a targeted fix. It isn't a general-purpose repair tool for problems unique to a single machine, and it can't help if the PC has no network connection during recovery. Early testing also suggests it may not work on older hardware. Even with those limits, QMR fills the last gap in a self-healing setup by handling failures that happen before any scheduled script has a chance to run. Built-in tools that keep Windows running on its own Task Scheduler automates maintenance, DISM repairs the component store, SFC restores protected system files, and Quick Machine Recovery handles boot failures. Together, they give Windows 11 a layered, largely hands-off way to keep itself healthy without installing any extra software.

item.title: These 3D prints are meant to break—that's the whole point
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.38
3D prints can be brittle and weak, depending on which materials you use and how you choose to print them. But some prints are designed to be broken, either as part of their core functionality or in order to protect something else. Here are some 3D prints that you might want to break. Snap-off shims Snap to decide which size you need 3D-printed shims can be made to size and are perfect for installing and fixing doors and windows that are out of plumb. There are two ways you can go about this: draw up and design a shim that fits perfectly every time you need one, or keep a few around and break them down to size with models like the cutaway shim or easy snap waffle shim. While 3D-printed parts are weak enough that bending can cause them to separate at the layer lines, even basic PLA is tough enough to withstand the sort of compressing force that these shims are designed to endure. They’re perfect for using up those last few grams of filament, too! Tamper-evident seals and locks Designed with a single use in mind Tamper-evident seals and locks are designed to be used just once. You attach them to whatever it is you want to monitor for interference, after which you have to break them in order to gain access. There are a few models to choose from here, including the popular tamper-evident lock and the much smaller tamper-evident bag lock. Both of these models have an excellent community rating, even if they’re probably not as reliable as commercially available solutions. Assuming you’re not securing police evidence or crime scenes, they’ll probably do the job just fine. Remember that these aren’t designed to keep people out like a standard lock, but rather to break easily if someone attempts to make their way in. Breakable surprise egg Add a surprise during the pause, then finish the print This breakable egg needs to be cracked in order to get to whatever is stored within it. Send it to your printer and then, when the print pauses, fill it with a surprise: toys, candy, or anything else you want. Resume the print and the contents will be sealed up inside, ready for someone to break open. At only 8g of filament per egg, you don’t need to feel too bad about plastic waste (justmake sure that you recycle or reuse the waste filament when you’re done). Be careful about putting chocolate and other meltable items inside the egg, since the heat from the print bed will cause them to soften. The Death Box Like the surprise egg but less cheery The Death Box follows the same basic principle as the surprise egg above, with a cheeky morbid twist. This simple yet sturdy print is designed to store a piece of paper, photograph, or other thin object. When the print pauses, add your items, then resume the print to seal them up. To retrieve them—whether that’s after your death or not—the box will need to be broken. The author has included two models: one’s a bit easier thanks to a weak spot, another that’s a lot harder to break. This doesn’t have to contain your last will and testament or instructions following your demise; you could use it to enclose a private note, the answers to a quiz, or anything else you want to save for a big reveal. Alternatively, print it using something sturdy, put a photo of yourself and a small blurb about who you are, and bury it in the backyard or entombed in the walls of your house as a time capsule. Drone propeller guards Break cheap guards, not propellers 3D-printed drone propeller guards are surprisingly popular, even though drones still feel like a relatively niche gadget. There are guards for a wide variety of models like the DJI’s Avata 2, Lito, Mini 3, and Mini 2 (SE). There are many more models online, from entire protective cages to generic prop guards for other drone types. These lightweight prints shouldn’t add a ton of weight to your drone when printed using light material. Some call for TPU for added flex, but most use cheap PLA that’s easy to print and cheap to replace should the worst happen. While it’s debatable that these are meant to be broken, it’s certainly preferable to break these as opposed to a more expensive part of your drone like the chassis or propeller. Beyond protecting a flying machine you may already own, did you know you can also use your 3D printer to create your own drone?

item.title: You don't need CAD skills to customize 3D models anymore
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.28
Have you seen the slew of new customizable 3D models that are on sites like MakerWorld lately? It's all thanks to a word you might never have heard of before — parametric. Parametric modeling has done more to improve the 3D printing world than almost anything else, and here's everything you need to know. Normal 3D printing files are one-size-fits-all And we all know how one-size-fits-all rarely actually fits well If you've been 3D printing for any length of time, then you've probably run into the problem where a 3D print file from a site like MakerWorld, Thingiverse, or anywhere else almost works. The hole is slightly too small, or the grid is a little too large. While you can easily scale a project in your slicer, that's often not the best solution. The problem with scaling is that everything scales equally. That might not sound like a problem, but for something like Gridfinity, that means the entire thing no longer fits the Gridfinity bins. So, the only option used to be trying to pull the model into a 3D CAD program and update it manually. It was cumbersome, never worked well, and it always took way more effort than it should have. However, parametric modeling completely changes that. Parametric modeling allows you to change parameters to fit your project It adds a level of customizability that just wasn't there before Parametric modeling isn't new. It's been around for years, but it was typically found only in CAD software. Still, though, I always loved it when I found someone who had a parametric 3D model I could just load into Autodesk Fusion and start changing parameters. The way parametric modeling works is by assigning a parameter to a dimension in the model instead of a dimension itself. Then, you define the dimension in a separate table. This is great because you can define something like "plyThickness" for the thickness of your plywood and use that for extrusions. Then, you can change that from 1/8 to 1/4 to 1/2 inch, and it just updates the model accordingly. These parameters can be used anywhere in the model, and they update dynamically. So, if you parameter affects. There have been a few instances where that hasn't happened for me, but it's typically because I did something wrong. But in the world of 3D printing, this is a much better way to design in CAD. You can make a parameter called "smallMagnet" and then print a test print, and if you need to change the size, you can just change the parameter instead of having to update each magnet hole individually. The problem was that, to use parametric modeling, you had to use the software that the model was originally designed in. Thankfully, in 2026, that's no longer a requirement. You no longer need CAD knowledge to edit parametric models It can be done right in your web browser now These days, you'll find parametric models right on sites like MakerWorld. This allows someone to design parametrically and then upload it to MakerWorld, and you just have to enter a few dimensions on the website. For example, take this screw generator. With it, you can generate just about any screw or nut you might need to 3D print, all from your browser without having to know CAD. Or there's this parametric post cap generator. All you have to do is insert the post size you have, and it designs the cap to fit your post. The sky is the limit here, and I love that parametric generators are now available in the browser. One of the best places to use parametric modeling is with Gridfinity. Instead of having to find dedicated websites to generate your grids, you can simply navigate to this customizable Gridfinity project on MakerWorld and input the dimensions you need. Need custom-sized Gridfinity bins? There's a parametric project for that, too. Parametric modeling also lets you do more than just customize dimensions. For instance, there's this custom LED name light box project where you can type a name in, and it generates the whole project for you. Or, this custom name pen holder project where you, again, just type a name and it creates a custom pen holder with the name. If . 3D printing has never been easier When I first started 3D printing around five years ago, it was still a tinkerer's hobby. In some ways, it still is. But these days, 3D printing is much more user-friendly and easier to get into than ever before. 3D printers now tune themselves out of the box in a matter of minutes, and there are more places to download files than ever before. So, if you've been wanting to try out 3D printing, there has never been a better time than now to give it a shot.

item.title: 6 beginner self-hosting projects you can run on any old PC
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.87
Your busted laptop from 2019 or that old desktop that has been gathering dust in a closet might not be suitable for use as a "normal" PC, but they have more than enough power to run useful services. You don't need a data center tucked under your desk to get started with self-hosting—almost any PC will do. These are six lightweight apps or services that you can run on almost any PC that'll still boot today without requiring an expensive RAM upgrade. Pi-hole Network-wide ad-block and tracker blocking Pi-hole is a classic self-hosting project because it is useful, easy to set up, and low-stakes if something breaks. A Pi-hole sits between the devices on your network and a DNS server on the internet, where it can effectively prevent specified websites from loading by referencing a blocklist. If you use the right blocklist, you can block ads, trackers, and even some malware. That makes it an especially useful project if you have a lot of smart devices on your network that don't support conventional ad blocking. Additionally, the Pi-hole's dashboard makes it easy to know which device is trying to access the internet, when, and the domain it is trying to connect to. If you're privacy conscious, that allows you to prevent many smart devices from "phoning home" without your permission. You can run a Pi-hole using Docker on almost any major operating system, but I typically install it using the official install script on Linux instead. Once it has been installed, you need to log into your router's admin panel (use the app or the web portal) and point the router's DNS server at the Pi-hole's local IP address. Then all you need to do is select a blocklist that you like. Vaultwarden Store your own passwords securely Bitwarden is an open-source password manager that normally relies on Bitwarden's official servers to store your passwords, but it isn't strictly necessary. If you want, you can host your own password server using Vaultwarden. Vaultwarden is an implementation of the normal Bitwarden Client API written in Rust. Critically, that means that you can use the official Bitwarden app on your phone or desktop—or the browser extension—normally to connect to it. You also get the premium features Bitwarden offers, like time-based one-time-passwords (TOTPs) and attachments at no cost. Vaultwarden only uses a few hundred megabytes of RAM (at most), so it'll run on pretty much anything. However, you're assuming total responsibility for maintaining robust backups of your passwords and making sure that your network is secured against would-be intruders. Syncthing Keep files moving between devices without a cloud account If you don't like using Google Drive or OneDrive every time you need to sync your files from one device to another, you could self-host Syncthing instead. Rather than rely on a cloud-based provider, Syncthing works by creating a continuous, encrypted peer-to-peer sync system between the devices you set up. Those devices could be anything, ranging from phones to personal computers to home servers. When you add an old PC into the mix as an always-on node, it functions a bit like your own personal central cloud server. Say you have three different devices on your network: A, B, and C, where B is your old PC working as an always-on node. If A and C need to sync their files, but they're not always online at the same time, they can both just send the files to be synced to B in the interim. When A comes online, B will send C's files to the A device and vice versa. Syncthing's footprint is pretty small, and usually only consumes a few hundred megabytes of RAM at a time. FreshRSS News and a feed without the algorithm One of my least favorite parts of the modern internet is algorithmically driven feeds. So, I switched to an RSS feed instead. FreshRSS is a simple, lightweight RSS aggregator that you can self-host. It offers a web UI and API support for mobile apps, so you can access it from any modern device. It allows you to follow blogs, subreddits, YouTube channels, and countless other things without a recommendation engine making decisions on your behalf. Uptime Kuma Monitoring everything you host Once your homelab has grown to more than a handful of services, manually keeping track of them all is a pain. Uptime Kuma is a self-hosted service that monitors them for you. If something goes wrong, you can have notifications sent to you via Discord, Telegram, Email, or ntfy. It isn't a system metrics tool, though. If you want an overview of your network's performance, or detailed CPU and RAM usage information, you'll need to look elsewhere. Homepage If you build a homelab, you need a dashboard If you're not running Caddy (or some other service) to give all of your services easily-memorable domain names, then keeping track of your services can get to be pretty tedious. I have more than 20 self-hosted services running on my network these days, and I have no hope of remembering whether Jellyfin or Navidrome live at 192.168.0.111 or 192.168.0.101. Fortunately, I don't have to enter an IP address manually most of the time. Homepage is a dashboard that provides an overview and link to all of the self-hosted services on my network. It integrates neatly with Pi-hole, Uptime Kuma, Proxmox, and Docker to provide tidy widgets that display the status of various services running on your network. The only slight downside is that you handle configuration via YAML files, which are a type of text file. They're human-readable, so you don't need to know C++ or Python to configure Homepage. Self-hosting doesn't need anything special None of the services on this list are especially demanding, and if you use Proxmox or Docker, you could probably run all of them on a single 10-year-old desktop PC with 8GB of RAM as long as you are careful. If you had 16GB of RAM, you'd easily be able to run a dozen lightweight services.

item.title: I started keeping an "offline" NAS. It’s the only backup I actually trust
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.03
Most home NAS units are designed to stay powered on and available 24/7. After all, if you want to ensure a backup is made, the best way to do that is keep your backup solution available all the time. However, I also run a small NAS that stays powered off and completely disconnected except for a backup that I run every month or so. As strange as it sounds, it is actually the backup that I trust and rely on the most. This is why. An offline NAS is my backup of last resort Disconnected and offline 95% of the time My offline NAS is my "backup of last resort." It isn't what I use to handle backups of the data that I use day to day for work or in my hobbies. Rather, it stores copies of irreplaceable photos, copies of important tax forms going back a decade or so, digital copies of my social security card, and other things like that. An offline NAS isn't a replacement for your regular NAS or cloud backup. It is a supplement to ensure that your most important files aren't lost. As such, I keep it offline unless I'm actively creating or using a backup. The hardware doesn't need to be anything fancy. You can use an old PC, a Raspberry Pi with a USB drive enclosure, an old Synology unit, or even just a bare drive in a dock. The most important thing is nothing can write to the drive without your direct intervention. . It can't be corrupted by a bad update or botched sync Always-on backups back up mistakes One of the problems that can occur with always-on backups is actually how good they are at mirroring exactly what you do. If you make a mistake and delete something from your PC or a file gets corrupted accidentally, that change can be backed up within minutes, depending on your settings. We've occasionally seen cases where a bad software update to either the NAS or the backup file system can break something too. An offline system mitigates all of those risks. It is almost certainly going to be offline when an unexpected update rolls out, and your file and folder updates are similarly insulated. If I were to corrupt a document with my current setup, I'd have weeks to spot the problem. Moreover, I deliberately don't update files that I haven't manually changed. That way, if a sync bug or a botched migration overwrites my entire photo library, I don't have to panic. I can just fire up the offline NAS, copy over my "cold storage" backup, and everything is fine. Ransomware and malware can't affect a drive that isn't connected Network isolation can be protection Unfortunately, some modern ransomware is specifically designed to find and infect networked storage. Some NAS manufacturers have features designed to mitigate that risk, but it still isn't a risk I want to take. An imperfect implementation can still leave you vulnerable. On the other hand, a device that is disconnected from power and the internet can't be hit with ransomware. The only window where my backup solution could be infected is during a backup phase, but that risk is easy to mitigate—double-check your PC before you perform a backup. It isn't affected by random power surges or wear and tear A disconnected device doesn't care about a power surge There is a physical safety advantage as well. Power surges and brownouts can damage electronics, but if your device is disconnected completely, you don't need to worry about it. You reduce wear and tear Mechanical hard drives are also subject to wear and tear, especially if they spin 24/7. On the other hand, a NAS that is only active for an hour or two every month (or whatever your backup window is) will have a much longer lifespan. SSDs need to be powered on intermittently or their risk of data loss increases. Mechanical hard drives are basically safe to leave off—it doesn't meaningfully affect their data retention. An offline backup is my version of cold storage Always-on backups are designed to protect your regular files against loss. I back up my work and hobby project files to a cloud server and a separate NAS daily. While losing them would be inconvenient and frustrating, it wouldn't devastate me—none of it is irreplaceable. On the other hand, the offline NAS shines when you need a backup that you want to insulate against every possible risk or attack avenue. If you have photos you can't replace, critical documents that you don't want to lose, or anything else like that, I'd recommend creating an always-offline NAS. So long as you're careful with it, and selective about the files you choose to back up, it'll be reliable and cost-effective for years. The only real tradeoff is convenience. You need to remember to transfer your latest f1040 during tax season or those pictures you scanned from a relative.

item.title: 4K remasters have an AI problem, and it's destroying the history of film
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.39
Most people probably assume that the latest 4K Blu-ray release of a movie is the definitive version with the highest quality. It's the version that you should buy to preserve that title for yourself at the highest quality. Right? For many films, the process of creating that 4K release does more harm than good, meaning you might end up buying an inauthentic presentation of your favorite flick because AI is now entering the chat. A 4K remaster should reveal an old film, not redesign it That belongs in a museum! What is the goal of a 4K remaster anyway? On the surface, it sounds pretty simple. A VHS tape, LaserDisc, DVD, or standard Blu-ray has a fixed amount of lines (for VHS and LaserDisc) or pixels that limit how much detail can be seen on-screen. So the goal is to increase that detail level to what 4K UHD offers. Which is about 8.3 million pixels. Four times that of a standard Blu-ray, and a silly amount of extra detail compared to older formats. Where does the extra detail come from? If the film was originally shot on actual film, then you can rescan the negatives at higher detail levels. 35mm film holds detail roughly equivalent to between 4K and 6K in digital formats. So when you remaster the movie with fresh scans, you can actually now see detail that was invisible in the original cut but was actually captured on-set. The issues arise when the original film was shot digitally. If a movie was shot in 1080p, then 1080p is the only ground-truth level of detail that film will ever have. To make the image appear sharper and more detailed, you need to use some form of upscaling process. AI upscaling has become the most advanced form of this process, but the AI is making up that extra detail from pure digital imagination, which can also sometimes include hallucinations. "True Lies," "Aliens," and shows what happens when AI starts guessing Now the humans look like aliens There's an excellent video by the YouTube channel Nerrel called AI Can Ruin Movies Now, Too - Aliens and True Lies on 4k, which uses those two titles to break down how AI upscalers are absolutely butchering movies, resulting in a 4K commercial release that is objectively worse than other lower-resolution formats. From giving actors uncanny, smooth, and waxlike skin to distorting or even hallucinating entire faces, it's shocking that any professional film editor would sign off on a final cut like this. What makes it even more egregious is that films like Aliens were indeed shot on celluloid. So there was no reason to use upscaling on a 2K intermediate master. However, doing a proper 4K version based on new film scans is expensive and time-consuming. So you're getting the cheapskate, low-effort 4K cut, and I guess they just hope no one notices. Film grain is part of the photograph, not dirt covering it The medium is the message AI is also one of the technologies used to remove film grain, although some people might call that "denoising." The thing is, film grain isn't a defect that has to be removed; it's the original texture of the medium used to make the movie. To me, it's like taking an oil painting and then treating it to look like it was made using an inkjet printer. An oil painting should look like it was made with oil-based paints, right? But even when those who remaster films argue that film grain is visual distortion that gets in the way of what the filmmaker wanted us to see, there's actually a technical reason why it can be a problem. Film grain makes it hard to compress a film because it's random and therefore gets in the way of repeatable data that can be thrown out. It's why Netflix had to invent a film grain effect. So the movie is compressed with no film grain, and then a filter is applied when it gets played back. It's a decent compromise but doesn't apply to 4K Blu-ray releases, only streamed movies. The remaster could be the only version anyone is allowed to see I have an extensive collection of DVDs and HD Blu-ray movies that I consider the versions that are worth keeping. If the original movie was not meant to have HDR and requires upscaling to hit 4K, then I might as well just let my TV or Blu-ray player do the upscaling based on that source, which is untouched by AI. The thing is, at least no one can come and mess with my discs and change the content. When it comes to streaming services like Disney, you're only likely to have access to that terrible AI-upscaled 4K version, and even when you "buy" a movie digitally, that's what you're going to get. Even the 1080p stream version will only be a downscaled stream of the butchered 4K master. I hate that I need to carefully check how a 4K movie was mastered before spending any money on it, but that's the world we live in now.

item.title: 4 "smart" home gadgets that don't need Wi-Fi or an app
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.18
I have a home filled with devices connected to my router, but I'm not fully convinced that these have made my home smarter. In fact, many of my favorite purchases, those I can recommend with an unequivocal yes, don't require an app at all. A night light that stays on when the power goes out It also doubles as a flashlight If there is one cheap upgrade you can make to your home that will absolutely improve your quality of life, it's this. Get a night light that stays on when you lose power. You'll never find yourself stranded in pitch dark. These night lights also serve as flashlights when you unplug them from the wall. I have a house filled with portable power stations I can use to turn the lights back on, but I need the flashlight to help me see our breaker panel in the first place! My phone is typically the most convenient light, but I don't always have it on me. Meanwhile, these night lights are practically shouting "Look at me!" I purchased several GE 4-in-1 Power Failure LED Night Lights from Amazon, and they were my favorite purchase of 2025. Mine relies on AA batteries, but there is a variant with a built-in battery you can switch to instead. Hot water dispenser Enjoy drinks without waiting for water to boil As an avid tea drinker, I loved my electric kettle. I also resigned it to the donate pile as soon as I was sent a Waterdrop M6CG countertop hot water dispenser. Owning one of these things is like having a Keurig without being limited to overpriced, wasteful K-Cups. Put your mug under the dispenser, choose the temperature, and walk away. When you come back, your tea will have steeped. Yet while the countertop hot water dispenser instantly displaced my kettle, I didn't use it for long. As a homeowner, I have the option for a built-in hot water dispenser instead. Waterdrop's K6 instant hot water dispenser now sits next to my kitchen faucet, and it's my favorite kitchen upgrade so far. Unlike the countertop version, it doesn't need to be manually refilled. It also offers more precise temperature controls. It may not have the attractiveness of a smart kettle, but I can still fill a teapot with instant hot water when I want to serve tea the traditional way. Samsung Music Frame A Bluetooth speaker that I want in every room of the house I have ambient music playing all throughout the day. It helps wake me up in the morning as I start to get my kids ready for school. It helps me concentrate as I write. Nothing complements ambient music, music that's intended to blend into the background, quite like a Bluetooth speaker that is just as non-intrusive. The Samsung Music Frame is that speaker. Samsung's picture frame shares its name with the Frame TV, but these are very different products. While the TV has an always-on matte display and comes with Tizen OS, the Music Frame is a traditional picture frame that happens to double as a Bluetooth speaker. It's up to you to supply a paper photo or pay extra for a custom canvas. If you funnel the power cord through the wall as I have, the only tell is the frame's thickness, which is bulkier than the other frames on my wall. The Music Frame technically integrates with Samsung SmartThings, the company's smart home platform, but you don't need to download that app at all to use the Frame as a speaker. Just plug it in, pair it, and start listening to sound that is surprisingly rich. The Music Frame isn't new, so while it remains pricey, you may be able to find one refurbished and heavily discounted, as I did. A battery-powered fan Airflow wherever you need it My home has central air conditioning, but if I have a choice between cranking up the AC and turning up a nearby fan, I'd rather feel air blowing against my skin. Yet even with ceiling fans in nearly every room, some areas still don't get the air. That is why SwitchBot's Circulator Floor Fan isn't a gimmick — it's actually one of my favorite additions to my home this past year. I love this fan so much that, even after being sent a free review sample, I very quickly purchased another one of my own. Like all SwitchBot products, this fan can connect to a SwitchBot hub, be controlled by an app, and integrate with all sorts of automations. That's not the best thing about it. What I love most is the fact that it's simply an attractive-looking battery-powered fan that's easy to pick up and move wherever I want it to be without having to drag around a cord or look for an outlet. I can now float a fan in the middle of our living room without introducing a tripping hazard. The built-in light also provides just enough ambiance to help me navigate spaces at night. The product functions just fine as a portable fan, without requiring an app for setup. Skipping the app makes a smart home more resilient I enjoy my share of smart home automations. It's nice having certain lights come on automatically in the evening and turn off in the morning. I like having ceiling fans that turn on and off based on whether I'm in the room. But these fail when my smart home hub loses power or the internet goes down. The products above are always useful, no matter what my networking is doing.

item.title: Google killed Duo, and Android video calling has never really recovered
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.11
Despite Google’s many attempts, Android has never had a solid iMessage or FaceTime equivalent. 10 years ago, it made a big play with two apps named Allo and Duo. Only the latter survived into the 2020s, and video calling on Android has never really recovered. If there’s one thing Android fans can agree on, it’s that Google’s approach to messaging has been messy. Most people remember the long list of failed text messaging apps, but it has had just as much luck with video calling. Duo was the company’s best attempt — and it was killed. The Pre-Duo Era Remember Hangouts? Google’s journey with video calling started in 2008 with Gmail. The company added Google Talk to its email service a month after the first Android phone launched. However, Google didn’t offer a video calling app for Android until 2011. That app was Google Talk, which had been included on every Android device since 2008. Not many people actually got a chance to use it, though, since it relied on having the newly released Android 2.3 Gingerbread. In classic Google fashion, it launched a competing product just two months later: Hangouts. To this day, Hangouts is Google’s best attempt at a unified messaging platform. It started as the group video calling part of Google+, the company’s infamous social media flop. Eventually, it replaced Google Talk video calls in Gmail, and later became its own standalone app with text messages and video calling in one. Google fleshed out Hangouts from 2013 to 2016. The Android app gained support for SMS, including the ability to send and receive from a browser. Google Voice was also integrated into Hangouts. Everyone who had a Google account could use Hangouts — it didn’t rely on phone numbers. Duo arrives to fix what isn’t broken And it almost works I was writing about Android back when Hangouts came and went. I remember how much people in the Android community loved it. For the first time, it felt like Google had a genuinely unified approach to messaging. Instant messaging between Google accounts, SMS with desktop sync, and video calling — all in one app. Sadly, Google didn’t feel the same way. At Google I/O 2016, the company announced two new apps: Allo and Duo. It was a two-prong approach to text messaging and video calling (and our first introduction to Google Assistant). Hangouts existed alongside them for a year until it was rebranded and split into two for enterprise customers. Now, Allo turned out to be a bigger failure than Google+ — the company abandoned it only two years after launch. Duo, on the other hand, stuck around much longer. Android’s messaging situation was a mess, but Duo created a much cleaner solution for video calling. Duo could be used with a phone number or a Google account. Contacts who had access to Duo were labeled, making it easy to know who you could call. Duo offered both video and audio-only calls, supported screen sharing and desktop, and it had a nifty feature called “Knock Knock” that showed the caller a live preview before they answered. The app also worked extremely well with low-bandwidth, rating higher than all its competitors. Before Duo, it wasn’t obvious to the average Android user which app they should use for video calling. Google was maintaining Hangouts, Hangouts Meet, Messenger (SMS), Voice, and GChat — none of which were clearly intended for basic video calls. Duo was the FaceTime equivalent Android so desperately needed. Google makes video calling boring again But maybe that’s okay Duo made it all the way until 2022 before Google decided to make a change yet again. It had been rumored that Google was going to fold Duo into Meet for a couple of years, and it finally happened. Duo had established itself as a simple, focused video calling app — all that went out the window with Meet. I mentioned that Hangouts was rebranded and split into two in 2017. Those two apps were Hangouts Chat and Hangouts Meet. For reasons unknown, Google decided to use a consumer-facing brand name for enterprise apps. Hangouts Meet was a Zoom-like video conferencing app for enterprise customers. In 2020, “Hangouts” was dropped, and it became “Google Meet.” It was still a Zoom competitor. Then, in 2022, the aforementioned Duo merger happened. The Duo app became “Google Meet,” and for a comically long time, there were two apps named “Google Meet” in the Play Store. Not complicated at all. Mercifully, the original enterprise-friendly Google Meet app was removed in 2024. Since then, all of Google’s video calling and conferencing is contained within the Meet app. It has Duo’s one-on-one video calling features and Zoom-like conference calling. The situation is pretty clear-cut now. If you want to do anything video call-related through Google, Meet is the app to open. It’s simple, but it also feels like Google gave up. Duo was a fresh, fun approach to video calls. Meet technically works, but it has all the pizzaz of Zoom — and no one wants to use Zoom to make personal calls. In the end, boring is better than complicated. I would have preferred to keep Duo around for video calls and Meet for conferencing, but Google had other ideas. Hopefully, we don’t have another shake-up on the horizon.

item.title: Universal USB-C docks are convenient, but old-school docking stations were actually better
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.03
My first laptops were usually office hand-me-down machines and one I remember most fondly was a Pentium 133 system that was pretty thin and light for its time. The coolest thing it came with was a docking station, but this wasn't what you'd think of as a laptop dock today. It was a device molded to fit the entire laptop, with a proprietary connector that ensured the peripherals in the dock, such as hard drives and CD-ROM drives, performed the same as any internal drive. All you had to do was come home, press the laptop into the dock until you heard a click. Now, I dock my Windows laptop using a USB-C dock that would work with almost any computer using a modern USB-C port. On a technical level, it's a superior solution and far more flexible, but I still think model-specific docks have a few things going for them. Old laptop docks were designed as part of the computer Fits like a glove Being built specifically for a given laptop or family of laptop computers is probably the thing I liked the most about old-school laptop docks. They were designed from the ground up to work with a specific laptop body, and so the designers could use that as a way to elevate the experience. That was often literally true, since some docks lifted the laptop, acting as a monitor riser and sometimes letting you type at a more comfortable angle. The idea wasn't necessary that you would always use an external display, so many of these docks helped make the laptop easier to use even if you didn't have an external monitor or other peripherals. While a single USB cable that connects everything and sometimes even charges your laptop is impressive, it just doesn't have the same cohesiveness. Proprietary connectors offered predictable performance It takes the "U" out of USB I've written before about how USB-C is a real mess of a standard and that's a major issue for docks. There are so many variables involved that if you take a random mix of dock, cable, and laptop, you actually have no real way of knowing what performance or capabilities you'll get when it's all plugged in without looking up spec sheets. This is especially true if your dock is also charging your laptop via USB-C, since whether the laptop gets as much power as it needs depends on the stars aligning just right. With proprietary docks, you're using the dedicated power supply designed for that laptop and dock combo. So not only do you have one less thing to plug in, you also know that your laptop is charging at the speed it should, and receiving exactly as much power as it needs. Modern USB-C docks turn one fast connection into several compromises Bottlenecks galore Even if you have a fast USB4 or Thunderbolt connection on your laptop, its total bandwidth is finite. All the devices connected to that port share that bandwidth, and the more things you plug in, the less bandwidth there is to go around. One advantage of proprietary docs is that all the peripherals don't share the same set of wires. If you look at something like the Dell E-Port docking station, you'll see the proprietary connector has numerous wires in parallel. So each set of ports gets a direct line to the bus and the controller it needs without having to share with other types of port. A USB-C plug cannot replace a proper docking mechanism It's a little flimsy, to be honest One of my biggest gripes with modern "universal" docks is that they're risky and fragile. It is stupidly easy to accidentally break off a USB-C plug in its port, and I have never liked having a dongle dangling. The best compromise I've found so far is using this attachable USB-C dock with my MacBook. It's connected using both USB-C ports and a dummy headphone jack. So that makes it pretty secure and stable. It also has proper power passthrough and is a little less annoying to connect than a typical dongle-style dock. Of course, this also gives up some of the flexibility of these USB-C docks, since this only works on MacBooks that have a very specific port layout. Still, I feel it's the best of both worlds at this point, giving me some of the advantages of old docking stations, while benefiting from the full bandwidth of two ports, therefore compromising less. Universal docks are more convenient—but less dependable I can't argue that modern USB-C docks that will work with any laptop sporting the same connection standard are amazing and convenient devices, but it does put the onus of making sure everything works on you as the customer. It's obviously more convenient to have a single docked setup where anyone with a modern laptop can plug in and get it all up and running in seconds, but the reality is that when you plug a modern universal dock into your laptop, you don't actually know that everything will work correctly, run at the best speeds, or in some cases even work at all.

item.title: I ditched store-bought organizers for these 4 3D prints I use every single day
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.01
Like most people, I've printed mostly decorative items and novelties since starting this hobby. I like an articulated dragon or a cool figure as much as the next person, but I honestly haven't unlocked that much true utility from these machines. That, of course, is entirely my fault. We've all seen the amazing things people can do with 3D printers when they have the talent and time, which I both lack, but there are actually a few 3D prints that I genuinely use every day, because they're better than the store-bought alternatives. The Bookshark Bookmark by blecheimer It's nothing to be scared of This might be one of the simplest things I've ever printed, but the Bookshark bookmark is also one of the most ingenious because of it. I am a voracious reader, and I have been all my life. I also tend to read half a dozen books at once, and I have plenty of anthologies where I might go a few weeks or months between short stories. In other words, I need a lot of bookmarks to keep track of my reading. I first printed out some Booksharks because I thought they looked cool. There's a little stopper under the shark fin part, so when your book is closed, it looks like a shark swimming in the ocean. However, as I started using these, I quickly stopped using all my store-bought bookmarks. Booksharks are just so small, easy, and reliable to use that I never reach for anything else. They also use very little material, and on a modern printer you can knock one out in a minute or two, or even a whole plate full of them. I like using multicolor filament so that my Booksharks are all different colors, but I guess you could deliberately print them in sets of colors for a color-coded system. Strong Locking Cable Clip by neoyarus Those cables aren't going anywhere I've tried a lot of 3D-printed cable management solutions over the years. Some have worked better than others, but in the end, I've actually settled on this brilliant locking cable clip. The print-in-place hinge is already impressive enough, but neoyarus has really thought this one through. There are 16 sizes, supporting one to sixteen cables. There are four different mounting options, and the clip at the end really is easy to open and close. I have a little trolley with my handheld gaming consoles, VR headset, and other miscellaneous gadgets to charge, and using some double-sided tape to attach one of these clips to the back has been a godsend to stop my charging cables from flopping all over the place when I unplug my PlayStation Vita or Meta Quest 3. Under Desk Headphone Mount by Chickenface This one finally has me hooked I always seem to be drowning in headphones, so I've tried every reasonable store-bought headphone mount you can think of. I've tried the ones that have a suction cup for your desk, magnetic ones that stick to your desk's legs, and, of course, the type that slips over your desk's edge. I always accidentally knock that last type off the desk at some point, so I'm not a fan. Chickenface has taken a previous design and remixed it into a very elegant under-desk headphone hook. There's a variant with and without a screw hole. You can use adhesive to attach the former, but I personally don't trust that. All I needed was a short wood screw and a screwdriver that fit through the bottom guide hole, and I had the hook fitted in less than 30 seconds with a rock-solid attachment. If you have a desk with existing screws that are in the right place, you can even just remove the screw and replace it with the hook in between. The screw holes are countersunk, so you probably don't need a longer screw in most cases. Print in place BAG CLIPS by Shadow_Flash1234 It just tastes better when fresh I used to use clothing pegs to keep open bags closed, to prevent things from getting stale or bugs from getting in. Then I saw people 3D-printing bag clips, and that seemed like a potentially better solution. The thing is, most of the designs I tried either break too easily, or they do a much worse job of keeping the bag closed than a spring-loaded peg. Shadow_Flash1234's BAG CLIP design has none of those issues. It has a built-in clip and is under tension when it's closed. The little clips do eventually break after repeated openings, but they are fast and cheap to print, and good for long-term use for things you don't need often, like flour bags. It's the simple things that work best I've tried lots of supposedly helpful gadgets that have just too many moving parts, or ask for too much of typical filament.

item.title: MediaTek's first 2nm flagship chip is here — meet the new Dimensity 9600 Pro
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.43
What you need to know - MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 Pro is the company's first 2nm flagship chipset, promising better performance and efficiency. - The new 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU delivers up to 17% faster single-core performance while using significantly less power. - MediaTek's upgraded NPU supports on-device AI models with up to 30 billion parameters while improving AI power efficiency. MediaTek has officially taken the wraps off its latest flagship smartphone chipset, called the Dimensity 9600 Pro. And it's the company's first flagship chip built on a 2nm process. The new flagship smartphone season is almost upon us, and chipset makers have started unveiling their next generation of processors. Qualcomm is set to announce its next flagship Snapdragon chipsets later this month, but MediaTek has beaten it to the punch by unveiling its first 2nm chipset. Called the Dimensity 9600 Pro, MediaTek says its new chipset combines flagship performance and power efficiency with advanced agentic AI experiences. The chip features a 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU design, which MediaTek says delivers an impressive 61% reduction in multi-core power consumption. The architecture consists of two C2 Ultra cores clocked at up to 4.55GHz, three C2 Pro cores running at up to 4.35GHz, and another three C2 Pro cores clocked at up to 3.1GHz. MediaTek says single-core performance has improved by up to 17%, while multi-core performance is up to 15% higher than the previous generation, all while consuming less power. Of course, there's also a big focus on agentic AI experiences. MediaTek says the chipset's new dual-NPU architecture and Agentic AI Engine are designed to power the next generation of on-device AI. Its second-generation Super Efficient NPU reportedly reduces AI power consumption by up to 40%, while delivering 51% higher LLM prefill performance and 55% higher token generation per watt. The Dimensity 9600 Pro can also support AI models with up to 30 billion parameters directly on the device, which should allow more complex AI tasks to run without constantly relying on the cloud. There's also a larger 34.5MB cache, alongside support for LPDDR6 memory and UFS 5.0 storage for the first time. MediaTek says its new Scheduling Engine can intelligently allocate computing power and memory resources between hardware and software, allowing multiple apps to continue running smoothly in the background while using fewer resources. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Gaming is getting a significant upgrade as well. The new G2-Ultra NX GPU delivers up to 27% higher peak performance while consuming 24% less power. MediaTek says the GPU can deliver what it calls console-grade gaming on-device at up to 185fps. For cameras, there's a new Imagiq 1290 ISP, which MediaTek says will enable more advanced computational photography and content creation features on upcoming smartphones. There aren't any smartphones powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro just yet, but we shouldn't have to wait long before the first devices arrive. Apple's 2nm A20 Pro has already launched inside the iPhone 18 Pro series, while Qualcomm is expected to reveal its answer at Snapdragon Summit later this month. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket.
