item.title: Meta’s Phoenix mixed reality headset is finally starting to look real
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.12
What you need to know - Meta’s Project Phoenix is finally coming into focus after more than a year of rumors about a lightweight, high-end mixed-reality headset. - Phoenix looks more like smart glasses than a traditional VR headset, using nose pads and temple-mounted sensors. - An external compute puck appears to be part of the design. Whispers about Meta working on a lightweight, high-end mixed reality headset codenamed Project Phoenix have floated around the tech sphere for over a year. Now, we finally get our first real look at what Mark Zuckerberg's hardware team has been cooking up, and it seems Meta accidentally left the key under the mat. The images were revealed through Meta’s HorizonOS Prescription Lens package, which first appeared in August as a mostly blank system package, as noticed by UploadVR. An update in September showed detailed pictures of how prescription lens inserts attach to the Phoenix and how users scan a QR code to set them up. Interestingly, the hardware looks less like a traditional VR headset and more like chunky glasses. Phoenix uses nose pads instead of the bulky face interface of the Quest 3 and other XR headsets, with sensors along the temples. There’s also a cable coming from the left temple, seemingly confirming previous reports that Phoenix will use an external compute puck. It's a design that could change the way people think about wearing a mixed reality headset. If you’ve been using more traditional XR headsets, you’ll probably find it comforting to realize potential benefits here, like less weight on your face, but the compromise moves elsewhere: you’ll need to deal with a separate computing unit and a cable. For Meta, the greater challenge might be getting that extra hardware to feel invisible enough that Phoenix still feels like something you can casually wear, rather than another device you have to gear up for. There's another interesting clue here. The leaked setup stuff seems to be based on prescription inserts and controller-free interaction. Meta hasn’t officially announced Phoenix yet, but Meta Connect 2026 starts September 23 and has a session dedicated to controller-free interaction on its agenda. If Phoenix shows up there, we might finally learn whether Meta’s push toward lighter mixed reality headsets is a real shift in headset design, or just a clever way to move the weight somewhere else. item.title: Google just put the latest AI models through a brutal coding test — here's how they did
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.93
What you need to know - Google has launched Android Bench 2.0 to test AI models on complex Android development tasks that can take days. - The new benchmark includes tasks like upgrading dependencies, adding major features, and building Android apps from scratch. - GPT-6 Astra currently leads Google's new benchmark with a 28% pass rate, while Gemini 3.8 Flash scored just 8%. Google has announced Android Bench 2.0, an updated version of its benchmark for evaluating how well large language models (LLMs) and AI agents handle complex Android development tasks. Earlier this year, Google introduced the first version of Android Bench to measure how AI models perform on real-world Android development work. The company has now updated the benchmark with Android Bench 2.0, which is designed to evaluate models and agents against more complex tasks that better reflect actual software development. One of the biggest additions is what Google calls long-horizon tasks (LHTs). These are significantly more complex development jobs that could take a human engineer several days or even a week to complete. Google says the first version of Android Bench, along with many other early AI coding benchmarks, focused primarily on smaller, incremental changes. Android Bench 2.0 is designed to raise that bar with tasks such as upgrading dependencies, adding major new features, and even building Android apps from scratch. With Android Bench 2.0, Google has changed how models are graded. Rather than relying entirely on a binary pass-or-fail system, Android Bench 2.0 uses "continuous scoring." The company says this provides a more "meaningful indication" of how well a model performed, even when it wasn't able to fully complete a task. Google has already tested several of the latest AI models using the new benchmark, including Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, among others. According to the results, GPT-6 Astra currently sits at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate. Gemini 3.8 Flash, meanwhile, scored just 8%. Google says testing models against the LHT dataset should give it a better understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, while also providing developers with more practical guidance about which models are better suited for different Android development tasks. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The updated Android Bench 2.0 leaderboard is available now, and Google says it plans to continue expanding it with more models and results over time. item.title: iQOO 16 display leaks were true: Samsung's 2K 165Hz panel is official
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.87
What you need to know - The iQOO 16 is set to debut as the first smartphone with a 2K resolution OLED display running at a 165Hz refresh rate. - Co-developed with Samsung Display on a dedicated production line, the panel marks the Android debut of Samsung's latest M16 luminescent material and LEAD 2.0 architecture. - The screen reaches 2,800 nits global peak brightness (10,000 nits local peak), features 508 PPI, and delivers sub-pixel-level calibration for color accuracy. Rumor has it that the iQOO 16 will be released soon, and iQOO has now confirmed one of the upgrades that could make this gaming-focused flagship stand out from the crowd. The next phone from the company is said to be the first to sport a 2K OLED panel with a 165Hz refresh rate from Samsung, which iQOO is calling a smartphone first. The announcement also confirms earlier reports that the iQOO 16 would sport Samsung’s newer M16 OLED technology. The company says the phone will be the first Android smartphone to use the material, along with its new 2K LEAD 2.0 technology. For context, we saw the original LEAD OLED panel debut with the iQOO 15. LEAD 2.0 has been developed in partnership with Samsung, built on a dedicated production line just for iQOO’s flagship. The two companies also designed a custom high-refresh-rate display IC and a dedicated production line for the phone. The panel is rated at 2,800 nits for global brightness and 10,000 nits for local brightness. It also offers 508 ppi, wide P3 color coverage, DC dimming, and better brightness and color uniformity than the iQOO 15. iQOO also claims sub-pixel-level calibration leads to extremely tight color accuracy. There is also a less obvious upgrade here: Samsung recently said the new display uses roughly 31 percent less power at 150 nits than a similarly sized 1.5K panel. That’s particularly useful, as improving both resolution and refresh rate often comes with a battery cost. The target is clearly gaming. The display features 500Hz multi-touch sampling and 5,000Hz instantaneous sampling rate, while iQOO’s Q-Flex technology focuses on reducing input lag. There’s also 3,300Hz PWM dimming and many eye-comfort features. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The iQOO 16 is expected to launch in China sometime near the end of September. If the rest of the hardware is up to the mark as this display, the top gaming flagships out there will have a serious new competitor on their hands. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Meta's next smart glasses could solve a big privacy concern by ditching the camera
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.75
What you need to know - Meta is reportedly developing Luna smart glasses without a camera, with a launch possible as soon as next month. - Luna will reportedly feature six microphones, six speakers, and a dedicated button for quickly accessing Meta AI. - Meta is also developing Phoenix AR glasses with virtual workspaces and movie screens, reportedly coming in 2027. Meta is reportedly preparing to enter a slightly different category of the smart glasses market with a new pair that doesn't have any cameras. Smart glasses have faced plenty of scrutiny over the past few months, and privacy has always been one of the biggest concerns surrounding models with built-in cameras. Meta has taken several steps recently to prevent users from tampering with the capture LED and secretly recording people, but the privacy concerns and perception around camera-equipped smart glasses still remain. Now, it looks like Meta is preparing an alternative for people who want smart glasses without the camera. According to a report from The Information, Meta is developing a new pair of camera-free smart glasses and could begin shipping them as soon as next month. The new model will reportedly be called Luna and could be unveiled at the Connect developer conference next week. The glasses are expected to be available in two designs, called Clubmaster and Burbank. While Luna won't have a camera, it will still pack plenty of hardware for accessing Meta AI. The glasses will reportedly feature six microphones and six speakers aimed at the user's ears. This will allow users to talk directly with Meta's AI chatbot without pulling out their phone. The glasses are also expected to retain a dedicated button on the side for quick access to Meta AI. Removing the camera will reportedly allow Meta to slim down Luna considerably. The new model is expected to look and feel much closer to a conventional pair of glasses, which could make them more appealing to people who don't necessarily want the bulk or privacy concerns that come with camera-equipped smart glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Luna isn't the only new pair of glasses Meta is reportedly working on, though. The company is also developing its own augmented reality glasses, reportedly called Phoenix. Meta is reportedly preparing a major demo of Phoenix that could show us a different way of video calling. The glasses will reportedly be capable of displaying virtual workspaces and large virtual movie screens. Phoenix is still further away, though, with the AR glasses currently expected to arrive sometime in 2027. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. item.title: Steam Frame costs $1,059, but Android games could give it an edge
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.70
What you need to know - Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, while the 1TB model jumps to $1,299. - Android games are supported, giving the headset access to existing Android APKs without requiring completely separate ports. - Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 + 16GB RAM powers the headset, with SteamOS handling native games and compatibility layers. Valve has finally put a price tag on the Steam Frame, its new wireless VR headset that aims to blur the line between a standalone gaming device and a PC accessory. The catch? It won’t be as simple as clicking “buy” to get one. The Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, with the 1TB model costing $1,299. Each headset has tracked controllers, and Valve is bundling Half-Life: Alyx with the device, the company announced. It can play supported games locally or stream more demanding titles from a PC. It’ll also support Android games, with developers using the same Android APKs they already use to bring mobile titles to the Meta Quest. This could give the Frame access to a much larger game library without developers needing to build entirely separate versions for Valve’s headset. The Frame also supports wireless PC streaming with the 6GHz dongle that Valve bundles in. Under the hood, the Frame is packed with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and 16GB of RAM, with native software and compatibility layers handled by SteamOS. The storage options are also worth a closer look. You can upgrade from 256GB to 1TB for $240, but the Frame also has a microSD slot. So if your main game stream is from a PC, there may be little reason to pay extra for the bigger model. Valve had originally said it wanted the Steam Frame to cost less than the $999 Index, but the final starting price puts it $60 above that benchmark. Rising memory and component costs have complicated the pricing strategy of Valve’s hardware, as seen with the Steam Machine. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Availability will also be controlled by a reservation system, with sign-ups running until September 17 and purchase invitations starting September 18. The Steam Frame is clearly not aimed at the budget VR crowd at $1,059. Valve is betting its Steam library, Android support, wireless PC streaming, and standalone abilities will justify the premium. item.title: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Software matters
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.58
Heavyweight The iPhone Duo is heavier and thicker than Android foldables, but that isn’t going to make too much of a difference in day-to-day use. The plus point is that it has IP68 ingress protection, and a build quality that’s different to anything else we’ve seen on Android. Also, the software is the biggest differentiator, and the little I’ve seen of this makes me highly interested to use the iPhone Duo. Sublime Make no mistake: the Xiaomi 18 Fold has the best design of any wide foldable, and Xiaomi deserves credit for slotting in a dedicated tele lens into the device. It is a full 35g lighter than the iPhone Duo, but you still somehow get a huge 6,000mAh battery. The custom Xring 03 silicon is intriguing, and the only issue with the 18 Fold is that it is limited to China, so you don’t get the best software — there’s no Play Store or other Google services. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Design and display I like the design of wide foldables as they’re much easier to hold and use than traditional book-style devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The iPhone Duo looks interesting thanks to the 5.4-inch outer panel, and it unfolds to a 7.6-inch inner panel. The Xiaomi 18 Fold has similarly-sized displays as well, but when it comes to resolution, the iPhone Duo comes out ahead. That said, the biggest issue with the iPhone Duo is the weight; at 254g, it is the heaviest of any 2026 foldable, and the Xiaomi 18 Fold is 35g lighter. Now, to give you some context, it is 5g heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but the point stands that it is a hefty device. Obviously, we’ll need to see how that makes a difference in daily use; weight distribution matters a lot on a foldable, and I’ll share findings once I used the Duo. What I like is that the Duo gets IP68 dust and water resistance. It is the only foldable other Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold and 10 Pro Fold to have this feature, and it will make a genuine difference in regular use. The 18 Fold has IP58 and IP59 ingress protection, and it should do a good enough job in outdoor use. Also, the design itself is exquisite on the Duo, and the blue color looks stunning. Something you don’t see (but will make a difference) is the inner panel. The iPhone Duo uses layers of ultra-thin glass sandwiched over the panels, and it should give it much better resilience against deformation — which is an issue with most foldables. Xiaomi, to its credit, delivered what is arguably the best-looking wide foldable in the 18 Fold, and the svelte design along with the bright red hue is brilliant. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Hardware What’s notable about the internals is that both foldables use custom silicon. The iPhone Duo uses the latest A20 Pro, and the 2nm platform has much better power than last year, and it should deliver meaningful upgrades on the battery side of things. Xiaomi is using the Xring 03 silicon with the 18 Fold, and I’m excited to get my hands so I can test it — it’s not often we get a new player that can beat Qualcomm at its own game. Xiaomi also has a distinct advantage with the battery, and the 18 Fold has a 6,000mAh battery that easily lasts over a day. the iPhone Duo should last a day as well, but this is something I’ll need to test. The 18 Fold has 67W USB PD charging tech, but what I like is that the iPhone Duo has 25W MagSafe, making it that much more convenient to use. Annoyingly, Xiaomi doesn’t have built-in magnets, so you can’t just use a Qi 2.2 charger with the device. | Category | Apple iPhone Duo | Xiaomi 18 Fold | | Display | Outer: 5.4-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED, 2034x1398 Inner: 7.6-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED, 2670x1878 | Outer: 5.38-inch LTPO AMOLED, 1712x1168 Inner: 7.58-inch LTPO AMOLED, 2364x1672 | | Operating System | iOS 27, at least seven updates | Android 17 | | Chipset | Apple A20 Pro, 2nm | Xiaomi XRing O3, 3nm | | RAM | 12GB | 12GB/16GB | | Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB | | Rear cameras | Main: 48MP f/1.6, sensor-shift OIS Wide-angle: 48MP f/2.2 | Main: 200MP f/1.7, OIS Tele: 50MP f/2.8, 3x tele Wide-angle: 50MP f/2.4 | | Front camera | 12MP | 16MP | | Ingress Protection | IP68 | IP58/IP59 | | Battery | 4,700mAh | 6,000mAh | | Charging | 40W, 25W MagSafe/Qi 2 | 67W PD 3.0, 50W HyperCharge | | Dimensions | Folded: 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm Unfolded: 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm | Folded: 83.6 x 117.8 x 10.7mm Unfolded:163.8 x 117.8 x 5.0mm | | Weight | 254g | 219g | | Colors | Night Sky, Star White | Red, Rose gold, Silver, Grey | The iPhone Duo has two 48MP cameras — a main camera and wide-angle lens — but you don’t get a telephoto lens. This is annoying, as the tele lens is the one I use the most. That’s why it’s refreshing to see Xiaomi providing the lens on the 18 Fold; its foldable has a 200MP main camera, 50MP tele lens with 3x optical zoom, and a 50MP wide-angle lens. Just having a tele lens gives the device a huge advantage, and Xiaomi is the only brand doing so on a wide foldable. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Software Where the iPhone Duo has a sizable lead is the software; it’s clear that iOS 27 has plenty of custom features to maximize the real estate on the foldable. What’s great to see is that the toggles and the taskbar are oriented on the right, and while it’s a small thing, it makes a difference in usability. The main problem with the Xiaomi 18 Fold is that it is limited to China, so you have to use the Chinese iteration of the brand’s skin. There are issues with push notifications, aggressive memory management, and there’s no Play Store or Google services out of the box. If you're an enthusiast and have used Chinese software previously, you can wrangle the 18 Fold to work the way you want (I plan on doing that), but it is a hassle. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Which should you buy? I’ll make this easy: if you like the look of a wide foldable, you should get the iPhone Duo. Although the Xiaomi 18 Fold has arguably better internals, the software is not ideal, and I wouldn’t recommend getting it as a result. Xiaomi needs to do a better job bringing its foldables to global regions, because the 18 Fold deserves a wide rollout. Of course, the iPhone Duo is costlier than any other iPhone, but not by too much than the latest Pro models. There's no doubt that the 18 Fold gives you a better overall value (as these things go), but with Xiaomi choosing not to launch the foldable globally, this is a moot point. Heavyweight The iPhone Duo is the default choice if you need a wide foldable. The Xiaomi 18 Fold has better internals, but the Duo arguably has the better software, and it is launching in over 75 countries. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd. item.title: Google continues to fix Android 17 issues with a QPR2 Beta 5 release for Pixels
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.42
What you need to know - Google is rolling out Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 to Pixel testers, solving several issues, such as an unexpected reboot problem. - The company is also fixing another Bluetooth problem; however, this one involves a bug when changing device type. - Beta 4 at the end of August marked QPR2 entering Platform Stability, meaning we're headed down the final stretch toward launch. Get your Pixels ready. Google is rolling out another beta for its next quarterly Android 17 update. The company detailed everything enrolled testers will find on Reddit. If you're looking for the update, you might find one of two build numbers. Google states users with a Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, 7 Pro, 7a, Pixel Fold, or Pixel Tablet will download vCP41.260828.005.A6. If you have any other eligible Pixel device, you will find vCP41.260828.004.A8. The company is fixing a few problems users have reported throughout QPR2's testing. One fix is coming in for a system instability issue. The patch notes state this fix should solve the "unexpected device reboots during continuous UI scrolling in media-heavy applications." Another fix aims to solve an issue with the Pixel's side buttons for volume control. Users noticed that while casting media, pressing these buttons wouldn't surface the volume slider UI. Google states a fix for this issue is rolling out. Additionally, enhanced HDR was stuck for several users on the Issue Tracker. Google says its fix should solve the issue of the feature "remaining enabled despite being turned off in user settings." The remainder of the patch notes is as follows: - Changing a Bluetooth device type in settings failed to update its icon visually - Fixed a text-rendering issue that caused unexpected background highlights to appear when typing in search fields, and resolved a navigation routing issue that prevented Private Space from unlocking correctly - Launching Google Wallet via the power button shortcut caused the touchscreen to become unresponsive - Camera crashes during panorama processing - Bluetooth audio experiences noise and distortion after completing or answering a call The Final Stretch Beta 5 is fixing up some lingering issues, but it was QPR2 Beta 4 that we were really excited about. The end of August saw Android 17 QPR2 enter the Platform Stability phase. This is a standard milestone for Google's software development. It locks in the OS' APIs, ushering it down the final stretch. We're starting to wrap things up, but there's still work to do—for everyone. Similarly, Google was fixing quite a few bugs last month. Pixel Bluetooth is apparently still giving it some trouble. In August, Google fixed a Bluetooth call audio issue that saw user calls getting erroneously put through the phone's speaker. Other issues included a broken gesture problem and strange UI freezing. item.title: Triple launch: Boox debuts Note Air6 C and Palma 3 just in time for fall binge-reading
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.22
What you need to know - Boox launched three new ePaper tablets today (Sept 16), starting with the 10.3-inch HD color ePaper Note Air6 C. - The company is also expanding its Note series with the 8.5-inch Note Mini C and its next Palma, the Palma 3 with a redesigned premium frame. - The Note Air6 C is available now for $579, while the Mini C and Palma 3 are "coming soon," those will start at $579 and $339, respectively. Onyx Boox launched a trio of ePaper tablets today (Sept. 16), just in time for the chillier months. Each tablet features a built-in front light, capable of reading in any situation. This morning, Boox detailed its press release for the Note Air6 C, Palma 3, and the Note Mini C. Reading and writing are the hallmarks of these tablets, and we're beginning with the Boox Note Air6 C. "Available now," the Note Air6 C continues what Boox states is its "most popular series." Consumers will find a 10.3-inch HD color ePaper display with a 4nm octa-core processor and "Dual Tone" to adjust the screen's warm and cooler tones for a softer eye experience. The tactile writing experience is something Boox reiterates as a positive note from many Air C-series consumers. The Air6 C delivers that with a native Notes app with Outline, Tag, and Search tools. This Notes app features a "Dual Note" feature, letting consumers open two separate notes "horizontally or vertically." What's more, Boox states the tablet fully supports Android 16 and the Google Play Store. Reading is another major highlight for Boox tablets. The post states it delivers a "40% reduction in page turn speed compared to its predecessor," thanks to its BSR technology. Additionally, the tablet offers 6GB of RAM, 64GB of storage, and includes the Boox Pen3 stylus. The Boox Note Air6 C is available today for $579. The tablet will become available on Amazon soon. On the other hand, we have two more ePaper tablets that are "launching soon." The first is another addition to the Boox Note series: the Note Mini C. This smaller, 8.5-inch color ePaper display reportedly balances "portability and readability." Boox spoke highly of its one-handed use in its overview of the tablet. With the smaller size, Boox says it has kept its PDF legibility intact for users. The included InkSight Magnetic Active Stylus has been redesigned with a side button and a stronger magnetic connection. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Boox made sure to provide the Note Mini C with the same front-light treatment. It states the tablet features "Dual-Tone" adjustable warm and cool tones. This should provide an easy-on-the-eye experience, especially when using the device for prolonged periods. BSR technology assists the Mini C's lag-free scrolling for documents and websites. Android 16 and access to the Play Store are included as well. Once the Mini C arrives, consumers can utilize its 6/64GB configuration and 3,150mAh battery. Boox states the Note Mini C will "launch soon" for $579 in the U.S., with Amazon availability to follow. The Palma series gets another If we're talking portability and the one-handed experience, it's hard not to mention Boox's Palma series. Luckily for consumers, the Palma 3 was announced this morning. The Palma 3 features a 6.1-inch ePaper display. Boox adds that it's improved the screen with "deeper blacks and higher contrast." However, the Palma 3's redesigned frame is also earning attention. According to the post, Boox integrated "fine stationary" tactility. It replaced the plastic body with anodized aluminum to emulate a more premium feel. The fiber-glass back panel reinforces that ambition of a premium ePaper tablet. The Palma 3 also features the "Dual Tone" front light tech for warm and cooler tones, alongside an Ambient Light Sensor. Boox says this sensor will adjust the device's brightness depending on your surroundings. Similar to the other two devices launched today, the Palma 3 features Android 16 and Google Play Store support. Other specs include 6GB of RAM and 128GB of storage. The 3,950mAh battery is said to provide "days of deep reading" on a single charge. The Boox Palma 3 will launch soon for $339. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: A mysterious Google Wear OS fitness tracker just appeared at the FCC
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.21
What you need to know - A mysterious Google-made wearable has appeared at the FCC with clues suggesting it could run Wear OS. - The device reportedly skips Wi-Fi and relies on Bluetooth LE, suggesting it may be a fitness tracker. - GPS support and a metal frame are also listed, while ADB testing suggests some form of Wear OS software. - The device could sit between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch, potentially filling the gap left by Fitbit Charge. A mysterious new Wear OS fitness tracker has been spotted at the FCC, and there are a few clues suggesting it could be an upcoming Google Pixel or Fitbit-branded device. Google has been enjoying success with both the Pixel Watch lineup and the recently launched Fitbit Air, and it looks like the company could be preparing to expand its fitness tracking lineup even further. As spotted by 9to5Google, a mysterious new Google-made device has now appeared in an FCC listing. The device, described as a "Wireless Device," carries the model number G8BL6 and is manufactured by Goertek, a company that has previously manufactured several generations of Pixel Buds. Interestingly, the FCC listing suggests there's no Wi-Fi connectivity onboard. Instead, the device appears to rely entirely on Bluetooth LE. There are also clues suggesting the device could run some form of Wear OS, as the EUT operation test setup specifically mentions ADB testing. In terms of other connectivity, the mysterious device reportedly supports GPS or GNSS and features a metal frame that will also act as its antenna. The lack of Wi-Fi is particularly interesting, since most traditional Wear OS smartwatches have supported Wi-Fi. That could suggest we're looking at a different type of wearable altogether, potentially a more traditional fitness tracker rather than another Pixel Watch. And there might already be another clue. During the Pixel 11 launch, Google briefly showed an unannounced fitness tracker with a small display in one of its teasers, and there's a chance this FCC listing could be related to that device. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If so, the new wearable could potentially sit somewhere between the Fitbit Air and Google's more expensive Pixel Watch lineup. It's also worth remembering that Fitbit hasn't updated its Charge lineup since 2023, so this device could fit quite nicely into that missing middle ground. item.title: Ultrahuman, HealthEx team up: your medical records step forward for 'always-on' insights
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.72
What you need to know - Ultrahuman and HealthEx partner to bring the HealthEx PowerPlug for $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr in the app. - HealthEx brings your official medical records into the app, and Ultrahuman's biomarkers/Ring data is placed alongside it for better insights into your wellbeing. - Ultrahuman states this PowerPlug will also generate a "Visit Pack" full of data that's listed with your records to make your next visit more insightful. Medical records are often a tricky obstacle to navigate. This week, Ultrahuman announced a partnership that streamlines appointments, tests, and even surgeries. This morning (Sept. 17), Ultrahuman announced a partnership with HealthEx in a press release, bringing the HealthEx PowerPlug to its app. The company states the PowerPlug will "combine a member’s medical records with continuous biomarkers" from its smart ring "in a secure, transparent, and consented manner." This will roll out over the week; however, Ultrahuman shared details on how this new PowerPlug will work. Ultrahuman members will need to verify their identity to activate HealthEx's capabilities. This will automatically locate your health records from places you've received care before. Ultrahuman states HealthEx has nationwide reach, thanks to the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA). Additionally, users can choose which care sites the HealthEx PowerPlug accesses. This is done via your consent, and you can stop sharing any records at any time. Priyanka Agarwal, M.D., MBA, co-founder and CEO of HealthEx, said, "When members choose to connect the two through HealthEx, they arrive at their next appointment with the most complete health picture, helping them arrive better prepared for that conversation." Getting down to brass tacks, the HealthEx PowerPlug aims to place your entire medical history in one convenient place for you and your doctor. Ultrahuman states this new feature "maps 532 conditions" based on your medications and procedures. Incorporating your biomarkers only enhances its usefulness. Your previous diagnosis and new medications will be displayed alongside the daily measurements your Ultrahuman Ring captures of your heart. Your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, and deep sleep are all factored in. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If a follow-up has been missed, or a condition/medication record hasn't been checked, the HealthEx PowerPlug will surface it for your attention. Users can bring this up as a question during their next doctor's visit. Additionally, Ultrahuman highlights its "Visit Pack." This is a collection of your medication information—a "doctor-ready summary"—tied to your wearable data. The company states, "The PowerPlug also flags questions and tests to raise with their doctor based on their reports." Take care I've had to deal with medical records, or medical information in general several times. This hasn't been for me, but for family. And it can be a headache at times. The long waits, the misinformation because someone got their wires crossed. I can appreciate what Ultrahuman is trying to do by bringing in HealthEx. Its smart ring already captures a wealth of data about your body. It kind of sounds like a no-brainer to put that side-by-side with your records Research states the average doctor's visit lasts ~15 minutes. What's more, the information about your health is typically scattered. This PowerPlug with HealthEx aims to make that process a little less strenuous. The HealthEx PowerPlug has started rolling out today (Sept. 17) for users in the U.S. Users can access this PowerPlug from the Ultrahuman PowerPlugs tab in the Ultrahuman app. However, it costs $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr. If you're interested in viewing your "longitudinal health history," Ultrahuman states this is free through HealthEx Wallet. Ultrahuman and HealthEx plan to do more following the PowerPlug's debut. Vitamin D, GLP-1, and Respiratory Health should arrive sometime in the future. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: Galaxy SmartTag 3 leaks: Samsung's redesign might not be better than the last
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.39
What you need to know - Galaxy SmartTag 3 rumors continue, suggesting Samsung could redesign the little tracker into a squircle shape, like the Galaxy Watch 8 and 9. - The tracker is reportedly arriving in white and black; however, Samsung has removed the built-in loop, meaning consumers may have to shell out more cash for a case with a loop. - Recent rumors suggested the SmartTag 3 could debut with the Galaxy S26 FE, but that never happened as the phone showed up solo late last month. Samsung's next smart tracker has been long overdue—three years, to be exact. Rumors continue in September, suggesting a reworked design is in the cards. Alleged renderings obtained by SammyGuru claim Samsung has redesigned the Galaxy SmartTag 3 with a familiar shape (via 9to5Google). The publication mentions this, too: the SmartTag 3 might take on a squircle shape, similar to the Galaxy Watch 8 and 9 series. A thicker, colored outer portion encases a silver (metallic) center. Rumors add that the SmartTag 3 could arrive in white and black. The latter trades in a silvery metallic center for a black, almost brushed metal aesthetic. The post highlights a few expectations, such as (improved) Bluetooth and UWB (ultra-wideband), like its previous model. What's more, the "NFC-based Lost Mode" is also suspected to continue in this next generation. The tracker's battery specifications are still unknown, but here's hoping that the SmartTag 3's longevity hasn't taken a hit. There's no dodging the elephant in the room. While the SmartTag 3 appears to take on a squircle shape, the alleged renderings highlight that it's missing a built-in mounting solution. According to the publication, consumers might have to shell out extra cash for a "separate case with an attachment loop." As far as pricing is concerned, the publication cites alleged "retailer listings." The SmartTag 3 could stay ~$30 in the U.S.; however, consumers in Europe might see a slight price increase of a few bucks (or... euros). This change is certainly a choice We've been playing around and tracking with the Galaxy SmartTag 2 since 2023. What's interesting is that the tracker also reworked its design from the original tag. It brought in a wider attachment loop. Consumers could get a case for it that would provide another loop (more of a keyring-style). But rumors from July finally got us thinking about a SmartTag 3 after three years. A tipster on social media claimed the next tag could debut sometime in September, alongside the Galaxy S26 FE. That didn't end up happening. The S26 FE debuted late in August. So there's a chance we're looking at a solo launch for the SmartTag 3, or perhaps something closer to the Galaxy Tab S12 debut this year. item.title: Nothing's Headphone 1 is going Pro? Rumors allege upgrades and a 'premium' feel are possible
item.description:

What you need to know - Rumors now say Nothing is getting closer to a new audio product launch dubbed the "Headphone 1 Pro" late in September. - The device could enter a more premium aesthetic for consumers with a $399 price tag, 60 hours battery life, improved ANC, and a triple audio driver setup. - The original Headphone 1 were pretty good, and could've arguably been one of the best (if not the best) audio product of 2025. Nothing's first over-ear headphones made a splash when they debuted. Now, rumors suggest the company wants to make even more noise with a "Pro" model. Late this week, a post by Dealabs suggests Nothing is developing a "Headphone 1 Pro" model, and a launch could be closer than we think (via 9to5Google). As with any device, especially one marked by "Pro," design changes/improvements are possible. The publication claims the Pro headphones could feature "aluminum and glass" on their body. The idea could be to not only separate the Pro from the base model, but also to solidify a "premium" aesthetic, as the post notes. White and black colorways are supposedly likely once this (allegedly) hits the market around September 29, 2026. However, rumors claim Nothing plans to make the Pro tag matter with a triple audio driver. Improved bass, sharper audio precision, and improved treble were mentioned. Whispers allege real-time "adaptive" ANC that could outshine the original's. Battery life is another highlight. The Pro model could offer 60 hours of playback time. What's not clear is whether this is with ANC active or not. The original model could run for 35 hours with ANC on and 80 hours with it off. If this higher number concerns the former, that could be a huge boon to consumers. There's nothing official, but rumors claim the Headphone 1 Pro could run consumers $399 in the U.S. The original model was good The idea of a Pro headphone from Nothing sounds intriguing. I'm not really a fan of wearing over-ear headphones out or away from my computer. I'm a gamer, so that's usually when I'll ever wear something like this. But there's a huge market for over-ear headphones. Music is probably the best thing for them. You can connect them to your phone, get a workout in, or hop on the bus or train and immerse yourself in sound. That's what I'd like from Nothing. If it's going Pro, go immersive, too. If you take a quick step back to when the Headphone 1 launched, Nothing stuck them with a $299 price tag in the U.S. The Pro model would ask for ~$100 more, if we're to believe these early rumors. Anyway, Nothing wanted to make a bold statement with these headphones. The device brought back real, physical buttons, rollers, and paddles that make the experience more manageable. There were pieces of aluminum that accented the Headphone 1. The Pro version could take that up a bit, and with more glass, too. In our experience, the Headphone 1 was a good piece of hardware. In fact, it was arguably one of the best audio products of 2025. Considering the positioning of the controls, the Headphone 1 made it easy to control our music. What's more, since these buttons are physical, we avoided those accidental song skips or pauses. item.title: Snap SPECS can work and play—AI intelligence platform 'anticipates' your needs
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.99
What you need to know - Snap revealed its upcoming SPECS smart glasses in full this midweek, stating they are available for pre-order for $2,196 in the U.S. ahead of a late fall launch. - SPECS browser lets users stream content from HBO Max and YouTube, as well as music from Spotify and educational content. - The glasses offer in-display real-time translation with subtitles and directions while walking in big cities, with Tripadvisor for finding food and landmarks. - The Snap SPECS are preparing to launch in the U.S., U.K., and France. Snap's new smart glasses, SPECS, are finally here. For the time being, pre-orders are open, but Snap is getting candid about everything in its human-centric computing glasses. Snap announced an "all-new experience" coming to the growing world of smart glasses with SPECS. These glasses are reportedly "built around how you interact with the world, and the AI-native operating system is designed to help you get things done through natural interactions using your hands and voice." To get us going, Snap says SPECS are designed for work and play—and we're starting with play. The SPECS browser lets users stream content from YouTube, HBO Max, and more on a virtual 115-inch display, placed roughly 10 ft away. Thanks to an HBO Max partnership, Snap says it's bringing the world of Harry Potter to SPECS in time for the HBO Original Series Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, premiering on Christmas. Elsewhere, work with the NBA and WNBA will bring "interactive basketball experiences" to SPECS users. Watching sports or shows and movies isn't all the SPECS is good for. Snap says you can also listen to your favorite tunes with Spotify. Additionally, learning is made easier with an "interactive recreation" of the Apollo 11 moon mission. For your day-to-day, Snap says SPECS offers several AR experiences. With "Translation," you'll find real-time, in-display subtitles (supports 60 languages). "Navigation" provides similar assistance, and Tripadvisor helps users find places to eat, landmarks, and more. The Shopify Catalog is another feature that brings 3D products right into your vision, placeable in the space around you. "Connected Lens" is a feature that lets two SPECS users "share digital experiences in the same physical space." What's more, since Snap is the parent company of Snapchat, you'll find an experience that fits the smart glasses space. Privacy is another aspect that Snap states it takes seriously. It says its glasses do not record the world around you, nor do they constantly capture and save audio. There's even more to unpack about the Snap SPECS. For now, you can pre-order the glasses for $2,195 with a $200 refundable deposit at SPECS.com. Shipping is expected to begin later this fall in the U.S., the U.K., and France. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android However, if you're feeling hesitant, you can look forward to a trip to Los Angeles on October 1 and visit SPECS First Look at Westfield Century City. Hands-on demos and a meet-and-greet with the SPECS team will await you there. Snap adds that the SPECS glasses have been equipped with a new Charging Case with Cellular. Sold separately, this provides "four additional charges and offers cellular connectivity through participating wireless carriers." To get this done in the U.S., Snap partnered with Verizon for a Connected Case bundle at $2,395. It adds, "Verizon will offer eligible customers financing options, including a 36 month payment plan. Connected Wearable data plans are available from $10/month for Verizon customers and from $20/month for non-Verizon customers." AI that anticipates AI is a feature that ties the Snap SPECS together. According to the post, SPECS Intelligence is an "anticipatory" AI platform that "builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose." The point of SPECS Intelligence is not only to help you reach your goals, but to know and be proactive about your assistance. Snap states that this AI platform was built to "anticipate when help would be useful and surface relevant information and actions at the right moment." This would replace the need for users to constantly have to prompt the AI to do something or fetch something. This platform is useful with your connected data and the physical world. Snap states SPECS Intelligence can bring "relevant information" directly into view while outside. SPECS Intelligence will work with iPhone, Mac, and, of course, the glasses. Beginning today (Sept. 16), users can download the iOS SPECS app and try SPECS Intelligence. There is also a waitlist that you can join for the AI platform within the app "for invitation-only early access to the fuller SPECS Intelligence experience on Mac." item.title: BMX's GaNsta 140W may just be the 4-port GaN travel charger you need
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.63
It was when I started running out of storage boxes that I realized I may have too many GaN chargers. I joke that if you casually throw a GaN charger in my home, you're bound to hit another one. Anyway, I have dozens of these things lying around, and having tested just about every major charger released in the last three years, I know what a good charger needs to offer. So when I got started with the BMX GaNsta 140W (as puns go, the name gets an 8/10), it was clear that the charger ticked a lot of the right boxes. It has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, foldable blade pins with EU, UK, and AU converters that make it easy to travel with, and 140W power over USB PD 3.1. Oh, and it gets an LCD panel that shows real-time charging details out of each port, which is a must-have in a GaN charger in 2026. The GaNsta costs $89 as of writing, which is $10 pricier than Anker's charger, and $30 more than the last-gen 160W UGREEN Nexode Pro, both of which also have LCD screens. The GaNsta is a little smaller than other 4-port chargers, but not enough that you'd notice the difference. Build quality is decent, and I didn't see any issues in the two months I used it. I tested the charger with my Find X9 Ultra, Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 17 Pro, iPad Pro M4, and a dozen or so accessories — including 160W power banks — and it turned out to be reliable in day-to-day use. I like that each port's power output is clearly labeled, and it takes a lot of the guesswork out of figuring out which port to use. The USB-C1 and C2 ports individually go up to 140W over the USB PD 3.1 protocol, and I tested this using a standalone power meter (Power-Z KM003C). I also like that the area around the ports has a slotted design to prevent scratches; this is a thoughtful design choice that makes a difference. The LCD screen is the real star of the show. It shows real-time charging details, power going out of each port, and heat levels. The latter isn't quite as useful as you don't normally see thermal issues on a 140W charger, but it's there. And as AI needs to be shoehorned into every product these days, this thermal management feature is assisted by AI (however that works). Anyway, what you need to know is that even with all ports in use, the GaNsta doesn't have any issues with overheating. You also get emoticons on the panel, and you can easily cycle through the various menus via the button at the bottom. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android With four ports available, you get the ability to charge four devices at once. Of course, the total power budget is limited when all ports are in use, and with the GaNsta, you get 125W cumulatively: 65W + 45W + 7.5W + 7.5W. I would've liked to see 65W on both the C1 and C2 ports — like the latest Nexode Pro 160W charger — but that isn't the case. That said, if you're just going to leave four devices to charge overnight, the GaNsta 140W does a decent enough job. The inclusion of a USB-C to USB-C cable along with travel plugs is a good move, and the size of the charger means you can easily throw it into a travel bag. What I'm not too sure about is the pricing; it is costlier than its rivals, and if you're willing to shell out $89, the new Nexode Pro 160W is a better deal at $99 as it has a retractable cable. If you don't need the built-in cable and like the travel-related accessories, the GaNsta 140W is a good choice. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd. item.title: I've used Meta Ray-Ban Display for a year, and I like them, but it still feels like something is missing
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.31
Android Central Verdict Meta Ray-Ban Display represents a massive milestone in the smart glasses industry. These glasses look like a normal pair of thick-framed glasses, have all the best features of non-display Meta AI glasses from Ray-Ban and Oakley, and even sport a single display in the right lens. The Neural gesture band that ships with the glasses provides a revolutionary new input method that feels strangely natural, but the monocular display can be jarring for certain content, like videos. Gestures all work incredibly well, but there's simply not enough to do on these glasses, even after nearly a year of development. Pros - +Incredible innovation - +Look like a normal pair of thick-framed glasses - +Amazing gesture controls - +Neural Band haptic feedback feels great - +Meta has a brilliant history of long-term product support Cons - -Thick and heavy - -Battery life is limiting - -Not enough to do - -Monocular display can be jarring Why you can trust Android Central Two years ago, I had the privilege of going hands-on with Meta Orion glasses. It was the first time I'd used a pair of AR glasses that didn't feel like a massively compromised experience, and while they weren't quite ready for prime time, I knew a proper consumer version wasn't far off. Sure enough, Meta debuted Ray-Ban Display glasses at last year's Meta Connect show in September. They're not quite the full vision Orion showed me was possible, but they made the right concessions to deliver good-looking frames at a good price. Now, a year later, I'm asking the question: have they been worth it, and should you buy them, or should you wait for the next big release? What can Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses do? Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses retail for $799 and are available at stores like Best Buy, where you can stop in and try a pair on. These support a narrow prescription range, so be sure to get your prescription filled when you order, since the lenses can't be easily swapped out after ordering. Ray-Ban Display glasses feature a display in the right lens only to reduce weight and battery use. This is a full-color display and doesn't have the warping or light bleed found in similar glasses like Even Realities G2 or MemoMind One. The sophisticated lenses and displays are a hallmark of Meta's glasses and a major difference from the competition. I spoke with Lumus, the manufacturer of the waveguide displays Meta uses, to better understand how the tech works. In a nutshell, these full-color optics are built for privacy and clarity. People cannot see your display, even if they put their face right up to the outside of your glasses. Meta's software is also substantially more robust and mature than any other smart glasses platform I've used to date. It integrates directly with popular fitness services like Garmin and Strava, and supports all of Meta's apps and services, like WhatsApp and Instagram. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Viewing Instagram feeds on the display is novel, though it's a bit visually tiring since the display is in only one lens. You'll never have an issue seeing things since the display gets so bright (yes, even in direct sunlight), but the monocular vision can be very jarring for some tasks. Reading messages, navigating, checking notifications, and controlling music are all perfect examples of how this hardware shines. Even taking pictures with the built-in viewfinder feels like a major step-up from Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 glasses, which have no display and can only give you audio feedback. Like those glasses, Ray-Ban Display also has built-in microphones and speakers and can do everything those can do (plus more). The camera quality is excellent, and you can even zoom in using the camera viewfinder, which isn't something supported on non-display Meta AI glasses. Updates and apps make all the difference When Meta launched Ray-Ban Display last year, it very much felt like a beta product. The glasses had tons of promise, but the vision clearly wasn't complete. It didn't even ship with the handwriting recognition feature that Mark Zuckerberg proudly showed off on stage at last year's Connect. One year later, Display not only has that and every other promised feature, but it also sports some fresh features Meta didn't initially show off. My favorite feature addition so far is app support, but this comes with a big caveat. Apps all require smartphone connectivity to work, and you'll need to add them through a beta UI panel on the Meta AI app on your phone. The easiest way to find them is the Meta Glasses Apps website, which gives you a QR code you can scan with your phone to get it quickly added to your glasses app list. The problem with the current crop of apps is that only 26 are available. Clearly, Meta is having just as hard a time convincing developers to make content for these glasses as it did convincing the same developers to make 2D apps for its Quest headsets. And that's really the core problem with Meta Ray-Ban Display Glasses. While Meta has proven itself time and time again to deliver incredible support and regular updates to its excellent hardware products, the company continues to have a difficult time courting developers for its ecosystems. The band is still the best (and worst) part Meta's Neural Band, which is required to interact with most of Ray-Ban Display's UI, is truly brilliant. The band is vitally important to the experience because you can interact with the glasses without pointing or holding your hand in the air. Keep your hands in your pockets, if you like, or just leave them in your lap. It's effortless and brilliant. The degree of control it delivers over the floating glasses UI is astounding, and the haptic feedback you receive with each interaction is paramount to making the glasses feel like a more authentic experience. It's essentially the touchscreen of the smart glasses world. The band is ultra-responsive and never misses a beat. You interact with the glasses' UI through gestures the band picks up, understanding the nuances of muscle movement and electrical signals. The first time you respond to a message by writing with your fingers or adjust music volume by turning an invisible nob is going to blow your mind. I'm someone who dislikes wearing watches all day because they irritate my wrist, especially when I'm writing, but Meta's comfortable cloth construction feels different. However, the worst part about needing the Neural Band is that you have to remember to charge it. Battery life is slightly longer than the glasses, but you'll still need to charge it once per day. Like most smartwatches, this one uses a bespoke charger that doesn't work with anything else. That also means that if you lose the charger (like I did), you won't be able to use your glasses until you find the charger or buy a new one. Should you buy it? The short answer is no; most people should not buy these glasses. While they represent a big step up in capability compared to standard Meta AI glasses, there simply aren't enough reasons for the average person to spend twice the amount of money (or more) on them versus a pair without a display. I love what Meta built here and think it's a great template for upcoming smart glasses that will inevitably be lighter, have thinner frames, better battery life, and more functionality. For now, though, these are an amazing tech toy that's perfect for Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Whether it's VR, smart home gadgets, or something else that beeps and boops, he's been writing about it since 2011. item.title: 'There's one never-ending challenge working for IKEA: cable management' — how Xbox collaborated with the Swedish designers to help solve the biggest problems for gamers while also making beautiful furniture
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.66
When I first saw the IKEA x Xbox collaboration at this year's Gamescom, I was struck by two conflicting ideas. With its multi-functional side table, TV stand, and decorative controller box, this is some smartly made furniture with some genuinely helpful uses. Then, with a thumbstick stool and a D-pad cushion, it's also one of the silliest things I've seen. Taken as a whole, you can see it's a mix of the playful and the practical. After I spoke to designers at both IKEA and Xbox at the show, it turns out that was the point all along. "That was present throughout the journey because it's important," explained Philip Dilé, product developer for IKEA of Sweden. "Playing games is playful; it is fun. Solving people's needs connected to that can be very functional and practical. We tried to balance that, for sure. "We wanted to make things that are relevant for people who play games. Something that reflects you, or that you feel allows you to express yourself...but the object itself is a beautiful piece of home furnishing." It's a philosophy echoed by Carl Ledbetter, partner head of design at Xbox: "Just like when we design a console, it can be as quiet as people want it. They can put it back and let it recede into their environment. Or they can pull it forward and have it be very expressive. And I think some of those same qualities are in these products in the YXSTABY collection." Ledbetter used the controller display box and the TV stand as examples of this. With the former, it's ideal for enthusiast gamers who like to collect controllers and show off their favorite designs in a dedicated gaming space. Meanwhile, with the latter, it serves a "dual life" — whether it's sitting in the corner while you're watching shows and movies, or wheeled front and centre for an intense gaming session. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. "That was a big part of our philosophy: how do we make products that can adapt to how people want to use them? Either be as expressive as possible, or just be part of your world," summarised Ledbetter. You can see that approach clearly in all of the more practical products from the collection. Take the side table. Closed up and next to your sofa, it could be mistaken for another piece of clean and minimalist furniture you'd find in IKEA. Open up the sliding doors on the front, though, and inside there's space specifically designed to store controllers, headsets, and battery packs — plus the all-important cable management and power connectivity options you need to keep your tech charged between sessions. "This came up time and time again: cable management, charging stuff — where do you put it when you're done? People don't want it all over the place," said Ledbetter. And Dilé agreed: "We looked at it from the perspective of: what does gaming throughout the home look like? Because, of course, people play at their desks, in the living room, on the couch. In so many different ways. For us, it was important to cater for a lot of these different needs. "And there's one never-ending challenge working for IKEA: cable management. It always comes up over and over again. I think it's a very real frustration for people. "Take the TV stand, for example. Yeah, you need to have the console there; you need to have somewhere to charge the controllers, somewhere to put a headset. That was one of the benefits of working together with someone like Xbox that knows gaming, and the hardware, and the players. That made the brief really, really clear." And even though designing for gamers was a big part of their brief, both teams were also well aware that they wanted products that a non-gamer would be happy to live in their home. This meant offering something that wasn't bedazzled with RGB lighting and garish colors. "You need to cater for gamers, but also for non-gamers or people who are living with gamers, or people who want to have the functionality but still want to have a nice home," said Dilé. "[We wanted to create] things that maybe your spouse or the people you live with also want to put in your home. These aren't just things that you accept because of your hobby. That was an important balance for us. "There are so many people who play games, so it’s incredibly diverse. We really wanted to showcase that you can have that [gaming] experience and still have beautiful products that blend into your home to create a nice environment that you want to live in." That led Ledbetter to reminisce about the first meeting between both parties, where they both discovered they shared very similar design philosophies and were keen to get both of their respective design teams together to bounce around ideas. The result is this YXSTABY collection — nine products encompassing everything from stools, seats and cushions, to TV stands, storage and display cases — set to launch in October later this year. A weird and wonderful mix of items that speak to both the fun side of gaming and the practical needs in the home. Ledbetter summed up his hopes for the collection as follows: "Think about it: we create these controllers, and we sell millions of controllers, but we're not in charge of the controller’s home. We make the controller, and then where does it go? We don’t know. So, now, there's this opportunity between IKEA and Xbox to build that home. It felt like a completion of that journey." item.title: Quote of the day by pioneer Douglas Engelbart: 'The digital revolution is even more significant than the invention of writing or printing' — an audacious claim about interactive computing
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.56
It's hard to imagine how we'd interact with computers today without the work of engineer and inventor Douglas Engelbart, who pioneered many aspects of computer science and also invented the computer mouse. The breadth and depth of his work led him to believe that humanity's digital era could be the most significant in its history. The digital revolution Engelbart, then a researcher at the Stanford Research Institute where he led the development of interactive computing, was delivering a demonstration now considered by many as legendary. This article is part of TechRadar Pro's QOTD project to provide an insight into the minds of the brightest and most recognized figures in the technology industry today and in years gone by. Read the full series here. This spoken presentation, known as 'The Mother of All Demos', involved a 90-minute showcase in which his team described their progress to a captivated audience. Engelbart wasn't standing at a podium, but at a computer that was based 30 miles away in his research lab. The event cycled between spoken passages, live demos, and different members of the team using teleconferencing to speak about different technologies. A new era During this talk, he delivered his opinion that their work, which would lay the foundation for advancements in the years to come, was a more important contribution than both writing – and even printing. This was an incredibly bold prediction, because he was comparing the digital revolution to core aspects of the human condition. Writing and printing fundamentally opened pathways for sustainable knowledge transfer, allowing humanity to pass on and build on progress over the course of millennia. If anybody was poised to know the significance of the computing era, it was Eglebart. His work was at the heart of many of the technologies that we take for granted today, including the humble computer mouse. In 1964, he built a small, carved wooden block featuring a single button on top and two metal wheels beneath to track movement. He went on to demonstrate this for the first time at his 1968 demo. item.description:

- China's UBTech has revealed its new robot factory - The facility can produce 10,000 androids a year - It uses many autonomous robots in the production process Forget AI agents and ChatGPT, fully autonomous robots are the next high-tech frontier, with companies across the globe racing to perfect their android creations. And Chinese firm UBTech has taken a big step in that direction with its new smart factory that can produce 10,000 robots a year — and it might change manufacturing forever. The factory is the first of its kind in the world, according to the Seoul Economic Daily. It’s located in Liuzhou, in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region and is focused on producing UBTech’s Walker S and Cruzr robot series. And the factory itself makes heavy use of humanoid robots and driverless vehicles, perhaps providing a glimpse of the future of production and manufacturing. Cruzr Y1 and Cruzr S2 androids unload materials and stack, load and transport them, while collaborative robots take part in the final assembly process that finalizes each product. These final-stage robots work in tandem with human operators and include autonomous vehicles and rotating workbenches. In a separate development, UBTech says it has launched “the industry’s first fully automated three-dimensional warehouse,” according to the Seoul Economic Daily. This can store 112 robots in 65 square meters of space, supposedly utilizing 50% more space than a facility with similar floor space. Expanding capacity UBTech said it has been able to create its robot factory thanks to the strong supply chain that exists in China. According to UBTech vice president Fang Jianxin, “This foundation is rooted in the many engineers, scientists and application scenarios China has accumulated over the past 10 to 20 years, which has formed a very strong supply chain base, manufacturing capability and research and development capacity.” China has been ramping up its robot production in recent years, with the National Bureau of Statistics of China noting that output hit 98,677 units in July, an increase of 30.2% on the previous year. And 635,056 robots were created between January 2026 and July 2026, an uptick of 28.5% year on year. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. item.title: How the mighty have fallen — the notorious Stuxnet malware source code has been replicated and posted on GitHub for all to see
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.43
- A pseudonymous GitHub account has published what it calls a reconstruction of Stuxnet malware that purportedly took out a fifth of Iran's centrifuges before being discovered - The original source has never surfaced, and the 'Stuxnet' moniker that the account uses comes from Symantec's coining of the name weeks after it was discovered - The code remains unverified and untested, with some users indicating that it is likely an AI-generated replication of the original binaries' behavior, which has been widely documented A GitHub account has published what it describes as a faithful reconstruction of Stuxnet, the worm that sabotaged Iranian uranium-enrichment centrifuges. It also became the first piece of software widely accepted as having caused physical destruction in the real world, highlighting how malicious software can often do much more harm to people and hardware than just stealing or manipulating data. The repository surfaced via a Show HN submission, which mainstream media outlets then picked up, highlighting the as-yet-unknown researcher's reverse-engineered code. Not the first or last Stuxnet repository The original Stuxnet source, written by whoever built it, has never been leaked and did not leak last week. The repository's README explicitly states that it is a reconstruction assembled from decompiled binaries, and those binaries have been in public circulation since Belarusian firm VirusBlokAda pulled samples from an Iranian customer's machines in June 2010. Everything that followed, including Symantec's W32.Stuxnet Dossier and Ralph Langner's To Kill a Centrifuge, was built on those samples and how they reacted in test environments. This is also not the first time readable C-language code aiming to replicate Stuxnet has been published online. Malware researcher Amr Thabet published a decompilation of the MRxNet rootkit carrying a 2010 to 2011 copyright notice. Christian Roggia followed with a dropper decompilation called open-myrtus, copyrighted 2012 to 2014, which has since been forked into a long chain of repositories. The irony is that if such code were a faithful replication of the infamous malware, it would not have mentioned "Stuxnet" in multiple places, including registry keys. This is because the moniker is not one the developers likely used, but one Symantec switched to from its original 'W32.Temphid' identifier. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The thread where it was first brought to attention by a user called Sadpainy also has mixed views from developers, many of whom have branded it 'AI slop' or a 'fake' that relies on a mixture of already existing repositories, even as the about page on its GitHub repo states that it was reproduced by the researcher for educational purposes and is designed to only work on Windows XP and Windows 7. For those looking to test it, a virtual machine might be their best bet, especially given Stuxnet's ability to physically damage hardware, but it is also a stark reminder of what a rogue AI agent could do if left unchecked without specific instructions or safeguards. "Everyone's going to learn it all together, and if you're a big Guild Wars fan, you'll know what some of the species are and some of the characters or some of the locations," the studio head said. "But for the most part, everybody is on equal footing." The direction also means the studio could draw more players by launching the game on both PC and PlayStation 5; it's unclear right now whether the game could eventually get an Xbox release as well. item.title: Will Samsung and Qualcomm’s organic bridge technology make AI processors more powerful and cheaper to produce?
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.12
- A collaboration between Samsung and Qualcomm aims to harness 'organic bridge' technology to reduce costs for AI CPUs - The process is being developed for 2.1D packaging, a lower-cost integration than 2.5D , where silicon, glass, or ceramic materials are used - Resins and composites are among the organic materials typically used in semiconductor integration Samsung and Qualcomm have collaborated on a new type of CPU that takes advantage of organic materials for integration between layers, rather than silicon or its alternatives. Described as an “organic bridge,” the technology is intended for AI semiconductors. The development of what has been named 2.1D packaging is aimed at reducing costs in AI chip fabrication, where 2.5D packaging is typically used. 2.5D chips rely on silicon, glass, or ceramic for connectivity between layers of microcircuits. With 2.1D, however, the use of organic material improves bandwidth. The organic bridge The key element of the 2.1D packaging is the organic bridge. It’s a technology adopted (and shrunk down) from PCB manufacture, and can reduce reduce production costs while boosting assembly. In short, it is a mass producer’s dream. Rather than the silicon (or an inorganic alternative), the organic bridge is a layer cut from resin or polymer. Its purpose is to connect multiple microcircuit dies, while providing insulation, as with silicon. However, the organic bridge has been proved to be more efficient, and can be produced more easily at scale. In addition, the organic bridge solves the supply chain issues surrounding silicon. Development of the technology for die fabrication appears to have commenced around October 2024, when a patent for “interconnected bridge” technology was filed. With the drive towards increased AI data centers in full swing, the 2.1D processor packaging could prove pivotal in delivering the predicted benefits of artificial intelligence. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Multiple partners Qualcomm isn’t the only partner Samsung is working with on organic bridge technology. Various other companies have also expressed an interest in developing chips with 2.1D packaging. The significance of the drive to build 2.1D packaging for AI chips has not gone unnoticed by other companies in the tech industry. Korean magazine TheElec suggests that other Samsung customers are interested in working with the giant’s Samsung Electro-Mechanics subsidiary to develop 2.1D. If true, this would suggest that 2.1D is being widely considered as one solution to the the cost and energy demands of AI processing. Samsung isn’t the only chip maker working on 2.1D packaging. Intel Foundry Services has its own process in development, as does TSMC, which has expanded into 2.1D packaging after dominating the 2.5D market. It seems that work between Samsung and Qualcomm has been ongoing for the past year, which indicates that it might be some time before any production-ready AI chips with 2.1D packaging are available. item.title: Chinese scientists achieve 10 billion writing cycles in major future memory endurance breakthrough that improves endurance by 100x
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.09
- Future memory could be more durable thanks to developments with wurtzite ferroelectrics materials - A new structural design has enabled a demonstration of 10 billion writing cycles, around 100 times the previous limit - The breakthrough was made by scientists from the Xidian University working with the City University of Hong Kong and Fudan University. Next generation memory for future AI systems will need far faster and more durable performance, and scientific researchers in China seem to have made a breakthrough, demonstrating a new design which can complete some 10 billion writing cycles, 100 times more than the previous limit. This development – by teams at the Xidian University working with the City University of Hong Kong and Fudan University – is one of the most significant breakthroughs in memory development, and relies on the discovery of a quirk in the behavior of Nitrogen atoms. Dense, low-power memory chips now seem to be a realistic possibility for a future demanding ever-scaling AI processing. Wurtzite ferroelectrics Creating faster memory and storage with greater capacity while keeping the energy requirements low is the holy grail of computing. Over the past few years, research has increasingly focused on wurtzite ferroelectrics (polar crystal materials) such as aluminium scandium nitride (AlScN), which has the advantage of being compatible with semiconductor manufacturing processes currently in use. It also offers that low energy target, along with the superior switching speed required by fast storage. Until now, the main challenge had been reliability. Testing of repeated switching in previously developed AlScN chips had resulted in failure after around 100 million writing cycles, but the researchers have found a solution. Nitrogen cornfields So, why has this breakthrough been made now? The previous failed attempts led researchers into deeper investigation as to why the AlScN chips would top out at 100 million cycles, which is where they found the problem: missing nitrogen atoms. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Wang Ruiqing, is a doctoral researcher at Xidian University and one of the authors of the research paper on the study, recently published in journal Science. “Think of ferroelectric material as a neatly planted cornfield,” Wang said, “with nitrogen vacancies representing spots where seedlings are missing.” The defects were not the problem itself, however, but rather their behavior during switching. Rather than remain stationary, the nitrogen vacancies would move, and even group together. The consequence of this was the creation of “pathways” that allowed electricity to leak. Upon discovering this, the team designed a structure to minimise the nitrogen vacancies, slowing the deterioration of the material. “In the past, researchers knew that the devices failed and could observe some of the symptoms, but no one had been able to explain at the atomic scale what was moving, how they were moving and how that movement ultimately caused failure.” Wang added. If successful, AlScN-based RAM and storage could form the backbone of future server farms and provide the framework for greater LLM and artificial intelligence adoption.
