item.title: Alienware Gaming Laptops in Canada (2026): Specs, Prices, and Upgrade Paths
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.25
Quick Answer: In Canada, the Alienware 15 is the entry point to the Alienware lineup, with up to RTX 5060 graphics and up to 32GB of user-upgradeable memory, at 2.25 kg — a single device for everyday gaming alongside work, school, and other productivity. Stepping up, the Alienware 16X Aurora tops out at up to RTX 5070 Ti graphics and Intel Core Ultra 9 processors, the configuration to look at for demanding games and creative work. Canadian gamers already know that not every gaming laptop spec sheet travels well across the border. Frustratingly, a configuration or price listed in the US may not be available in Canada, and even the GPU or Windows edition can differ north of the 49th parallel. So, it’s worth checking the local lineup before getting your heart set on your dream rig. From there, you can narrow your choices based on your priorities for performance and upgrade potential, as well as practical considerations like size and weight. For Alienware buyers, the choice comes down to the capabilities you care about most. Dell’s Alienware 16X Aurora is the more performance-focused machine, while the Alienware 15 is the smaller and lighter of the two, offering an accessible entry to the Alienware experience without sacrificing high quality and performance at a lower starting price. Below is an overview of the specific details Canadian shoppers need to know before they buy either the Alienware 16X Aurora or the Alienware 15. What Should Canadian Shoppers Look for in a 2026 Alienware Gaming Laptop? Start with the configuration that’s actually available in Canada, then work backward from your budget and the games and other workloads you plan to run, as well as the upgrade paths available for each option. A few quirks and considerations to sort through up front: - The configurations on offer in Canada: Laptop makers don’t always offer the same processor, GPU, memory, or display combinations in every market, so check the Canadian product page rather than assuming a US configuration is available locally - The price of your preferred configuration: Use the starting price as a baseline, then check how your specs and preferences affect the total - What you can upgrade later: Both Windows laptops give you some flexibility to make changes down the line (for example, adding more RAM or expanding SSD storage), so it’s prudent to prioritize components that are harder to replace or upgrade later (e.g., the processor or display) - How the laptop fits into your routine: Features such as Stealth Mode, USB-C charging capabilities, and chassis size become more relevant if the same PC also has to show up at school or work Alienware Gaming Laptops in Canada: Key Specs at a Glance Here’s a quick chart for seeing how each option stacks up. How Do Canadian Alienware Configurations and Prices Compare? The Alienware 15 sits at the lower end of the price range, while the 16X Aurora offers several higher-performance configurations. This entry-level configuration pairs an Intel Core 5 210H processor with RTX 4050 graphics, 16GB of DDR5 memory, a 512GB SSD, and a 15.3-inch 165Hz WUXGA display. It’s the lower-cost route for buyers focused on portability and a multi-use device for gaming and more. This configuration steps up to an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, RTX 5070 graphics, 16GB of DDR5 memory, a 1TB SSD, and a 240Hz WQXGA OLED display. It’s a stronger fit for buyers who want more gaming performance and a higher-end display. At the upper end of the current Canadian lineup, this configuration combines an RTX 5070 Ti with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, 32GB of DDR5 memory, a 1TB SSD, and the same 240Hz WQXGA OLED display. The extra spend primarily gets you the higher-tier GPU and twice the memory of the RTX 5070 configuration above. Can a High-Performance Gaming Laptop Double as an Understated Work Machine? Both Alienware models are designed for settings where you may not want your laptop to look or behave like a stereotypical gaming rig (like a Monday-morning status meeting or an afternoon working from your neighbourhood cafe). The Alienware 15 is especially easy to picture as part of a hybrid-work routine. Its polycarbonate-resin chassis and Nova Black finish keep the aesthetic classic and understated. At a minimum weight of 2.2 kg (4.85 pounds), it slides easily into a backpack for class or work tote for the commute. The device’s 180-degree hinge is another practical feature for anyone working at an awkwardly small desk or sharing their screen with a colleague across the table. The 16X Aurora has that same crossover appeal. An anodized aluminum exterior and clean silhouette keep the styling restrained. And when the work itself gets demanding, the laptop has the processing and graphics power for tasks like video editing or casual work in CAD or 3D software. On both laptops, Stealth Mode—activated by tapping F7 on your keyboard—lets you tone down the lighting and fan noise when you’re in a meeting or shared space, so your laptop doesn't draw unwanted attention from nosy classmates or coworkers. Are Entry-Level Alienware Laptops Easy to Upgrade Down the Line? Both laptops offer options for user upgrades to memory and storage, although the 16X Aurora offers more expansion flexibility than the Alienware 15. Some important details: Memory Both models use two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, so RAM is replaceable rather than soldered in. The Alienware 15 supports up to 32GB, while the 16X Aurora supports up to 64GB, so you can start modestly and add memory later if your games or creative applications get more demanding. Storage The Alienware 15 has one M.2 SSD slot, so increasing storage means replacing the existing drive with a larger capacity. The 16X Aurora has two M.2 SSD slots, which gives you the option to add a second drive as your game library or project files grow. Which Canadian Alienware Laptop Fits Your Budget? For Canadian buyers, the Alienware 15 is the lower-priced of the two, and the Alienware 16X Aurora is where the higher-tier GPU and display options live. The decision on how far to stretch your budget will depend on your needs and gameplay preferences: if your laptop has to move between classes, meetings, and back to your home or dorm room, the Alienware 15 may offer a more enticing balance of cost, performance, and portability. If 1440p-class gaming or heavier multitasking are higher on your list, the 16X Aurora gives you more room to scale up. What is the maximum GPU ceiling on the Canadian Alienware 16X Aurora? The Alienware 16X Aurora is currently available in Canada with up to an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU. Is single-channel RAM on the Alienware 15 a performance bottleneck? Single-channel RAM can limit memory bandwidth in some workloads, but the Alienware 15 has two user-accessible DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, which leaves room to add or replace memory later. How does Stealth Mode work on the Alienware 16X Aurora and Alienware 15? Stealth Mode turns off AlienFX lighting and switches the laptop to Quiet mode; simply hit the F7 key on your keyboard to activate the feature. Can you power the Alienware 15 using a standard USB-C charger? Yes. The Alienware 15 supports USB-C Power Delivery charging at up to 100W, so a general-purpose 100W (5A) USB-C charger works as a backup to the AC adapter for productivity, not gaming. USB-C Power Delivery on the Alienware 15 supplies enough power for writing a paper, building a presentation, or taking notes when the main adapter is out of reach. Gaming and other demanding workloads draw more than 100W, so those sessions need the dedicated AC power adapter included with the Alienware 15. Does the Alienware 16X Aurora feature Element 31 thermal cooling? No. Dell Technologies specifies Element 31 for its Area-51 laptops; the 16X Aurora instead uses a Cryo-Chamber cooling design. How much can Canadian shoppers save during Dell seasonal promotions? Savings vary by specific promotion and configuration; Dell Canada is currently advertising gaming PC deals of up to CAD $1,500 off select systems.

item.title: US Takes Down Long-Running DDoS Site 'NightmareStresser'
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.19
The FBI has seized a notorious site called “NightmareStresser” that’s been fueling hundreds of thousands DDoS attacks to knock services offline. Since at least 2020, NightmareStresser had sold access to users looking to launch Distributed Denial-of-Service attacks, which can overwhelm and disrupt access to internet services. But on Tuesday, the Justice Department announced the FBI had used court-authorized orders to seize domains belonging to the DDoS provider. “According to the seizure warrant affidavit, the NightmareStresser Booter service targeted in this operation was used to launch hundreds of thousands of actual or attempted DDoS attacks targeting victims worldwide since 2022,” the department added. The site’s main domain at nightmare-stresser.com has since been replaced with an FBI seizure notice. Back in 2022, federal agents previously seized the group’s other domain at nightmarestresser.com while charging six suspects behind dozens of DDoS-for-hire services. NightmareStresser had over 566,000 registered users, providing an easy way for anyone to launch a DDoS attack, according to a 2023 report from cybersecurity provider Searchlight Cyber. The site was charging between €25 to €19,999 for a variety of DDoS methods and intensities. NightmareStresser itself touted: “Backed by the most experienced minds in the DDoS industry, it now stands tall as the longest-running, most powerful, and most respected platform of its kind. For over 8 relentless years, NightmareStresser hasn’t gone down.” Although the site portrayed itself as offering stress-testing services, the FBI says NightmareStresser's actual customers were using the service "to facilitate attacks on victims in the District of Alaska and across the United States." The FBI’s takedown is part of Operation PowerOFF, an ongoing effort from international law enforcement to crack down on DDoS services. Still, it’s possible NightmareStresser could return with a new site. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Sunnier Days Ahead? Solar Panels Are Now So Cheap It's Upending the Business World
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.16
Solar panels are so cheap now that in many places around the world, if a business isn't running on solar energy, it's going to struggle to compete. But as the Financial Times reports, the influx of cheap panels is placing new strains on the grid, and the underlying business model of utility companies which see shrinking profits alongside an explosion in self-generation. At the start of this century, solar panels were priced around $5 per watt they generated. Today, that's more like $0.12 per watt, almost entirely driven by China's enormous production of solar panels, which are currently estimated to be in the region of 1.36 terawatts per year. But where this more affordable form of green energy was initially mostly used in hard-to-reach places or in economies where decarbonizing was attractive, the low cost has now made it a fundamental part of some businesses. The FT cites a cement producer in Northern Pakistan that sees solar energy as a necessity to survive. With its rivals already using solar, it is struggling to compete on price because the others' low energy costs allow them to be more competitive, regardless of fluctuations in fuel pricing impacted by global trade and conflict. This is becoming increasing prevalent in developing countries. Estimates from the green-energy-focused think tank Ember suggest that African countries will jointly bring online over 17GW of solar power generation in 2026. This in turns helps them replace otherwise carbon-generating sources, like kerosene lamps and charcoal-cooking fires. Although the US government has stymied some attempts to accelerate solar roll out, plug-in solar is still making inroads, allowing for smaller solar setups, even on balconies, to flourish. The UK recently legalized these new plug-in systems and they are expected to see swift adoption under the looming shadow of the US-Iran war and its ongoing energy turbulence. But while some businesses are buoyed by the technology, traditional utility companies face new challenges. With so many homes and businesses switching to solar, often those with larger energy usage, utility firms are contending with reduced revenue, and less reliable demand. Cloudy days suddenly see millions more homes and businesses demanding energy from the grid, where otherwise they would rely on their own solar power. On top of that, national grids not designed with two-way power transmission in mind are straining under the exploding solar generation capacity. Day-long blackouts in Spain and Portugal in 2025 have been linked to the grid not being adapted to the increasing capacity for solar generation from individual homes and businesses. As more and more people move off-grid for the majority of their electricity, too, it raises questions about who should be paying for grid infrastructure and maintenance. But raising prices on remaining customers further risks punishing those who can't afford or physically fit solar panels on to their home. Part of the solution may be using AI to better manage grid loads and the influx of solar energy, with smart forecasting that uses weather patterns to provide a more responsive energy grid. While designing a modern power grid may be more complex and remain costly in the near-term, the genie is not going back in the solar bottle. As global disturbances push up fuel prices and increase uncertainty, a growing majority of people just want stable, affordable power. Solar looks set to be the best way to achieve that. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal Review: Stellar Carpet Suction Meets Subpar Mopping
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.80
The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal is a hybrid robot vacuum and mop with serious strengths and some drawbacks. It handled stubborn carpet debris effortlessly and navigated tricky floor plans without bumping into toys. Yet it struggled to pick up all pet hair and fell short on mopping, smearing messes across the floor. If you have a pet-free home with mostly carpeted flooring, it’s worth considering, but its $1,299 price puts it above more well-rounded premium models. The Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni ($1,099.99) remains our Editors' Choice thanks to its lower price, similar vacuum performance, and stellar mop design. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal has an understated design with just enough accents to avoid appearing bland. It isn't overly large, but it’s not quite small enough to squeeze under most furniture. The front of the disc-shaped Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal robot holds its namesake feature. In an indent on the bumper, alongside a 3D RGB sensor and an UltraRange Camera, is its UV module, which uses ultraviolet light to detect invisible stains needing extra attention. The top features a raised, mostly square tower with rounded edges that houses a 360 LiDAR module for navigation. At the front of the top is a hidden touch control panel with buttons that light up when the robot is working. The water droplet button starts a mopping cycle, while the icon with curved spokes on a wheel starts a vacuuming cycle. Press and hold both the vacuum and mop buttons together to start a whole-home combo clean. Between them is a home icon with a power symbol in the middle; press this button to send the robot back to its dock, or hold it to turn the cleaner on/off. A red icon will appear if there's an error, and a blue Wi-Fi icon illuminates during setup. Press the lever at the back of the top to release a section containing the dustbin, detachable mop pad, and water tank. The mop is a flat trapezoid with rounded edges that runs the width of the body. During operation, the hypersonic mopping process vibrates the pad 100 times per minute. The bottom of the robot also features a central, rotating brush roll that alternates curved bristles and plastic fins. Flanking the brush roll are large retractable wheels, which can independently raise to help the vacuum get unstuck when it encounters obstacles. A separate, small wheel behind the mop can extend to lift the back of the robot, and thus its mop, when traversing carpets. The front of the bottom has an omnidirectional caster wheel and a side brush with three straight prongs. Edge sensors line the perimeter. You won’t have to flip the vacuum over or access its dustbin often, as the base station empties the robot's dustbin into a canister that can store up to 60 days' worth of debris while reducing foul smells with a replaceable air freshener. This bagless compartment pulls free from the base station by pressing a lever hidden in an indent on the right side. Once free, the bottom flips open when you press a separate orange button, and the opening is wide enough that dirt never got stuck when I was emptying the bin in testing. Just make sure you’re emptying it over a waste can with a large mouth so it encircles the entire reservoir. Under a lid on top of the base sit the clean and dirty water reservoirs, which should allow up to 30 days of maintenance-free mopping with normal use. There's no separate compartment for cleaning solution, as on some other robot floor cleaners, but it comes with a 12-ounce bottle that you pour into the clean reservoir. Note that the lids on the reservoirs aren’t attached. I almost dumped dirty water all over myself because I was expecting the lid to flip open, and it came off entirely. To prevent the carpet from getting wet, the base station can remove the robot's mop pad for dry runs. During combined runs, the robot will vacuum carpeted areas first without the mop attached, then return to the base to pick up the mop before targeting rooms with hard floors. After a cleaning run, the base washes the mop with water heated to 185 degrees Fahrenheit and dries it with 175-degree air. I appreciate all the extras Shark includes with the PowerDetect UV Reveal. In addition to the aforementioned cleaning solution and air freshener, it comes with a replacement side brush. Unpacking everything takes a few minutes, as is typical for a bigger machine. Then, the setup is pretty quick. You’ll need to find a spot for the base station on a hard floor, near an outlet, with a strong Wi-Fi signal. The base needs a foot of clearance on each side and two feet of free space in front so the robot can move freely. Snap the front ramp into place, then insert the anti-odor cartridge, and fill the clean tank with tap water and cleaning solution. Finally, plug in the base, and you’ll see the front indicator light illuminate, indicating it’s powered on. Next, push the side brush into place until it clicks, then roll the robot into the base station and, within moments, it’ll power on with a jingle of chimes. From there, you’ll need to download the Shark Clean app (available for Android and iOS), create an account, and add a device. It’ll then walk you through connecting the robot to your Wi-Fi network, giving it a name, going through terms and conditions, and installing updates. Once the app is set, it prompts you to send the robot on a mapping run. In testing, the PowerDetect UV Reveal completed its exploratory trek of my 1,500-square-foot, two-bedroom apartment in 10 minutes and 55 seconds. The Ecovacs Deebot X8 only needed 7 minutes and 48 seconds to map my place, but the extra couple of minutes didn’t bother me. The vacuum was a little loud while mapping, as though its suction was engaged, and it emptied its dustbin afterward, even though it wasn't cleaning. The map's perimeter was oddly shaped, but it still looked good overall. The app then instructs you to send the robot on its first cleaning run to verify and complete the map and to discover the locations of area rugs and carpet. This process took roughly an hour. You can then manually merge, split, or rename rooms, or add no-ho zones to the map. When manually editing the map, I found it a bit fiddly to change the perimeter between rooms. Additionally, I couldn’t make the no-go zone small enough to block off just the litter box area in my office. Once the map is set in the app, a button below it starts a whole-home clean, and pulls up options to vacuum, mop, or vacuum and mop. You can choose from three vacuum suction levels, three water flow levels for mopping, and whether to enable UV Stain Detect. The app lets you select a spot on the map or specific rooms for targeted cleaning, but, oddly, only for a vacuum or mop run. You can’t start a combined run on a smaller selected area; it only applies to the whole floor plan. As another limitation, the app doesn’t let you save multiple maps, and overwrites older ones when you make a new one. Otherwise, the settings menu in the upper left lets you create a schedule and configure device options such as enabling Do Not Disturb times, changing button sounds, and turning on the Under Glow Lights, which illuminate when errors, stains, or particularly dirty areas are detected. From this menu, you can also connect the robot to Amazon and Google for voice control. After its two mapping runs, I started a whole-home combo run with the Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. It finished in 105 minutes, with a couple of pit stops at the base station to empty the dirt, again taking longer than X8 (77 minutes) on this task, but it covered the floor thoroughly. It left its mop in its base station while vacuuming the throw rug in my bedroom, and my carpeted living room and office. After it retrieved the mop, it covered the rest of the rooms, including the remaining space in my bedroom. When traversing the same throw rug with the mop attached, it lifted its tail into the air like it was doing a downward-dog yoga pose, looking goofy in the process, but successfully avoiding any contact between the mop and the rug. After the run, my floors mostly looked good, with a few strands of cat hair left here and there. On subsequent runs, I’d occasionally find clumps of hair left near chair and table legs. The PowerDetect also sometimes struggles with cords. It ran over them on several runs, but mostly managed to untangle itself with its independently lifting wheels. I did have to rescue it once when it managed to get itself fully wrapped within a tangle of cords. Aside from cords, the PowerDetect excels at obstacle avoidance. I tested this by scattering cat toys of various shapes and sizes on the floor, and it found its way around all of them without bumping into or running over any. I test battery life by running whole-home cleaning cycles on the default power level until the robot stops and returns to the base station to charge. I consider 60 minutes the functional minimum for covering a small home, and 90 minutes a passing grade for medium- to large-sized spaces. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal lasted for 141 minutes. That’s an impressive result that beats the Deebot X8 (134 minutes) and most other premium models, but falls short of our all-time battery champ, the Ecovacs Deebot X11 (180 minutes). For measured vacuum testing, I assess performance on 100 square feet of carpet and hardwood, using two types of debris: rice (representing everyday debris) and sand (representing stubborn debris). I distribute a specific amount of debris onto a precleaned floor and weigh the robot's dustbin before and after each test run to determine how much it picked up. The PowerDetect picked up 46% of sand on the carpet, beating the X8 (37%) and other recent premium models, and falling only a few points short of the Dyson 360 Vis Nav, which earned the highest-ever score on the test at 53.6%. On hardwood, the PowerDetect picked up 97% of the rice, an excellent result on this relatively easy test. It effectively cleans along walls and avoids flinging dirt with its side brush. With sand on hardwood, it also avoided spreading the debris, but collected only 62.7%. The X8, for comparison, captured 90% of rice and 82.3% of sand on hardwood. The PowerDetect picked cleaned my carpeted test space in an average of 9 minutes and 41 seconds, and my hardwood space in 9 minutes and 8 seconds. While its cleaning time on carpet is similar to that of other recent high-end models, it proved particularly fast in my hardwood testing space, beating most competitors by a couple of minutes. The Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal struggled in my mopping stress test. For this test, I spread 0.25 ounces of raspberry jelly in a single area on my kitchen floor, and then send the robot on a combined cleaning run targeting the room. The PowerDetect clearly detected the stain. It stopped over it, let the mop scrub for a few seconds, then returned later in the cycle for an additional pass. With the extra attention, it managed to remove almost all residue from the initial stain area, but it spread some seeds and even a couple of globs of jelly to other nearby parts of the room. The whole kitchen floor felt a touch sticky to me afterward. The design of the flat, vibrating mop is the culprit. Roborock has used a similar mop design on its hybrid models for years, and the Saros 10 similarly struggled in this stress test. Newer designs, such as the self-refreshing roller mop on the Ecovacs Deebot X8 and X11, perform much better. Even spinning mop pads, like those on the Roborock Qrevo Curv, outperform a single vibrating pad. Final Thoughts Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. If your home is mostly carpeted and free of pets, the Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal delivers powerful suction and smart, hassle-free dock automation. However, its vibrating mop pad simply can't handle tough, sticky messes on hard floors, and it drops the ball on heavy pet shedding. Given its steep price tag, you'll get significantly better performance and value from our Editors' Choice winner, the Ecovacs Deebot X8 Pro Omni, which mops better, handles pet hair cleanly, and costs less. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Duda Website Builder Review: Powerful, Flexible, and Packed With Features
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.75
Simplicity is Duda's selling point. We've tested many website builders for years, and this one lets you quickly and easily build attractive websites that look great on desktops, smartphones, and tablets. Despite high-end tiers that target professionals, Duda lets you create handsome sites even if you have little design or technical knowledge. Since our last review, Duda has also enhanced its AI tools. Featuring numerous templates, strong e-commerce tools, and a top-tier editor, the slick and powerful Duda is an Editors' Choice winner for website builders alongside Wix, which stands out for its fantastic free tier. Duda lacks a free tier, but you can sample the service using its 14-day free trial. It has three paid tiers that focus on collaborative websites. The first is Basic ($25 per month, $19 per month if billed annually), which lets a single user create one website. However, Basic limits your customer support contact method to email. Team is the next tier up ($39 per month, $29 per month if billed annually). It increases the maximum team size to three, adds chat and phone support, and lets visitors leave site comments. The Team tier is where Duda focuses on web agencies, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and web hosting services, with client billing and management options, as well as white-label analytics, included. In fact, the next tier is called Agency ($69 per month, $52 per month if billed annually). It lets you build up to four websites, rope in six team members, and build widgets to give your site unique capabilities. Beyond these main tiers, Duda offers a White Label tier ($199 per month, $149 per month if billed annually) with more enterprise customization. Duda also has a full-on custom option if you need managed services and 24/7 dedicated support, but you must contact the company for a quote. Each plan comes with unlimited storage and monthly data transfers. Although each paid tier is built for a certain number of sites, you can add more for an additional monthly fee. This fee depends on your subscription plan: $19 per site per month for the Basic tier and $17 per site per month for the other tiers. E-commerce also costs extra. The standard e-commerce add-on is $7 per month for a maximum of 100 products in your digital storefront. For an additional $20 per month, you can sell up to 2,500 products, sell on Amazon and eBay, and even create multilingual stores. The top-end e-commerce plan costs $45 per month and lets you sell unlimited products and leverage a Square point-of-sale system. All these costs add up, since they're added onto the base subscription price, and can threaten to push Duda out of the realm of the casual user. Wix's business plans start at $36 per month. To start a new site, you choose from more than 100 attractive, modern templates. There's a search bar if you're looking for a specific template, but Duda has many other sorting options. You can look by overall color or filter by categories, such as Online, Travel, Restaurant & Food, and Blog. Duda makes it simple to see everything it offers, unlike Squarespace and other website builders, which have questionnaires to help narrow the template hunt. After clicking a template thumbnail, you'll see a panel showing how the template looks on a phone or tablet. You can even see how the template looks on all three device types—desktop, smartphone, and tablet—at once. That's better than what many site builders do. Strikingly, for example, has just one preview. However, you can resize the browser window to see how it will look on smaller screens. Once you choose a template for your Duda site and start customizing, you can't easily switch templates later, as you can with Squarespace or Simvoly. You have to basically reset your site. That's because Duda sites aren't responsive in the strictest sense, though they fit the search engines' criteria for mobile presentation. This means they don't stretch and compress all elements as you resize the browser window. Duda uses the term responsive—not incorrectly—when describing sites it builds to mean that the presentation reformats based on whether you're viewing it in a desktop browser, tablet, or smartphone. Duda's approach means you get a lot more control over your site design and can tweak it to look different on mobile. If you want to completely rebuild your site, you can at least save some data (like images and store content) so you don't need to start from scratch with a new template. You can also manually tweak the JavaScript. Duda also has Flex templates, which are advanced editing options that let you create fully responsive sites. As a newer feature, though, it offers just a handful of templates. You can add Flex sections to traditional Duda templates, giving you more freedom to arrange elements within those sections of your site. You can even restrict Flex editing to certain team members. You build your site using the selected template, which is pre-populated with dummy content. You can pull images and other content directly from an existing site or Facebook page. For more on getting started building your site, read our primer on how to create a website. We started with the DigiStore template. The site builder interface features an intuitive left sidebar with tools for managing and designing your site. These let you customize your theme colors, text, and navigation, as well as add and manage pages and site settings from choices on the left panel. An arrow lets you collapse this sidebar for a helpful, full-page view. Also helpful are the Undo and Redo icons that work no matter what you're doing on the site. Ctrl-Z works, too. Furthermore, you can always get help by clicking a chat bubble icon at the bottom right—very handy. The basic page elements—images, text boxes, buttons, dividers—appear when you click the Widgets button. You may find this a bit confusing, as widgets are typically third-party goodies rather than basic site elements. You drag the elements onto your web page, as with Weebly and other competitors. Aside from Flex sections, you can only drop elements in allowed areas, but it's not hard to add columns or change spacing to customize the layout to your taste. In fact, we love how you can choose Add Row or Add Column right from a page's Row button, which appears when you hover over any section. Third-party items, such as Disqus and Facebook comment modules, are included in the Widgets group, but Duda lacks a large catalog of third-party integrations like those found in Wix. Duda has continued to update its limited App Store with a handful of new selections, such as SimplyBook.me and Zuppler for Restaurants. However, using a web builder like Bluehost WonderSuite connects you to the much more expansive WordPress plug-in ecosystem. Upon launching Duda, you see the latest service updates, including new apps, templates, and features. Duda also integrates with services such as OpenTable, PayPal, vCita, and Yelp. For example, its integration with Yext embeds structured schema data into your website, making it easier for other sites to machine-read it. This helps search engines parse your site. The service makes it a breeze to incorporate social sharing buttons, including Facebook Likes, comments, and albums; a Twitter/X feed; and a WordPress feed. When we added the Click-to-Call feature to our test site, it merely displayed our number, which smartphones display as a link that opens the phone dialer. Duda's editor works well thanks to its clean, consistent layout. Along the top is an ever-present toolbar that lets you switch pages, undo your last edit, save your work, preview your site, publish your site, and view your site in three different screen sizes. The toolbar also grants access to your Dashboard page, from which you can manage all your existing Duda sites, start new ones, and connect them to a personal domain. There's an option to purchase a new domain name through Google Domains or Hover, and Duda offers specific integrated help for using a custom domain obtained from the major domain name registrars. If you don't choose a custom domain, Duda assigns your site a URL (you can pick your own prefix if it's not already taken). If you've built pages but aren't ready to publish them, you can save your edits for later publication. Duda lets you schedule overall site publication at a specific date and time, as Weebly does. Whenever you hover over an item on your site, you see a button with relevant edit options. It also supports right-clicking, which gives you a context-sensitive menu for each element. This provides an easy way to edit, align, or remove content. You can move elements around the page and resize them, though, as with most mobile-friendly site builders, your choices of where to move items are limited. For a paragraph object, the context menu lets you pull content from another site, edit the text, format it, and even hide it for selected device types. Clicking a page navigation link in the site designer takes you to that page on your site; you don't have to select it from a page menu as in some other site builders, though there's also a dropdown menu for switching among your pages. The Manage Pages panel is simple and clear, with SEO and navigation options available under a gear icon. It also lets you import images and site info from an existing site. To add a new page to a site, you simply tap the +New page button. There's a selection of page types to choose from, including Blank, URL, About, Contact, Photo Gallery, List, and Complex Page. Pages can be password-protected via the Settings menu. Hovering over a page type's thumbnail shows its layout on the three device sizes. Duda also has a very serviceable blogging tool. This lets you save and preview posts that you can format and add images to taste. Every option dialog for every Duda site element includes a Settings tab that lets you edit spacing in pixels, the CSS code, and—for premium accounts—the actual HTML code for the element. The service lets you use Secure Sockets Layer certificates (SSL), so site visitors see HTTPS in the browser address bar. Most modern browsers make HTTPS connections by default; this level of security is especially important with the arrival of GDPR. Duda offers all the tools you need to stay compliant with privacy regulations for your European visitors. You can enable a cookie notification, implement a privacy policy, require opt-in consent for contact forms, and provide a way to delete personal data. In the end, building a site with Duda is a pleasure: The interface is mostly quick, unlike some builders that take a few seconds to load modules. As with most such services, moving objects around can be finicky, but Duda got us the results we wanted. To add images to your site, you can use the included stock photography, drag and drop photos from computer folders, or import images from online sources, such as Dropbox, Facebook, Flickr, or Instagram. The included stock photography selection has improved since our last test, turning up plenty of clothing rack shots when we searched for "thrift shop," for example. You can even enter an image's URL or perform a web image search to find the picture you want. Uploading multiple images at once? Not a problem, whether it's a whole folder or multiple selected images within it. You can crop, resize, and even open an embedded image editor for some online photo editing and effects. In testing, we added a clickable link and tooltip, and changed the Alt text in the image-editing dialog. If you need more control, a gear icon gives access to CSS and HTML code. There are many photo gallery options, including image size, frame style, spacing, and animation. We also like that once you add an associated Facebook page, any public images from that page appear in the Duda images manager. You can also connect an Instagram account, so your photo gallery can pull images from there. Duda offers separate site-builder views for desktop, smartphone, and tablet designs. Our test Duda site looked as good and felt just as comfortable to navigate on an iPhone as it did in a PC web browser. A cool option lets you hide any image on a device of your choice—desktop, tablet, or phone. Some content doesn't work well in the smaller formats, so this is a valuable option. The other side of mobile development is the ability to actually build or edit your site on a mobile device. Duda doesn't offer a mobile app for site building, unlike Weebly. Instead, it offers a mobile web version of the site builder. This features a touch-friendly design with a menu bar for adding and editing widgets. This also lets you add photos to your site right from the tablet. Duda has a suite of business-focused AI features meant to enhance your site-building experience. The AI SEO Assistant can generate relevant meta tags for your pages, and you can grant permission for team members to adjust tone and translate text with the AI Content Assistant. Duda's AI tools can also generate text and entire sites based on prompts. You can even pay extra to make your site more visible to AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini, with that subscription starting at $19 per month. These AI features feel targeted toward professionals rather than hobbyists, which makes sense for the service. Still, we recommend against using AI tools to build websites due to the many downsides. With Duda, you can add buttons that link to your Facebook, Twitter, and other social media accounts. As with Weebly, Duda offers many monochrome or color buttons in different sizes. An older-style Share bar also lets you add buttons, but these aren't customizable in the way the other buttons are, offering no choice of button designs or even which social networks are included. You're better off sticking with the Social Icons option. You can also include an on-page Twitter feed, a Facebook Like button, and Facebook comments. Duda includes a full sales system, with shopping carts and checkout pages like those you get with Squarespace, Weebly, and Wix. You can also plug PayPal buy buttons into any site page, add printable coupons for site visitors, and create customer memberships. Any Duda user can add a 10-page web store to their sites, assuming they've paid for the e-commerce add-on. The process is slick, clear, and guided. When you add a store under the e-commerce section, Duda builds a new page for your site with a demo catalog, and it displays a Help box explaining how to set it up. A tooltip tour explains your store page, shopping cart, search, and store management features. There's a separate Store Control Panel page where you add products and configure shipping and payment options. Credit card transactions automatically use SSL security. Another well-designed wizard takes you through the store setup process. Adding images and formatting text is easy, as is assigning categories and SKU numbers to your products. You can also change the localization to support non-US currencies. Shipping options are integrated with UPS and FedEx, or you can set custom rates. FirstData, PayPal, and Stripe are the available payment processing options. You can import product lists in CSV, LiteCommerce, and XCart formats. Finally, Duda supports selling digital downloads (which the company calls "e-goods"), but the maximum size varies depending on your e-commerce add-on. Standard allows up to 100 MB file sizes, Advanced goes up to 1GB, and Unlimited boosts that limit to 10GB. Duda has a few customer support options that largely depend on your service level. In other words, the more you pay, the better your support experience will be. As stated earlier, Basic only lets you email the support squad, while Agency adds screen share and web chat to communication options. More impressive in the Agency tier is the priority support. At this tier, contacting support first brings you to a bot that takes your questions and tries to funnel you toward an answer in Duda's Knowledge Base. If that doesn't suffice, you can "Get in Touch," which connects you with a live agent. In our test, it took less than 30 seconds to reach an agent, and we received answers to our questions 20 seconds later. Duda can also connect you with verified partners called Duda Experts to give you even more insightful advice on how to improve your site. The directory lists the services experts provide, the regions they are from, their ratings, and their rates. Reliable website uptime is one of the most important aspects of a hosting service. If your site is down, clients or customers will be unable to find you or access your products or services. Fortunately, Duda displays its uptime on its site, and the results are basically perfect. In short, Duda is stable and dependable. Final Thoughts Duda Website Builder - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Duda is a highly capable and user-friendly website-building service, offering many impressive features, especially in the realm of custom enterprise software for teams. It should be among your top considerations if you prioritize a site's look and functionality on mobile devices. Wix, another top pick, offers more integration with third-party services, a solid editor, automatic site creation, and a free tier. However, Duda has site traffic statistics that provide more details, and its editor is one of the best we've tested, especially for agencies. All this earns Duda our enthusiastic recommendation and an Editors' Choice award. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert My PCMag career began in 2013 as an intern. Now, I'm a senior writer, using the skills I acquired at Northwestern University to write about dating apps, meal kits, programming software, website builders, video streaming services, and video games. I was previously a senior editor at Geek.com and have written for The A.V. Club, Kotaku, and Paste Magazine. I'm the author of the gaming history book Video Game of the Year: A Year-by-Year Guide to the Best, Boldest, and Most Bizarre Games from Every Year Since 1977, and the reason everything you know about Street Sharks is a lie.

item.title: Adobe Lightroom Classic Review: The Leading Photo Workflow App for Pros
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.66
Adobe's Lightroom Classic is the longtime benchmark for photo workflow apps, thanks to its best-in-class organization and nondestructive Raw processing features. Hobbyists can get creative with a range of unbeatable color tools and quickly find photos of loved ones using robust keyword and face recognition filters. Meanwhile, pros who need to sort through large volumes of images should appreciate its recently improved assisted culling features. And despite the app's monthly subscription model, the cost is reasonable for photographers who want immediate access to its latest features. We've lowered Lightroom Classic's rating by half a star because it’s no longer head and shoulders above its competitors, but it's still a clear Editors' Choice winner. It shares that distinction with the more streamlined non-Classic Lightroom (which you get as part of the same subscription) and Adobe Photoshop, our top pick for pixel-level retouching and editing. Lightroom Classic is available only via subscription, starting with the Lightroom (1TB) plan. The plan is available for $17.99 per month, $11.99 per month (with an annual commitment for a total of $143.88), or $9.99 per month (billed annually at $119.88). A seven-day trial is available for all plans. Each plan comes with 1TB of cloud storage and both Lightroom Classic and Lightroom. The apps have the same core functionality but differ in their interfaces and some features, including their approaches to storage. Lightroom Classic works especially well with local photos on your computer (but can sync images to the cloud), while Lightroom puts your catalog in the cloud by default (which can add to your monthly bill if it swells beyond 1TB). For more details, read our in-depth comparison. The Creative Cloud Photography Plan (1TB), which costs $29.99 per month or $19.99 per month with an annual commitment, includes Photoshop. It's a better deal than paying for Photoshop à la carte—Adobe charges $22.99 per month (with an annual commitment) for Photoshop and a meager 100GB of storage. Photoshop provides pixel-based, destructive (also called raster) editing tools that aren’t available in Lightroom. Photographers who prefer to retouch images by hand or use more esoteric techniques like macro focus stacking will want to add Photoshop to their toolkit, but Lightroom does so much that Photoshop is no longer a strict requirement for many creative workflows. Naturally, Lightroom Classic is part of the full Creative Cloud suite, which costs $54.99 per month for the Standard edition or $69.99 per month for the Pro version, which includes more AI tools and credits. Both of those rates require an annual commitment. If you find Adobe’s subscription model distasteful, look into getting a perpetual license for Capture One ($349), DxO Photo Lab ($249.99), or Skylum Luminar ($129). Choosing an app with a perpetual license can reduce monthly subscription costs, but you miss out on the regular feature updates that a subscription model provides. It's also worth noting that Capture One's base Pro subscription plan ($18 per month, billed annually) costs more than Lightroom Classic. Adobe regularly updates Lightroom Classic with new features and support for the latest cameras and lenses. The app typically gets new features three to four times per year, with more frequent camera and lens compatibility fixes. Adobe does a fantastic job of keeping up with support for the newest digital cameras. The current version of Lightroom Classic at the time of writing is 15.5.1, released in August 2026. Here's what's new since the last time of the last review in July of 2025: - Assisted Culling improvements: Lightroom Classic uses face recognition to select photos where subjects’ eyes are open and sharp, helping you find the best portrait or group shot in a sequence. - Better identification of AI-edited images: You can now filter images based on AI Edits, with granular options for Has AI, Has Generative AI, and Needs AI Update. - Broader support for HDR file formats: The app lets you send 16- or 32-bit HDR images to an external editor (like Photoshop) with your choice of an sRGB, HDR Rec. 2020, or HDR Display P3 color space. - DNG rendering: Lightroom Classic now lets you render and export a DNG version of a photo with adjustments applied, a plus for creators who want to make additional adjustments in another application. - Improved Generate Remove: The software's generative remove and distraction removal tools now run faster and perform better, helping you target dust spots, distracting objects, or reflections in photos. Most of the updates from the last year are enhancements to existing features rather than all-new concepts. That’s a reflection of the software’s maturity; Lightroom Classic debuted back in 2007. Adobe also typically trots out new features in full version releases. Given previous development cycles, we expect a major release later this year. To install Lightroom Classic, you need a fairly up-to-date, 64-bit OS. It supports macOS 14 or later, Windows 10 (version 22H2 or later), and Windows 11 (version 21H2 or later). It works with both Intel- and Apple silicon-based Macs, but not natively on Windows on Arm PCs (unlike the other Lightroom). Otherwise, you need about 2GB of storage for installation, and a minimum of 8GB of RAM. Adobe recommends 16GB and an SSD for the best performance. Don't ignore these recommendations. Some advanced features take a while on 8GB systems, and physical disks can also be a bottleneck. I use a LaCie 6big Thunderbolt 3 RAID 5 hard drive array for my image archive, and I typically notice a delay when drives need to spin up and load an image. A Lightroom subscription includes access to mobile apps for Android, iOS, and iPadOS. With these apps, you can edit images you’ve synced to the cloud or photos on your mobile device. If you spend a lot of time editing on mobile, non-Classic Lightroom makes more sense on desktop, thanks to its more seamless cloud integration and a more consistent interface. However, you can still sync photos with Lightroom Classic. Lightroom Classic’s user experience hasn’t changed that much over the last couple of decades, even as its feature set has grown significantly. It breaks up its main screen into seven tabs: Library, Develop, Map, Book, Slideshow, Print, and Web. A cloud icon shows how much of your Adobe cloud storage you’re using and lets you sync on demand. The app puts folders, develop presets, and templates on the left, shows the image you’re working on in the center, information and tools on the right, and a film strip on the bottom so you can scroll through images. Most of Classic’s functions live in the Library and Develop tabs, so you'll spend most of your time there. The other tabs handle less frequent tasks. Map shows a global map and populates it with images that have GPS metadata, Book lets you create photo books that you can buy from Blurb, Slideshow replaces the old Kodak Carousel and lets you create MP4 movies with titles and transitions, Print prepares images for printing, and Web helps you publish a gallery website to show off your images. I’ve used Lightroom Classic regularly since its debut, first as a hobbyist photographer and, for the past 15 years, as a camera reviewer, so it’s fair to say I know Classic better than any other piece of software. I’m old and set in my ways, so I tend to struggle with photo apps with dramatically different layouts (I’m looking at you, Capture One). But even when I was starting out, I felt comfortable in Lightroom and struggled with its contemporary competition, Apple’s long-discontinued Aperture—and I say that as a dyed-in-the-wool Mac person. Don't forget about the top bar drop-down menu. If you’re ever trying to figure out how to do something and can’t find it, the searchable Help menu is worth a visit. Just type in the feature you’re looking for, and the menu will take you right to it. If you can’t figure something out, Adobe has an extensive library of support documents on its website, along with an active user group forum. If you’re still stuck on something after that, drop me an email, and I’ll do my best to assist. Lightroom uses a catalog system that imports and sorts images into its Library, leaving the organizational structure up to you. I sort everything into year-based folders with subfolders, but you might want to take a different approach. Wedding photographers, for example, might choose to organize by client name or even create a separate catalog file for each client. Lightroom loads only one catalog at a time, but it lets you freely swap between as many as you want to create. I like this approach—I prefer to keep just one huge catalog as I often need to go back and look at images from the various cameras I’ve reviewed over the years, but I can see why working photographers would want to spin up a different catalog for each client or start fresh each calendar year. Importing photos into the catalog is required; you can’t just edit directly from a drive or memory card. The Import screen pops up automatically when you insert a memory card into your computer, or you can load it manually by clicking Import (in the bottom-left corner of the app). You can select what you bring in and choose to add keywords during the process. Lightroom gives you flexibility on where you import them, though—you can spread a library across multiple folders, as well as internal or external drives. You can opt to convert proprietary Raw formats to Adobe DNG during import, though I don’t see much point in that. If you end up switching to a different photo editing app down the road, you’re better off with original files. You can also bring images into your catalog by using Tethered Capture, a mode that lets you connect and control a digital camera from your computer screen. Tethering is available for many major brands, and photos go straight into your computer and the Lightroom catalog. It’s a must-have feature if you work in a proper studio, but not super useful for hobbyists and event photogs who take pictures out in the world. The Library tab shows your catalog’s folder structure in its left panel, along with Collections (groups of images organized independent of the folder structure). This panel also provides quick access to supported Publish services, such as Adobe Stock and Flickr. Additional services are available via plug-ins. The right panel lets you access the Assisted Culling tool, add comments and keywords to images, and make quick exposure and color adjustments via the Quick Develop tool. The film strip at the bottom lets you page through images (tap the left or right keys to move back and forth) and includes tools to add a star rating, assign a color code, and flag images as picks or rejects. If your camera lets you assign star ratings to photos, Lightroom reads those automatically. All of these features genuinely help you pare down the photos you want to edit. Assisted Culling is a big hit for sports and wildlife photography, disciplines in which you often capture a high volume of images, intending to edit and publish only a few. Event photographers should find the star-rating and color-coding features handy for picking out the best images from the day. You can also quickly compare two photos (tap ‘c’), and click on an image to zoom in and check focus. One quick, but important note: Lightroom Classic won't import images it doesn't support. Adobe is quick to accommodate new Raw image formats, but if you get a brand-new camera on day one, you might have to wait a few weeks for Lightroom to read its file format. Among its competitors, Adobe is usually the first to support newly released cameras, but not always. The Develop panel, which resembles the Library tab, is the heart of Lightroom Classic. Its right-hand editing panel has a Histogram on top, with a row of six icons (Edit, Crop and Straighten, Remove, Red Eye Correction, Masking, and AI Edit Status). The Edit section includes slider-based tools for adjusting exposure and color, applying noise reduction, adding film grain, and more. It covers a lot of ground, but puts the features you’ll use most often (exposure and white balance) toward the top, and lets you suppress other options to one line so they don’t take up space. You can’t reorder them, however. It's crucial to understand that the changes you make to photos in Lightroom are nondestructive. Instead of changing information in an actual image, the software records changes in its catalog instead and only renders a finished photo with all of your edits baked in when you export it. This matches how pretty much every workflow application behaves, and I think it's the best way to go. Since Lightroom Classic never alters the original camera file, you can always go back to rework and freely experiment with an image. That's important because if you stick with photography long enough, your style and tastes will likely evolve—I recently looked at some photos I shot in my early days and was horrified by my early, garish processing. With Lightroom, I was able to rework my edits and am now happier with the results. And when you’re ready to share your photo with the world, you can easily export it in a wide variety of file formats (AVIF, DNG, JPG, JPG XL, PSD, PNG, TIFF). The Edit panel starts with a color profile, Adobe Color by default. Some preset options (such as RNI All Films 5 Pro) give images a stylized look, but Adobe also supports camera-matching profiles that mimic the colors of straight-out-of-camera JPGs from major brands. I especially like using the latter with Fujifilm cameras as Lightroom supports all of the company’s stylized Film Simulation looks. I appreciate the flexibility. You can either find or create a profile that matches your aesthetic. Or you can stick with Adobe's or your camera manufacturer's profiles. Raw images contain an incredible amount of color data, more than most screens can display, and the strength of Lightroom Classic (or any Raw converter for that matter) lies in its ability to tone exposure after capture. And you’ll want to make some adjustments—a Raw image is not a finished product, it’s a starting point that’s meant to be edited to taste. That said, you may be happy with what Lightroom shows right after import, since its default Adobe Color profile is naturalistic. Adobe puts Lightroom Classic’s exposure panel right near the top of the develop tools. It’s your starting point, with sliders to adjust the overall Exposure and Contrast of an image, or independently change the brightness of Highlights, Shadows, Whites, and Blacks. Everyone tones images differently, but I tend to go for a lower contrast look by moving Highlights and Whites to the left and Shadows and Blacks to the right. For a punchier photo, lower Shadows and Blacks and brighten Highlights and Whites. You can also go for a cool or warm tone by changing the White Balance. Use an eyedropper tool to set white balance from a neutral white, gray, or black area of an image, or choose a preset Kelvin temperature from a drop-down menu. If you want a punchier or paler color, you can try the Vibrance or Saturation sliders, though I caution you not to overdo it with either unless you're specifically going for a hyperrealistic look. Otherwise, you can raise or lower the microcontrast of an image using Clarity and Texture sliders, or sharpen a hazy shot with Dehaze. I try to use the Clarity and Texture options very conservatively; adding too much of either gives an image an unnatural look reminiscent of the worst examples of 2000s action films, while dialing them all the way back results in a diffused, soft-focus effect. Lightroom Classic's Detail panel includes the Super Resolution and Denoise tools, which respectively increase the pixel count and remove graininess. Both are useful if you’re cropping heavily or planning to make a large print. Super Resolution does a good job of adding detail without introducing AI hallucinations, unlike the upres features on phones like the Google Pixel 11 Pro. And it beats the in-camera version Canon includes in the EOS R5 Mark II and EOS R1 in terms of detail. I cover the Denoise feature in more detail further below (it’s part of Adobe’s AI toolset). The Transform tool can correct shots that aren’t quite level or suffer from keystone distortion with a single click. I struggle with getting shots perfectly level in the field and perhaps rely on the Level button too much, but it works reliably. If you’re going for an artsy look, you can use the Effects panel to add grain or a vignette. I like the ease of adding grain, as well as the option to adjust the amount, size, and roughness of the effect. Still, Adobe’s grain tends to look about the same from image to image, and doesn’t let you emulate different film stocks like you can with the Nik Collection tools, such as Color Efex and Silver Efex. That said, I use Lightroom Classic’s grain tool far more often than Nik's, simply because it’s quicker. With the latter, I have to export a TIFF and round-trip it back to my gallery. For social posts and my web gallery, Lightroom Classic’s convenience wins out, but if I were making a large print and wanted a filmic look, I’d go with Nik. Lens Profiles also come in handy. The vast majority of lenses for mirrorless camera systems are designed to work best with digital corrections to compensate for optical distortion and a vignette. Most digital cameras apply these automatically for JPGs, but you need to do it yourself for Raws. Lightroom Classic supports the vast majority of first-party and third-party lenses on the market. If you notice barrel or pincushion distortion or darkened corners when editing a photo, the first thing to do is to check if the Lens Profile correction setting is on. I’ve tested hundreds of lenses over the years, and Adobe’s profiles typically match in-camera corrections to a tee. Lightroom puts most of its useful tools in the Develop menu, but a quick right-click on an image opens more options, including the ability to stitch together panoramas or merge bracketed exposures into an HDR image that captures more dynamic range than even the best image sensors can in a single exposure. The right-click menu also shows some organization tools, including the option to create virtual copies of an image (so you can make different edits without taking up more room on your hard drive), group photos into stacks, or add a photo to a Quick Collection. These features are also available from the top menu and via hot keys. Generative AI has earned a bad name among creators, and for good reason. Adobe is as culpable as any AI brand, since you can use Firefly to create images from a text prompt, but the company takes a far more conservative approach than most with Lightroom Classic. Essentially, the app uses AI to improve its existing photo development tools. It doesn't put them in a separate section; instead, it maintains a summary of all AI edits on an image. This works alongside the C2PA Content Credentials system that embeds an image's editing history. It's helpful for photographers entering photo contests or working with agencies that want to see some provenance for a photo. Ultimately, it’s up to you to decide which AI tools are ethical to use and which aren’t. Where you land is likely tied to the type of photography you enjoy—photojournalists and documentarians should likely avoid it altogether, while digital creators, portrait and event photographers, and landscape artists who are used to burning, dodging, and retouching are likely to approach the tools more freely. If you often photograph events, sports, or wildlife, or simply prefer to keep your camera’s drive to Hi+ at all times, the AI Culling feature is for you. Lightroom analyzes sequences of images to identify the ones with the best focus and exposure, discarding the rejects and potentially saving you hours. Modern consumer cameras take photos at rates between 20 and 40fps, and high-end sports cameras like the Sony a9 III can hit 120fps, making it a little too easy to overshoot in the field. Assisted Culling takes some time to run. For instance, it needed about 10 minutes to check a batch of 2,500 images I shot at a local air show for focus, which it winnowed down to around 750 shots. Even so, that represents a net savings in editing time, so I count Assisted Culling as a smart use of AI. Noise Reduction has long been a feature in Lightroom Classic. By default, it removes color (chroma) noise from every image during import, so I won’t blame you if you didn’t notice. Its AI-driven Denoise tool instead attacks luminance noise, and does so more effectively than the old-school Luminance slider (which remains available). Generally, the AI Denoise tool removes grain more effectively while letting detail shine through, whereas the Luminance noise slider can soften an image if used too liberally. The only downside? The Denoise process takes a while to work—I tried it on an ISO 51200 shot of my detail test target captured with the Sony RX1R III, and it took about 20 seconds to analyze and apply noise reduction. Thankfully, you can apply Denoise to a batch of images, so you can grab a cup of coffee while Lightroom churns through a gallery. Lightroom lets you select someone’s face in a photo and find other instances of the person in your catalog. AI Face Recognition can help if you're bad at tagging friends in your snapshots or want to automatically add tags to the important members of a wedding party to make sure you get all the best shots with the bride and groom in frame. To get started, go to the top text menu, select View, and click on People. It performs fine, but I wish it extended to pets. I would also like to see support for descriptive natural language searches, such as "all images of bald eagles.” Lightroom has had a sensor dust removal tool for years, but it previously required you to select another area of the photo as a source. That wasn't a big problem if your dust spot was over a clear blue sky, but for removing actual specks of dirt from a product photo or a skin blemish from a portrait, the tool often fell short. Now, the AI-powered version looks at what you’re trying to remove (or clean up) and the surrounding area. The results are impressive. I shoot a lot of product photos of cameras and lenses with flash, and despite my best efforts, I always end up finding some spots of white dust or dirt that I missed—a matte black subject is unforgiving. Lightroom Classics’s Generative Remove does an outstanding job for this type of work. The tool isn’t just for dust, either. Lightroom can also remove reflections from surfaces, so you can freely shoot through glass even if you forgot to pack a circular polarizing filter. This works well—I tried it with some images I shot through glass at a trade show, and Lightroom cleaned them up. If I hadn't seen the originals, I wouldn't have guessed the images were edited. Finally, the technology can remove people from cityscapes and landscapes, which is handy for architectural and travel photographers who don't want to see tourists. Family photographers who want to send out a holiday card without exes in group shots might use it, too. People removal works quite well for the most part. I noticed that it could occasionally miss people who were diminutive in the frame, but it's easy enough to use a brush to manually tag anything the automatic detection misses, including inanimate distractions like trash cans, for that matter. Did you ever get back home after taking a photo and wish you had used a wider aperture to get the blurry background (bokeh) look? Or wish that you could adjust the look and intensity of bokeh like you can with your iPhone? Lightroom Classic's Lens Blur tool uses the same tech as the Masking tool to identify a subject and soften the background. Even better, it gives you control over the look of the blur, so you can choose between a 5-blade aperture, anamorphic, mirror lens, modern, or soap bubble look, as well as adjust the depth of field and change highlights to cat’s eye shapes. The blur tool can take a while to analyze complex images—as long as 20 seconds in some cases—and doesn’t always get the mapping spot-on initially. If the automatic depth mapping process misses it, you can manually add blur to an area of the frame with a brush tool. I like the results with this tool in some cases. For instance, I had to use an f/11 aperture at 30mm to keep both grave markers in focus in the preceding image, resulting in a deep-focus image. The Lens Blur tool effectively softens both the background and foreground while keeping the subjects in sharp focus. Masking is a powerful tool that lets editors apply selective edits (as opposed to global edits) to photos in Lightroom Classic. In the old days, this was a manual process in Photoshop that required careful use of the Lasso tool to draw an outline over a subject. Adobe now uses its AI engine to identify subjects or objects, the sky, or the background, which you can then edit independently of the rest of the image. It’s handy to be able to apply selective color effects, brighten a subject captured against a backlight, darken a sky in a landscape image to add some drama, or turn a portrait background into nothing to mimic the look of a studio shoot. Because Lightroom Classic’s edits are nondestructive, you'll need to render and export your images for archiving, printing, or uploading. The Export window offers granular control over file naming, resolution, formats, and locations, and supports plug-ins for direct uploads to Flickr, Mylio, Smugmug, and other popular cloud photo storage options. The Export window also lets you create and save presets, which are handy for quick right-click exports of an image. It's also possible to add watermarks. As mentioned, Lightroom Classic also lets you create layouts for printing, photo books with Blurb, or web-based photo galleries. These tools aren’t available in the non-Classic flavor of Lightroom. I run Lightroom Classic on two different systems regularly, a 2022 Mac Studio M1 Max with 64GB of memory for any serious photo work, and an Intel-based 2019 MacBook Pro i9 with 64GB RAM for quick edits when I’m not in my home office. I’m generally happy with how the software performs on both. Aside from waiting for my RAID disk to spin up from sleep, I don’t see any lag when making basic edits or when using advanced tools that run locally. I’ve yet to see a Raw file that can choke Lightroom, including images from cameras like the 100MP Fujifilm GFX100S and the 66MP Sony a7R VI. That said, both of these systems have plenty of RAM. When I tried Lightroom Classic with an 8GB MacBook Neo, I noticed some delay when zooming into photos at full resolution and using the AI Denoise and dust spot removal tools. Lightroom Classic's AI features obviously perform better on newer, more powerful hardware. Michael Muchmore contributed to this article. Final Thoughts Adobe Lightroom Classic - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Lightroom Classic excels at pretty much everything you might want to do in the digital darkroom: basic retouching, granular exposure and color adjustments, effective noise reduction, and much more. And it does all this non-destructively. Moreover, we count its comprehensive keyword and sorting tools, consistent and segmented user experience, local catalog storage, and reasonably useful AI tools as major strengths. Yes, its subscription costs can add up over time, but Lightroom Classic easily delivers enough value and innovations to remain an Editors' Choice winner, alongside Lightroom, its cloud-based sibling that comes with the same subscription. Meanwhile, Photoshop, another Editors' Choice winner, is the undisputed leader in photo manipulation. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Series 11: Is the Upgrade Actually Worth It?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.65
Table of Contents Apple is going even harder on AI and health tracking with the Apple Watch Series 12, which packs a range of new features enabled by a faster S11 chip and an entirely redesigned health-sensing system. However, the Series 12 looks virtually identical to its predecessor and shares the same estimated battery life. Do these underlying updates add up to a smartwatch that actually feels new? After testing it side by side with the Series 11, here's how the two generations compare to help you decide whether it's worth the upgrade. Full Specs | Apple Watch Series 12 | Apple Watch Series 11 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S10 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 54.5 hours (tested) | 43 hours (tested) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: A Higher Premium for Larger Sizes While year-over-year pricing remains mostly unchanged, the Series 12 gets a bit pricier if you prefer a larger watch. Like the Series 11, the base 42mm aluminum GPS model starts at $399. However, jumping to the 46mm size now costs an extra $50, compared with the $30 premium on the Series 11. Upgrading to cellular remains a $100 add-on across both generations. Titanium models with cellular also keep their previous price points at $699 (42mm) and $749 (46mm). If you want something even more premium, the Series 12 introduces a new ceramic finish for $899 (42mm) and $949 (46mm). Winner: Tie Design: A New Ceramic Option and Fresh Finish Colors The two Apple Watches look nearly identical, though the aluminum and titanium Series 12 are just a millimeter wider and 1.5 grams heavier than their Series 11 counterparts. The color choices are slightly different, with the aluminum Series 12 swapping out silver and rose gold finishes for light gold and bronze, and titanium adding a radiant gold. Then there's the ceramic version, in white or blue. It adds another millimeter to the watch's height, width, and depth, and another six to eight grams in weight. Either way, you have more options with the Series 12. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 AI Features: S11 Chip Powers On-Device Audio Intelligence The Series 12 uses Apple's new S11 chip to enable Apple Intelligence features that the Series 11 lacks.
