The biggest addition is an upcoming feature called Audio Intelligence, which lets the Series 12 listen to everything around you all day, providing summaries of conversations and even rewinding parts to help you catch up. It can also recognize important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, and notify you if you're hard of hearing. Apple claims the S11 chip protects privacy with hardware-isolated onboard audio processing. It also says Audio Intelligence doesn't identify speakers and doesn't include identifying information in its output. If you're still uncertain, though, you can just turn the feature off. The Series 11 doesn't support Audio Intelligence at all, but it still has all the standard hands-free Siri functionality and other Apple Intelligence features. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Health and Fitness: Frequent Heart Tracking and Daily Readiness Score The Series 12 makes some big leaps in fitness and health tracking features. Apple has reworked its optical and electrical heart rate sensors, and now the watch measures your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day instead of only periodically, as the Series 11 does. The new watch also measures heart rate variability up to 24 times more often, with a new section of the Heart Rate app dedicated to the data. Apple claims it's the most accurate heart rate tracking in a wearable. Apple is also taking a more holistic approach to fitness with a new Apple Intelligence-powered readiness score that provides a number from 0 to 10 assessing your energy for the day, with a recommendation to go all-out, pace yourself, or rest and recover. The readiness score is exclusive to the Series 12, though the Series 11 offers other holistic scores for sleep and mindfulness. Outside of the improved heart rate sensors and readiness score, the Series 12 and Series 11 are equally equipped for general health and fitness. Both support on-demand blood oxygen and ECG readings, keep tabs on your sleep, and offer all the other fitness-tracking tools. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Battery Life: S11 Efficiency Yields Superior Real-World Endurance Apple is always conservative in its battery life estimates, and both the Series 11 and the Series 12 have the same 24-hour estimate. In our real-world testing, the Series 11 lasted 43 hours with the always-on display enabled. The Series 12 did even better. The new chip and health-sensing system make a big difference in efficiency, helping the Series 12 power through 54.5 hours in our testing before it needed to be plugged in. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Durability: Tougher Ceramic Shield 2 Glass for Aluminum Models The Series 12 has the same IP6X dustproof rating and is water-resistant to up to 164 feet, just like the Series 11. The aluminum version is a bit tougher, though, thanks to its new Ceramic Shield 2 glass (different from the ceramic case option), which Apple claims is 60% more durable than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Connectivity: Identical Wireless Specs and Cellular Options Both models pack identical connectivity specs: dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.3, L1 GPS, and Apple's Ultra Wideband chip for precision phone tracking. Choose a cellular model, and you get the exact same 5G and LTE radios regardless of which generation you buy. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Series 12 The Series 12 delivers where it matters most, making it a far more satisfying upgrade than the Series 11 was over the Series 10. You get significantly smarter health sensors, longer battery life, and new AI tools—all without a base-price increase. Unless you find a massive discount on last year's model, the Series 12 is well worth the money.

item.title: iOS 27 Is Reportedly Freezing iPhones After a Few Quick Swipes: Here's the Fix
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.57
Apple’s iOS 27 software began rolling out last weekend, and 9to5Mac has spotted a bug that freezes iPhones after a series of quick swipes across the home screen. Not every user may experience the issue, but for those who do, the freezing occurs when you swipe down from the top left of the home screen to draw the Notification Center, and before it launches, you quickly swipe down from the top right to open the Control Center. When the screen freezes, you’ll see the Notification Center’s Camera and Torch icons stuck on top of your screen, 9to5Mac says. I couldn’t replicate the issue on my iPhone 14 running iOS 27, but if you're facing it, there’s a simple fix: force-restart your iPhone. To do so, press and quickly release the Volume Up button on the left, then do the same with the Volume Down button, and finally hold the Power button on the right until the Apple logo appears. This should reboot your iPhone and restore normalcy, the report adds. On iPhones, a force-restart is different from a regular restart, which requires you to hold the Volume Up and Power buttons together and swipe across the Power Off slider that appears. Since screen-freezing issues can prevent your taps and swipes from registering on the display, a force restart using the physical buttons is the easiest way out. iOS 27 users have also been sharing ways to freeze iPhones using a few other methods. As it happens with major iOS releases each year, they have also been complaining about battery drain after upgrading to iOS 27. Apple’s iOS 26 release drew similar reactions last year, and the company responded, saying it’s quite normal for major software updates to temporarily affect battery life. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Your Computer Might Demand Your Age Soon, No Matter Where You Live
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.31
Age verification laws have moved beyond social media and porn. Three US states have passed laws requiring operating systems to collect users' ages, and the EFF's Aaron Mackey says he expects Apple, Google, and Microsoft to mandate age verification nationwide. Congress is discussing a federal law to this end, too. Come 2027, you might even have to scan your face or upload a photo ID to prove you're a legal adult before you can use your computer. This new front in the age verification battle comes after more than two dozen states passed laws targeting adult websites like PornHub, and Utah started cracking down on VPNs. Major OS developers aren't pushing back, but the open-source community has been vocal about the risks to your online privacy and the future of the web. The California Ripple Effect: How One State Law Controls the Globe Starting in 2027, California's Digital Age Assurance Act will require operating systems, including Windows, macOS, Android, and ChromeOS, to ask users for their age during device setup and share an age range with apps. California's amended law now exempts Linux distributions, in a win for the open-source community. Depending on how future laws evolve, that process could eventually involve government IDs, credit cards, or biometric verification. Aaron Mackey, deputy legal director at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, warns the effects won't stop at California’s borders. Because tech companies rarely build separate operating systems for different states, he says these systems will likely be rolled out "for everyone who uses [operating systems], including the billions of folks outside of California." Colorado followed California by passing a similar law, and Illinois did as well. The three states are unlikely to remain alone for long. Similar bills are advancing in other states, while the proposed federal Parents Decide Act would, if passed, expand age verification at the operating-system level nationwide. At WWDC 2026, Apple discussed age-based content restrictions across apps and websites for child accounts, which are mandatory for users aged 13 and under. You might have to prove your age to avoid this requirement, too. Apple recently introduced mandatory age verification for new accounts in Texas, and more states are likely to follow. "The open-source community was rightly anxious about how they would ever comply with this," comments Mackey on the amendment. However, that isn't the end of the story. "At the end of the day, this sort of age-gating regime will go into effect in January," he says, pointing out the requirement still applies to macOS and Windows computers, as well as phones and tablets. He says Apple, Google, and Microsoft likely won't implement different age verification systems in each state, but rather a single national system for practicality. Privacy advocates, open-source developers, and lawmakers are now battling over a question that could reshape the future of computing: Should your computer know your age before you can use it? Here's what you need to know so far. Where You Live (or Don't) Matters: The 3 States Leading the Push As of this writing, three states have OS age verification laws: - California has the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It applies to closed-source operating systems such as macOS and Windows. California's law no longer applies to Linux and other open-source operating systems after AB-1856 passed in September, 2026. - Colorado has bill SB26-051, which takes effect on July 1, 2028. It exempts open-source operating systems, such as Linux. - Illinois has the Children's Online Social Media Safety Act (HB5511), which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2028. Illinois' law applies to Linux and other open-source operating systems, unlike the laws in California and Colorado. California’s law is the first and serves as a model for other states. It requires that operating systems ask for your age when you set them up. Your OS must then share an age bracket signal with the applications running on your computer. Applications will see one of the following age ranges: under 13, 13-16, 16-18, or over 18. Application developers are then “deemed to have actual knowledge of the age range of the user.” They would have a legal duty to comply with any laws requiring different treatment of minors and could not plead ignorance of the device user's age. An application might need to restrict access or features for users under 18, in accordance with other laws, including the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA), which requires online services to handle the personal information of users under the age of 13 differently. This could affect dating, gaming, and social media apps, for example. California’s law doesn’t affect websites. However, a proposed California law would extend the age signal to the web. Face Scans, Passports, or Honor System? How Age Verification Will Work Under California’s law, as written, your operating system must ask for your age during the device setup process. Your operating system will accept that age without requiring identification. Attestation—in other words, simply declaring your age—is sufficient proof. Nichole Rocha, a data privacy attorney who represents Children Now, a California-based organization that backs the law, tells me that California’s bill was designed to protect privacy. “There’s no requirement for the uploading of a government ID, and that was intentional on the part of the author, [California state assembly member] Buffy Wicks,” she says. “I think the bill strikes an appropriate balance. You see other states requiring the uploading of government IDs, and that’s incredibly invasive,” says Rocha. She argues that research shows parents set up devices for minors and will enter a child's age accurately at that time. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification."
However, the EFF believes that operating system providers such as Apple, Google, and Microsoft will require more personal information. “While the law on paper doesn’t require strict age verification, I think in practice compliance will look a lot more like age verification,” Mackey says. He points out that there are fines and legal consequences if minors bypass age checks, and that companies will want to prevent minors from lying. “That involves more invasive forms of age verification that adult websites implement,” he says. That could mean providing a credit card, a facial scan, or a government ID during OS setup to verify that an adult was involved in the process. Microsoft's age verification system will cover both unverified and verified ages, with the latter requiring a facial scan or government document. Beyond California: The Federal Push to Track OS Users On the federal level, the Parents Decide Act, introduced in Congress in April, would require OS-level age checks in all states if it passes. Specifically, the proposed law says operating system providers must "require any user of the operating system to provide the date of birth of the user" to set up an account or use the OS. Adults would also have to provide their date of birth. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would also need to “issue regulations on how operating system providers can… verify the date of birth of a parent or legal guardian” if a minor is setting up a device. This could include government identification checks during device setup; implementation details would be up to the FTC. Similar language appears in other proposed bills. The Kids Online Safety Act, introduced in the Senate in 2025, would require the Secretary of Commerce to "conduct a study evaluating the most technologically feasible methods... to verify age at the device or operating system level." "I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states.”
Rocha doesn’t expect the federal government to take action. “Every year, things pop up in Congress that never get signed, right?” she says. “We just haven’t seen anything meaningful happen at the federal level in this space since the mid-1990s.” The EFF is concerned about the current legislative environment, however. "This is a trend we're seeing," says Mackey. "Lawmakers don't understand the technology, and they don't understand that these proposals are unpopular." Other states followed California and Colorado. As mentioned, Illinois legislators passed the Children’s Online Social Media Safety Act, HB5511. It requires the person setting up a device to declare only an age, without requiring proof of identity. “I hope that by doing privacy-protective and nuanced legislation in California, we’re serving as a model for the rest of the states,” says Rocha. Some states might require more personal identification. New York’s senate, for example, is discussing Bill 8102, which will require operating systems to determine user ages via “commercially reasonable age assurance methods.” Behind the Code: How Apps Will Silently Request Your Age Apps will get your age range from your operating system using an application programming interface (API). In other words, they’ll ask the operating system for your age range and get a response. Major operating system vendors are already implementing compliant APIs. Google offers the Play Age Signals API for Android apps on Google Play, while Apple offers the Declared Age Range API for iOS and macOS. Microsoft is adding a Windows Age API to Windows 11. The system software used by many Linux distributions now includes an age field for user accounts, too. Moving the Gatekeeper From Websites to Your Operating System The legislation discussed above moves age verification from the application or website layer to the device or operating system level. PornHub has urged Apple, Google, and Microsoft to implement OS-level age verification. With OS-level age verification, adult online services like PornHub would not need to confirm visitors' ages by collecting documentation themselves. Instead, the operating system would have that obligation. PornHub is already using Apple's iOS signals to verify visitors' ages in the UK. However, as mentioned, California law does not require the operating system to relay page signals from the web browser to a website. That’s surprising, given that age-verification laws in many states have targeted adult websites. Rocha says California’s lawmakers were trying to address the web in the original law, but “ran out of time.” California's Bill AB 1856 extended the age verification requirement to internet websites owned by application developers. For example, the law would apply to both Facebook's app and website. Web browser developers are already working on age-verification standards. Google’s Chromium and Apple’s Safari both support the Digital Credentials API to share government identification information with websites. If you save a driver's license or other government ID to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet on your phone, you can securely share your credentials with websites. Theoretically, you could use the same process to share an age you provided to your desktop operating system with a website, too. Why Open-Source Developers Are Fighting State Legislatures In addition to affecting Apple’s iOS and macOS, Google’s Android and ChromeOS, and Microsoft's Windows, some of these laws impact smaller open-source community operating systems, including Linux distributions. The open-source community is discussing age verification laws, and some projects have already commented publicly. GrapheneOS, a privacy-focused Android fork, has announced its intention to “remain usable by anyone around the world without requiring personal information, identification, or an account.” The project adds, “If GrapheneOS devices can't be sold in a region due to their regulations, so be it." “I think the open-source community is rightly very concerned about what’s happening here,” Mackey says of these laws. He points out that many open-source operating systems prioritize privacy and don’t want to collect user data or engage in surveillance. California now exempts operating systems distributed "under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software" after the passage of AB-1856. The EFF is pleased with this change, writing that "The bill is narrower now than it was before, and lawmakers clearly responded to concerns raised by EFF and the broader open-source community." It still takes issue with the concept of age-gating, however. Colorado's bill SB26-051, signed into law on June 4, 2026, exempts Linux distributions and other open-source software. Specifically, the law says it doesn't apply to "an operating system provider... that distributes an operating system... under license terms that permit a recipient to copy, redistribute, and modify the software." The Illinois age verification law, however, applies to Linux distributions and other open-source operating systems. Could VPNs Be Forced to Block Unverified Devices? California’s law doesn’t mention VPNs. However, under other laws or regulations, a VPN application might need to block access based on OS-level age signals. Or applications and websites might legally need to check the OS-level age signal to confirm user ages. A New Era of Hardware Tracking Although I spoke to lawyers for this piece, I’m not a lawyer. I’m a tech geek who’s been using computers and operating systems for decades. As far as I can see, there are two types of laws under discussion: those that ask for your age and those that require proof of your age. California’s law, as well as the laws passed in Colorado and Illinois, accept whatever you provide during device setup. This imposes additional legal requirements on operating system providers, including open-source communities, to design interfaces that collect users' ages. Rocha summarizes the California law’s approach: “We are going to try and protect as many children as possible in the most privacy-protecting way possible. And there will probably be some kids who get around the system, but the vast majority of kids will be protected by this.” Mackey is skeptical that you'll just be able to enter an age without any proof, however. He expects many companies will require more information to protect themselves from legal liability, despite good-faith exemptions in the amended bill. "I think it will be more invasive," he says. "We'll just have to see." “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely. It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws."
Legislation like the proposed bill in New York could require you to prove your age with a credit card, facial scan, government ID, or another method when setting up your device. A federal law could enforce this nationwide, depending on what the FTC requires. Future operating systems may require biometrics or identity document verification during device setup. I’m not a fan of either type of law. I don’t believe governments should require operating systems—especially small, open-source projects—to verify their users' personal information, or risk legal liability. I want privacy-centric operating systems that don’t collect any user data to continue existing. “The open internet as we know it allows people to access information anonymously, privately, and securely,” says Mackey. “It’s in danger by lawmakers who have good intentions but are writing broad laws.” Mackey doesn’t think these laws are inevitable, though. “My hope is that people are energized by this [debate] and recognize the opportunity that we can push back,” he says. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Which Claude Do You Use? Cowork and Design Move Into One Simple Interface
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.10
Anthropic’s Claude interface is unnecessarily complicated: Cowork, Chat, and Design are available in different places, but an imminent update will make it easier to use. Soon, Claude itself will automatically determine the best next step in response to a prompt. Anthropic says, "Claude can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have." This change comes after Anthropic found users were frustrated by the separation and often unsure which tool to use. Some projects started through Cowork weren't available in its other tools, and vice versa. Combining into a single interface will also give you easier access to Claude's creative tools, including the existing Design option and new Docs and Slides features. Docs allows you to make text documents using Claude models to generate the prose, while Slides makes presentations. Claude will draft each slide for you, and you can present them directly from the app or download them as a PDF or PowerPoint file. Claude Design launched earlier this year and focuses on visual work, such as one-pagers, graphics, or prototype documents. Claude Design, Docs, and Slides all remain in beta and will be available through a new Output button under the prompt box. This will also house Artifacts, Anthropic's shareable tools created by other users. These changes will first appear for Pro and Max subscribers, with their rollout set for the coming weeks across desktop, mobile, and the web. Free users will be able to access the updated platform at a later date. The same applies to those on Team plans and Enterprise logins, although an exact rollout window remains unclear. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: The iPhone 18 Pro Has a Secret Weapon That Busts Fake AI Photos
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.89
Fake, AI-generated, and manipulated images are everywhere. It's gotten to the point where your feed is inundated with fake photos and videos whenever you open a social media app. It's as if everyone can make Industrial Light & Magic-quality CG without the need for skill (or in many cases, taste). Because of this, the photo industry developed C2PA, a standard that digitally signs photos at the time of capture and tracks edits. Of course, it didn't take too long for Apple to add a similar feature to the iPhone, but in typical Apple fashion, the company decided to develop its own proprietary tech called Reference Image. I'm here to break down how Reference Image works, why you need the iPhone 18 Pro (or 18 Pro Max) to use it, and how it integrates with photo-editing workflows. What Is Reference Image and How Does It Catch Edits? Reference Image is a new feature that's exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. It embeds an original, unedited version of an image into every picture you take. The idea being that anyone with an iPhone, iPad, or Mac can look at your photo and see exactly how it's been edited versus what the camera captured. If someone sends you a photo that looks unreal or too good to be true, you can use Reference Image to compare it with what the camera actually saw. Reference Image is hardware-based, so it won't be added to older phones. Furthermore, it doesn't work with every camera on the iPhone 18 Pro; it's restricted to the main (1x, 24mm F1.48) lens. This is because it encrypts the original image on a sensor level, and the 0.5x (13mm), 4x (100mm), and front lenses haven't yet been redesigned to support it. Additionally, you'll need to go into the iPhone's Settings menu and enable Reference Image if you want to use it—it's disabled by default. Once enabled, Reference Image works transparently and thankfully doesn't take away any camera features. It supports Portrait mode, Photographic Styles, Apple ProRaw, and its other computational features. And it doesn't stop you from editing photos—you can still use Apple's Photos app to adjust color, exposure, or use generative AI. The twist is that if you send an edited photo to a friend, they can check and see what you've changed. It takes away the question of whether something actually happened, whether an image was created with generative AI tools, or whether the truth lies somewhere in between. At launch, you can view the original Reference Image on Apple devices only—iPhones, iPads, and Mac computers. That capability should expand in time. Apple already announced that developers will be able to add support for these platforms, and I expect it's only a matter of time before a toolkit rolls out for Windows systems and web apps. After all, the idea is that anyone can check the Reference Image to see if and how an image has been manipulated. Living in a Post-Truth Feed: Why Original Raw Data Still Matters I see Reference Image as a net positive. Tools that show if and how a photo has been manipulated are important. Generative AI is here, and in the short time since it went mainstream, it has gotten good enough to create photos out of nothing. Early AI images had flaws, people with the wrong number of fingers, signage with gibberish text, etc., but the latest engines create photos that can fool even the best-trained eye. We've been catapulted into a post-truth world, and it happened in the blink of an eye. Look, I won't pretend that documentary photography and photojournalism represent the objective truth; the photographer makes subjective decisions on what to leave out of the frame, which is enough to change a narrative or take a moment out of context. Lighting, angles, and shutter speed can be used to craft a narrative, too. These rules also apply to the darkroom. Regardless of whether you're working with an enlarger or software, there are edits that are acceptable, per journalistic standards. In the film days, you could dodge and burn when making a print, brightening or darkening an exposure, and in the digital era, it's typically fine to adjust exposure, open shadows, crunch blacks, or change white balance. But at the end of the day, the finished photo is still what the lens captured, recorded either onto digital silicon or photochemical film, and turned into a JPG or a print. Generative AI is cloud cuckoo land. Reference Image vs. C2PA: How Does Apple's Proprietary Tech Compare With Standards? The photo industry, in large, has recognized this. It's incongruous, but Adobe, the company that made Photoshop a verb, is adding AI tools to its image software and, at the same time, leading the charge on image authentication. Adobe has signed on to the C2PA standard, a system that embeds a copy of an unedited image into photos that have been digitally manipulated and lets anyone drop it into the Content Credentials web app to view the original image, along with a list of the edits that were made. Adobe builds the tracking feature into Lightroom and Photoshop, so you can use the editing tools you're used to while still proving you used a camera to capture the moment. The camera industry is on board, too. The C2PA standard and its practical implementation, Content Credentials, don't have universal support as of yet, but it's included in pro cameras from Canon, Leica, Nikon, and Sony, while Fujifilm and Panasonic promise to add it down the road. Apple has its reasons for building its own tool instead of simply adding C2PA signing to the iPhone. For one, Apple's tech works at a deeper level. Some digital cameras with Content Credentials, including the Leica M11-P, sign images with hardware-based encryption, while other brands use software-based signing. But none go as far as Apple's sensor-based approach. We've seen some examples of C2PA being spoofed; one researcher was able to fool the Nikon Z6III into signing an AI-generated image last year. Reference Image's sensor-level encryption is a lot harder to crack, at least on paper. And while Reference Image is currently exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, the system can work hand in hand with C2PA. You can take a signed ProRaw image into Adobe Lightroom Classic or Photoshop, edit it, and create a JPG with the Content Credentials breadcrumb for sharing. The wrinkle there is that the image you export won't include the embedded Reference Image. But viewers will be able to view the edits you made in Adobe on the Content Credentials site, and if the provenance of your photo is called into question, you can always revert to the original file on your iPhone and show the Reference Image. That's one of the advantages of Adobe's nondestructive approach to image processing—you're not changing the original image when you make edits, you're creating a new one. The Catch: Apple's Walled Garden Strikes Again While I'm happy that Apple recognizes the importance of provenance, I'm a little disappointed that it bucked an existing standard. The company decided to go with its own tech rather than join forces with the brands that have adopted C2PA—Adobe, the first name in creative software; Leica, the first name in photography; Sony, the only camera brand trusted by the Associated Press; and industry stalwarts Canon and Nikon. I'm also a little bummed that it's only included on one of the iPhone 18 Pro's four lenses, and that it's an opt-in feature. Still, the logic and technology behind Reference Image are sound, and with the rise of AI slop, it's a concept whose time has come. Here's hoping that it will expand to every lens when it's time for Apple to trot out the iPhone 19 Pro this time next year. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: $2,195 for Smart Glasses? Snap's New Specs Are an Engineering Marvel...With Two Massive Flaws
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.89
Snap officially launched its new Specs, lifting the curtain on a surprisingly robust feature set and a high-profile lineup of launch partners. With self-contained processing powering motion tracking, environment scanning, and gesture controls, these might be the most technically ambitious smart glasses on the market—easily outpacing the $799 Meta Ray-Ban Display in pure hardware sophistication. But at $2,195, Snap faces monumental hurdles before its bleeding-edge tech can win over everyday buyers. I’ll give the Specs a rigorous hands-on test once a pair lands in PC Labs. For now, here's a close look at how they work, what they can do, and where they fit in an increasingly chaotic wearable ecosystem. Finally, Waveguide Glasses Free From Your Phone The Specs are waveguide smart glasses, which means they have a built-in display that uses special patterns etched into the lenses to project an OLED-based image into your eyes while still letting you see clearly through them. The display is full-color, a rare feature that few other glasses of this type share. They work independently, handling all processing and interactions on the device, unlike other waveguide glasses I’ve tested that require a physical tether or wireless connection to a phone. The Specs need an internet connection, but that’s it. Outward-facing cameras feed the Specs data for spatial processing, enabling them to track your position with six degrees of freedom (6DOF), map your surroundings, and display interface elements that respond to where you are and what you’re looking at. Those cameras also enable hand tracking and gesture controls, giving the Specs the same kind of augmented and mixed reality experiences as the Apple Vision Pro ($3,499), the Samsung Galaxy XR ($1,799.99), and the upcoming XReal Aura. All three devices are much chunkier and obstruct your vision more than the Specs; the Vision Pro and Galaxy XR are full standalone headsets with mini-OLED panels that completely replace your view. The Aura uses bulkier prism displays that can occlude your view of the outside world, along with a separate, smartphone-sized control box physically tethered to the glasses with a wire. The Specs are designed to be worn out and about, using their display to provide useful information based on the world around you, wherever you are. Mixed reality headsets and prism display glasses, on the other hand, are intended to be used relatively stationary, or in a controlled environment; you don’t want to cross the street while wearing them. Incidentally, while I’ve denounced cameras in smart glasses in the past, the Specs actually justify them because they power spatial processing and head tracking, not just photography, which is better done on a phone. Waveguide displays have traditionally had a very limited field of view, meaning they can only show an image in a relatively small box in your vision. The Meta Ray-Ban Display, for example, has a 20-degree field of view and a resolution of 600 by 600. That’s puny compared with prism display smart glasses like the Viture Beast ($549), which have a 58-degree field of view and a 1,920-by-1,200 resolution. The Specs’ waveguide display swings for prism territory with a 51-degree field of view. Waveguide displays offer completely unimpeded vision, unlike prism displays, so if they can catch up in size, color, and detail, it might be a fundamental game-changer for all display-equipped smart glasses. The apparent trade-off that helps enable the big picture is that the Specs are very chunky and heavy. I’ll get to that detail in a bit. The Specs' on-the-go concept pairs with one of Snap’s biggest announcements around the launch, the reveal of an optional charging case with built-in cellular connectivity. The charging case uses Verizon’s network to keep the Specs connected without your phone or a wi-fi network. The case adds $200 to the Specs’ $2,195 price, with data plans at $10 per month for Verizon customers and $20 per month for non-Verizon customers. Even if the cellular case is optional, the Specs are the first pair of standalone smart glasses to incorporate a cellular connection into their concept. Before this, the only other example was an eSIM-equipped prototype RayNeo showed off at CES. Software Partners Bet Big on Lenses All of this tech isn’t very useful without software to take advantage of it, so Snap also showed off the collaborations and software partners it's working with. Specs use their own software platform that supports third-party development and publishing of apps known as Lenses. Snap showed off an NBA basketball trainer Lens that analyzes your shots, a TripAdvisor Lens that shows nearby reviews, a Spotify Lens that integrates music playback into the glasses, and an augmented reality game Lens from HBO Max promoting the upcoming Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone show. Besides the larger commercial partners, Snap highlighted some individual “visionaries” with their own Lenses based on their work, including a book-augmenting experience by Library Science founder Kaia Gerber, a classic tabletop dominoes game using two synced pairs of Specs by NBA All-Star Jimmy Butler, and a meditation tool from Korean actress and model Jung Ho-yeon. The Specs have their own built-in set of features, and are functional even without third-party Lenses. Snap didn’t highlight many of the individual features, but it offered glimpses of its own navigation and video call Lenses. It also confirmed that its web browser officially supports streaming video from HBO Max and YouTube, showing whatever you’re watching on the virtual equivalent of a 115-inch screen viewed from 10 feet away. As expected, AI features are built into the Specs as well, and here Snap is getting majorly ambitious. The company announced Specs Intelligence, an “anticipatory AI service” integrated into the glasses’ AI assistant that tries to perform tasks and show you information before you need it, without you having to ask. To quote the press release, “Before a meeting, it could highlight decisions to make, questions to ask, and things to remember.” Snap says that its employees can’t access any personal information used with Specs Intelligence and that the data won’t be used to train AI models or serve personalized ads. I’ve explained before why I’m skeptical of these claims from any company that uses AI, especially when visual data is also being processed. Two Huge Flaws Snap Can't Ignore Even if I’m wary of Snap Intelligence, I won’t call it a negative for the Specs, because they have two much bigger problems standing in the way of their success: 1. A Sky-High Price Tag The first, and by far the biggest hurdle the Specs face is the price. The glasses are $2,195, which is absurdly expensive regardless of how incredible the tech built into them is. It’s not quite Vision Pro bad, but it’s several hundred dollars more than the Galaxy XR ($1,800). With the cellular case included, they cost as much as three pairs of Meta Ray-Ban Displays. 2. Style and Comfort Take a Hit The second hurdle is the physical design. I won’t mince words: These are ugly glasses, with a chunky, glossy black frame flanked by two massive rectangular rims on the end pieces. They aren’t as bad as their predecessor, the bulkier Spectacles ‘24, but those were strictly development hardware and not intended for public use. I’m sorry, but even a world-famous fashion model can’t avoid looking at least kind of like a dork wearing these. The problem goes beyond style and into wearability. The glasses are so big that they can bend your ears. They’re also heavy, weighing about 4.7 ounces. That’s twice as heavy as the Meta Ray-Ban Display (2.5 ounces), and four times heavier than the Even G2 (1.3 ounces). If you’re going to wear smart glasses out and about for any amount of time, they have to be comfortable, and that looks like a problem for the Specs. High-Tech Eyewear Worth Watching A personal heads-up display you can use while walking around is one of the most appealing and promising concepts smart glasses present, but it hasn’t quite clicked just yet. I’ve reviewed several pairs of waveguide glasses, and so far, none have come together in a way I’m willing to wholeheartedly recommend without some major caveats. Monochrome green displays, awkward interfaces, and steep learning curves are the norm. In terms of sheer capabilities, the Specs seem to blow away everything I've seen so far. The tech used here seems incredible, and I’d love to see it become common across all display-equipped smart glasses. Testing them will tell whether all that tech justifies the sky-high price. If you want to take the plunge and have the cash to spare, the Specs are now available for preorder with a $200 refundable deposit and are expected to ship later this fall. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Cricket Wireless Starts Offering 5G Home Broadband
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.78
AT&T’s Cricket Wireless is starting to use its own brand to offer a 5G home broadband service. The new service is called Cricket 5G Home Internet and can start as low as $45 per month for existing customers with the carrier who enroll into auto-pay. The company is touting “predictable pricing, no annual contracts” and an easy setup process, with download speeds ranging from 90 to 300 Mbps. Cricket’s home internet isn’t fiber, but what’s called fixed-wireless access (FWA), which has been growing in popularity across the US. The internet technology uses excess 5G network capacity to deliver broadband-like speeds to the customer’s home. In 2023, AT&T began offering its own solution in AT&T Internet Air to compete with rival offerings from T-Mobile and Verizon. It looks like AT&T is now expanding the 5G home broadband to Cricket Wireless. That said, Cricket Wireless has been spotted offering a variant of AT&T Internet Air as early as November 2024 at certain stores, according to Wave7 Research. "This has been covered and documented in every Wave7 prepaid report for the last 22 months," says the research firm's principal Jeff Moore. Today, Cricket Wireless is highlighting the internet offering as a way for customers to save money. According to our best mobile network rankings, Cricket Wireless offers “the best average price per line per month at just a few cents over $30.” Cricket added: “Customers increasingly want the convenience of having their wireless and home internet services with one provider, and Cricket's new bundle offers a simple, value-packed way to bring those connections together.” For new customers, the company is also offering the home 5G internet service along with a Cricket Wireless cellular plan as a bundle for $75 per month. As a standalone offering, Cricket 5G Home Internet costs $65 per month without auto-pay. Cricket 5G Home Internet offers unlimited data and uploads of between 8 to 30 Mbps. But you can expect a latency between 30 to 65 milliseconds, or what’s higher than the 9 millisecond average for home broadband, according to Speedtest.net parent Ookla. You can check out our review of AT&T Internet Air to get an idea of the service. For faster, gigabit speeds, Cricket has been offering "Quantum Fiber from AT&T" in select areas. Cricket 5G Home Internet isn’t available everywhere; interested users can check by visiting the company’s service map. Another caveat is that customers need to pay a one-time $49.99 fee for the gateway equipment to receive the 5G access at home. But set up takes less than 15 minutes, the company says. "In rare cases, if your usage is contributing to congestion on the network, Cricket will greatly reduce your speed for a min. of 30 min," the carrier also noted. "Cricket may temporarily slow data speeds if the network is busy." Editor's note: This story has been updated to note Wave7 Research previously spotted Cricket offering AT&T Internet Air back in 2024. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Avira Free Antivirus for Mac Review: Good Baseline Protection Gated by Paywalls
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.69
Windows has evolved over the decades, but it still requires patching to shore up security. By comparison, macOS was built from the ground up with security in mind. Macs do still get hit by malware, even ransomware. You need antivirus protection for your Macs, but you don’t necessarily have to pay for it. Avira Free Antivirus for Mac doesn't cost a thing. If you can afford to pay for protection, though, our Editors’ Choice winners do quite a bit more. Bitdefender Antivirus Plus and Norton AntiVirus Plus both earn perfect or near-perfect lab scores and include powerful security features beyond the basics, making them our top picks for protecting your Mac. Most Mac antivirus apps require macOS 10.15 or later. This only makes sense, given that Apple keeps adding security enhancements. Avira supports macOS versions back to 10.15 (Catalina). If you're stuck using an old operating system, you may need to consider a different Mac antivirus. Bitdefender, ClamXAV, K7 AntiVirus, and Panda offer support dating back to Yosemite (10.10). Yosemite was released 12 years ago, so one of these could be a better fit for an older Mac. There's a big range of prices for Mac-based antivirus support. At the high end, McAfee Total Protection lists at $89.99 per year to protect one Mac, the same as Intego One. One common pricing plan among antivirus apps we've reviewed is just under $40 per year for one license. ESET Cyber Security, G Data Antivirus, and Trend Micro Antivirus are in that group. Another cluster at just under $50 includes Bitdefender, F-Secure Internet Security, Panda Dome Essential, and Webroot Essentials. And then there’s Norton, which runs just under $60. As for Avira, you don’t have to pay one red cent. Like AVG AntiVirus and Avast One Free, it's totally free. Gen Digital owns Avira. Gen also owns Avast, AVG, LifeLock, Norton, and a host of other companies. This giant collection didn’t happen all at once. In 2016, Avast acquired AVG. Before long, the two product lines were using the same antivirus engine. Around the same time, Norton acquired LifeLock. In 2020, Norton acquired Avira. Shortly thereafter, Avira acquired BullGuard, but within a couple of years, Norton shut down the BullGuard brand and migrated its customers to Norton AntiVirus. Rounding out the collection, Norton acquired Avast/AVG in 2021 and created Gen as the parent company for all of them. Since 2023, Avast, AVG, and Norton have all relied on the same antivirus engine, called the Gen Stack. Not surprisingly, all three earned precisely the same scores in my hands-on malware blocking test. When I tested Avira Free Security on Windows, Avira scored the same as the other three. It’s not officially using the Gen Stack, but it still lined right up with the rest. As with the Windows version, Avira installs quickly on the Mac. The installer suggests you might prefer to purchase a license for Avira Prime, the first of many upsell attempts. After installation, Avira offers to run a Smart Scan. I skipped that initial scan to avoid any possible interference with timing tests. A redesign several years ago brought the macOS antivirus closer in appearance to the Windows version. The main window features a simple menu down the left, like Avira Free Security. But where the Windows apps just have Status, Security, Privacy, and Performance down the left side, the macOS edition adds two or three submenu items below each. As in the Windows edition, the rest of the window features oversized icons representing Security, Privacy, and Performance, with a button to run what Avira calls a Smart scan. More about the Smart scan later. When evaluating Windows antivirus utilities for malware protection, I rely on various testing apps I've coded and refined over the years. I have nothing similar for macOS, as my many hand-coded testing tools (and my coding skills in general) are Windows-only. For Mac antivirus, I rely heavily on independent testing labs to determine which antivirus tools are most capable. Two of the four independent antivirus testing labs I follow report on macOS antivirus. The experts at AV-Test Institute rate antivirus utilities on three criteria: how well they protect against malware, how little they impact performance, and how carefully they avoid interfering with usability by flagging valid programs as malicious. With six points available for Protection, Performance, and Usability, the maximum score is 18. In this lab’s latest report, all but two of the tested apps reached 18 points. Both Trend Micro and Avira took poor scores in the essential protection test, 4.5 for Trend Micro and 3.5 for Avira. Avira’s total of 16.5 is the lowest among the tested apps. AV-Comparatives rates each antivirus app on its all-important ability to defend against Mac-oriented malware, assigning a simple percentage score. The lab also rates how well each app handles less-risky PUAs (potentially unwanted applications) and checks its ability to detect Windows malware. Of course, Windows malware samples couldn’t infect a Mac, but removing them prevents your Mac from becoming a carrier. For many years, Avira’s antivirus technology has turned in top marks in these tests. However, Avira didn’t participate in the latest AV-Comparatives tests. Avast, AVG, ESET, and Norton are the big winners for Mac antivirus lab tests. All four earned a perfect 18 points from AV-Test and a near-perfect 99.9% from AV-Comparatives. These four also managed 100% detection of Windows-based malware. On the flip side, well over two-thirds of the Mac antiviruses I track don’t boast even one lab test result. I ran my own simple test of Avira’s ability to detect Windows malware, challenging it to clean a USB drive containing samples from my Windows-focused testing. As noted, automatic scanning of USB drives is a Prime-only feature, but as soon as I opened the infested folder, Avira got to work, quickly and silently wiping out 74% of the samples. Cross-checking my notes for the Windows edition, I found that both editions removed precisely the same set of samples, including all ransomware samples. Once again, malware coded for Windows cannot infect a Mac. Even so, it’s impressive that the Mac protection in Aura eliminated 100% of the Windows-centered samples. Webroot came close with 99%, followed by Surfshark with 94%. On the MacBook Air I use for testing, a quick scan finished in barely a second. The full scan took 41 minutes, a bit faster than the average of 47 minutes. Out of the box, Avira schedules a weekly quick scan. You can change the quick scan schedule to daily or monthly, and optionally schedule a full scan daily, weekly, or monthly. Clicking Protection Options in the left-rail menu opens a simple page with three toggles: Real-time Protection, Download Protection, and USB Protection. You can turn off the first two, but don’t do that! USB protection, meaning automatic scanning of any mounted USB drive, is unavailable unless you upgrade to the feature-complete cross-platform Avira Prime suite. That’s not a big loss, as dragging the USB icon onto Avira for scanning is a snap. Phishing pages are fraudulent sites that attempt to steal your login credentials by imitating legitimate websites. Crafting a fake bank site and tricking people into revealing their passwords is easy. Plenty of users have no clue about how to spot a phishing scam. Certainly, creating a phishing page is far easier than coding a Trojan that can actively steal and exfiltrate those passwords, all while evading detection by antivirus programs. In addition, malware is platform-specific, whereas phishing works across platforms. If you’re foolish enough to log into a fake banking page on the browser built into your smart toothbrush, you lose your credentials just the same as if you entered them in a browser on your Mac. Preventing access to such pages, or to pages containing malicious code, can be the first line of defense for an antivirus tool. Avira Free Antivirus does not directly protect against malicious or fraudulent URLs. That’s handled by Avira’s Browser Safety extension for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Opera (sorry, Mac purists—there’s no Safari extension). If you use Avira’s free antivirus for macOS, pair it with Avira's free Browser Safety extension. It’s easy to install in the browser of your choice; I installed it for Chrome and proceeded to test Avira's browser-based protection. For this test, I gather the latest phishing URLs I can find, including those that haven't yet been analyzed or blocklisted. I use one of my Windows-specific hand-coded tools to launch each URL and record results in three browsers, Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, each protected by the browser's own built-in protection. As for the Mac antivirus under test, my analysis tool only runs on Windows, so I test it by hand on the Mac. I’ve grown quite adept at the button-mashing involved in copying and pasting each URL from the list of suspects into the browser. I ran this test simultaneously with my test of Avira Free Security on Windows, using the same list of phishing URLs. For testing purposes, I discard any URL that doesn’t load properly in any browser and any URL that doesn't actively attempt to capture login credentials. Analyzing the confirmed phishing pages, I found that Avira's detection rate was a perfect 100%, exactly as it was under Windows. It makes sense that the scores match since both used the same Chrome extension. Eight competing Mac antivirus apps also reached 100% in their latest phishing tests, including Bitdefender, McAfee, Sophos Home Premium, and Webroot. As it does on Windows, Browser Safety also actively prevents advertisers and others from tracking you. Or rather, it does so if you turn on that feature. Click the browser toolbar button, click the settings gear, and enable Block web tracking. A small numeric overlay on the toolbar button indicates how many trackers it found on the current page. You can click to see more details, but you don’t have the option to fine-tune what it blocks, as you do with Bitdefender and other competitors. Like Browser Safety, the free Avira Safe Shopping extension is something Mac users must chase down and install separately. This extension aims to save you money when shopping online. When coupons are available for the shopping sites you visit, they are displayed. It also tries to find a better deal for each item you put in the cart. In testing, I saw coupons for many major sites but couldn’t find a single “better deal” offer. In any case, previous testing turned up alleged deals that came in at a higher price. I remain doubtful about the value of this feature. With Avira’s Windows-based free security tool, you click Privacy in the left-rail menu to view a page of privacy-related features. These include feature-limited versions of Avira’s VPN and password manager, a secure file-shredding deletion tool, and a tool to tune privacy settings in Windows and popular apps. In the macOS edition, you access the VPN and password manager via submenu items in that left-rail menu. Clicking the button to get VPN support takes you to the page where you can download the separate free edition of Avira Phantom VPN. Please read our review for a full description of the VPN. The Windows edition doesn’t let you choose a VPN location—it makes its own choice. In testing, I found that on the Mac, I could select a country or city for my VPN server. However, free VPN usage is still limited to 500MB of bandwidth per month. This limitation means you can’t afford to use the VPN all the time. I watched YouTube videos for 5-10 minutes and used up about 10% of my monthly data allotment. Clicking on the password management component sends you to its online home. You log into your Avira account and, on first use, create a strong, memorable master password. Be sure to install the browser extension in Chrome, Firefox, or Safari to get the full range of features. This tool handles basic tasks like capturing login credentials you enter, replaying them as needed, and syncing across all your devices. You can enable two-factor authentication, which functions by texting a code to your smartphone. But it doesn’t offer form-filling, secure sharing, digital inheritance, or other top-tier features. See our review of Avira Password Manager to learn more. The third macOS privacy feature, Cookie Cleaner, isn’t available unless you upgrade to Avira Prime. On Windows, all modern browsers support clearing cookies and other saved data by pressing Ctrl+Shift+Del. You can still access cleanup features in browsers on macOS, but there isn’t a universal key combo. Even so, I wouldn’t purchase Prime just to get the Cookie Cleaner. Under Performance, in the left-rail menu, you find Junk Cleaner, Startup Apps Manager, and Uninstaller. Junk Cleaner is available in the free edition; the other two require an upgrade. Like the Optimizer in the Windows edition, Junk Cleaner searches for files that can be safely deleted to free up disk space. It even announces, “You can clean all these items without deleting something important.” You can proceed straight to cleanup or pause and view the app’s findings. On my test Mac, Junk Cleaner reported finding cache files, downloads, and logs. By default, it selected all but downloads for deletion. Just as in the Windows app, it reported how much space it freed and offered to free up even more space if I upgraded to Prime. I mentioned that Avira runs a Smart Scan upon installation. You can also run this scan anytime by clicking a button on the main window. On Windows, this scan covers Privacy Issues, Performance Issues, Viruses, Outdated apps, and Network threats (though the free edition won’t deal with findings in some of these areas). The Mac edition is simpler, sticking to Security, Privacy, and Performance. A Smart Scan on my test Mac finished in less than a minute. Under security, it found the Mac virus-free. In the privacy realm, it reported finding browser tracking cookies and noted that my Email is not monitored for exposure on the dark web. The performance scan, equivalent to the Junk Cleaner, found the same junk files. When I clicked to fix the issues, it didn’t actually do anything. The Chrome browser trackers remained, as did the junk files. And my email was still not monitored. Taking care of those items would—you guessed it—require an upgrade to Avira Prime. At the bottom of the main screen's left-side menu is a highlighted item titled Get Prime. Clicking it gives you a laundry list of Avira Prime's virtues, which costs $109.99 per year to protect up to five devices. You may also see a recommendation for Avira Prime Family, which costs $134.99 per year for 25 devices. If you’re strictly a macOS household, I don’t see any reason to go for Prime. Personal VIP tech support is nice—free users only get FAQs and community support forums—but not at $109.99 per year. Windows users get more benefits from Avira Prime. Final Thoughts Avira Free Antivirus for Mac - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Avira Free Antivirus for Mac has a history of perfect lab scores, but at present its only score is poor. It did hit 100% in our hands-on phishing protection test, matching its Windows counterpart. It doesn’t offer as many features as the free suite on Windows, though, and many visible features require an upgrade. Avast and AVG also offer free antivirus utilities for macOS, so you may want to try them before you settle on a free protector. If you can lay out some cash on antivirus for your Mac, Bitdefender Antivirus Plus and Norton AntiVirus Plus both aced tests by one lab and earned high scores from another. Bitdefender includes advanced features such as ransomware protection for your documents and backups, while Norton includes a firewall, a password manager, a secure browser, and more. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert When the IBM PC was new, I served as the president of the San Francisco PC User Group for three years. That’s how I met PCMag’s editorial team, who brought me on board in 1986. In the years since that fateful meeting, I’ve become PCMag’s expert on security, privacy, and identity protection, putting antivirus tools, security suites, and all kinds of security software through their paces. Before my current security gig, I supplied PCMag readers with tips and solutions on using popular applications, operating systems, and programming languages in my "User to User" and "Ask Neil" columns, which began in 1990 and ran for almost 20 years. Along the way, I wrote more than 40 utility articles, as well as Delphi Programming for Dummies and six other books covering DOS, Windows, and programming. I also reviewed thousands of products of all kinds, ranging from early Sierra Online adventure games to AOL’s precursor Q-Link. In the early 2000s, I turned my focus to security and the growing antivirus industry. After years of working with antivirus, I’m known throughout the security industry as an expert on evaluating antivirus tools. I serve as an advisory board member for the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO), an international nonprofit group dedicated to coordinating and improving testing of anti-malware solutions.

item.title: Celebrate Pokémon’s 30th Anniversary by Cashing Out Your Rare Card Collection
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.24
Much like the pocket monsters themselves, the Pokémon trading card game (TCG) market has evolved from a casual hobby into a lucrative, high-stakes alternative asset. You know what I mean if you've ever tried to purchase a set from the Pokémon Center: the long queues are ridiculous. The market for top-tier chase cards is red hot, driven entirely by hype for a select few mascot singles. On Feb. 16, 2026, Logan Paul broke trading card records by selling his PSA 10-graded Pikachu Illustrator card (and diamond-encrusted slab-holder) for a dizzying $16.49 million. It's a flip for the record books, and you can join the party by making flips of your own. With Pokémon’s 30th anniversary in full swing, use this guide as your roadmap to navigate the wild and wonderful world of selling Pokémon cards online. These recommended apps and services will help you price, grade, and sell cards—and swiftly ship them to buyers. 1. Price Your Pokémon Cards With TCGPlayer and Other Apps Knowing your card's worth is important before listing it for sale. The popular TCGPlayer app (available for Android and iOS) is a valuable resource. Its handy scanning feature lets you quickly identify cards and view real-time pricing data based on recent sales completed on TCGPlayer. Each listing features market price history, recent sales, the number of cards available, and other useful metrics. You should gather data from multiple resources to better assess a card's value. Like TCGPlayer, Collectr is an Android and iOS app that lets you browse card listings and metrics. Alternative apps include Alt and Card Ladder. Alt is a great listing and auction app that focuses heavily on graded cards (more on that in a bit). Card Ladder has listings, too, but offers a subscription for tracking and growing your card collection. Of course, eBay never fails to feature Pokémon card listings, so make it a point to check the prices for sold cards. Note that some services double as platforms for selling your cards, streamlining the selling process. Armed with this information, you can establish a baseline selling price. But before moving on to that step, you must consider grading your Pokémon cards to amass big bucks. 2. Grade Your Pokémon Cards to Add Value Say you snag a rare Special Illustration Charizard ex from the Pokémon Scarlet & Violet 151 set, which currently goes for more than $350 raw as of this writing. You'll want it graded by an authentication company to get the full value from a sale. The most high-profile service is Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA). You'll often see PSA-graded cards for sale online. PSA has Android and iOS apps for scanning cards and submitting grading orders. It also lets you track these orders and even post your listing on eBay for easy selling. A graded Pokémon card gives it far more legitimacy. Why? The process verifies the card's authenticity and gives it a quality grade (i.e., Heavily Played, Mint, or Gem Mint), making it more valuable than an ungraded card. The process takes time. Depending on your submission tier, it can take anywhere from 20 to 100 business days for PSA to grade your Pokémon cards. However, you should factor in an extra few weeks for mail transit and intake processing before the grading clock officially starts. Grading isn't free. PSA charges $59.99 for its entry-level Standard tier to grade a single card. A PSA Collectors Club subscription (starting at $149 per year) drops this price to $24.99 per card with bulk orders of at least 20 cards. There is also an upcharge if the card’s post-grade value exceeds the limit of the tier you chose. This means that if you submit a card at a lower tier, but it receives a PSA 10 worth more than $1,000, PSA will upcharge you to the corresponding higher tier (such as Express) to match its true market value before shipping the slabbed card back to you. It is very important that you pre-screen your cards with the apps mentioned in the section above, and purchase the appropriate grading tier to avoid any mid-process upcharge. Group submission is a good way to mitigate subscription and pricing fees. PSA dealers run these submissions and aggregate cards from multiple collectors into one batch. You can browse online for local hobby leagues and hobby shops (such as Bleecker Trading in New York City) that offer group submissions. GameStop (yes, the video game store) also offers group card submissions. If you want to swing a profit, there's no financial incentive to grade Pokemon cards that sell for less than a grading fee—unless you're confident the card will increase in value later. Don't bother sending inexpensive cards for grading; sell these raw or in bulk instead. You should also consider alternative services that may offer lower-cost grading. Beckett (now owned by PSA's parent company), Certified Collectibles Group (CGC), and Sportscard Guaranty Corporation (also owned by PSA's parent company) are other options. Shop around to find a grading service that fits your budget. That said, if you pull a rare Pokémon card and want cash now, you don't necessarily need to get it graded, provided you're OK with not getting full value on the sale. List it on eBay or social media with high-quality photos; someone may take it off your hands. 3. Sell Your Pokémon Cards Online You've researched your Pokémon cards and know their worth, whether graded or not. Now you're ready to sell. But where should you list them? There are many options. If you're comfortable working through traditional selling apps, check out Alt, eBay, or TCGPlayer. If you're big into social media, platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatNot let you sell to live viewers. The selling process is fairly simple. The TCGPlayer app has a scanner to quickly identify cards and pull up market details. Then, you create a detailed listing title that states the card's name, language, grading, and signature information. Ensure the listing's description includes the necessary card descriptor language, damage, grading or modifications, and quantity. Publish it to go live and let the community seek it out. If you use social media, remember that interaction and engagement are key. For example, you should post Pokémon cards on an Instagram feed and discuss their grades. Likewise, Facebook has numerous groups packed with buyers, collectors, and sellers. WhatNot, on the other hand, is a unique auction and marketplace that combines live feeds and auctioning with audience engagement. It also lets you run giveaways and raffles, making it a fun alternative to traditional selling platforms. Similarly, TikTok users can create a shop to sell their inventory by leveraging the platform's robust live-streaming and video features. As vanilla as it sounds, eBay is often your best tool for selling Pokémon cards. Use the Buy it Now selling option to choose a specific card price. If you have many cards you'd like to sell quickly, use Auctions to let people bid on your stack. You can quickly establish a good reputation by selling honestly and providing accurate card descriptions. All selling services have commissions and fees to consider. Long story short, eBay, TCGPlayer, and the like all take a cut from your sales. Shipping fees are another factor. You may want to entice buyers with free shipping, but consider the out-of-pocket shipping costs. Be sure to carefully review the seller fees from services like eBay and TCGPlayer to understand the additional fees you might incur. 4. Pack Your Pokémon Cards You want the cards you sell to arrive in the best possible condition. Damage during shipping is an easy way to ruin your reputation, so use protection. BCW and UltraPro are the big names in the card-protection space. Penny sleeves, toploaders, and team bags are the absolute baseline protections. Penny sleeves (roughly $4 for a pack of 100) are designed to protect a single card from surface scratches: never try to stuff multiple cards into one. For high-value single cards, you want to slide that sleeved card into a rigid plastic toploader to prevent it from bending. If you're selling in bulk, team bags (roughly $6 for a pack of 100) can hold 25-75 cards together to prevent them from sliding around in transit. For extra security, tape your toploaders or team bags shut with painter's tape (the blue type) to keep your cards from slipping out of the opening. Painter's tape is a good choice because its adhesive is neither particularly strong nor particularly sticky, making it easy to remove without potentially damaging anything. Selling an individual card? Slide the single penny sleeve into a rigid toploader opening-first, then apply your tape. Toploaders are highly durable plastic cases, and a fantastic choice for safeguarding individual cards. You can pick up a pack of 25 top loaders for roughly $5. As a general rule, pack your cards like you would expect to receive them. 5. Ship Your Pokémon Cards Depending on the card's value, you may want to take additional steps to protect it. If the cards are inexpensive (say, under $20), simply slip those top loaders or team bags into a padded envelope for shipping. If they cost more than $20, sandwich the top loaders or team bags between two pieces of cardboard and secure them with painter's tape. Avoid rubber bands, which can warp the edges if compressed. Place the cards into a bubble mailer envelope and ship them via a courier, such as FedEx, UPS, or USPS. If you want additional security (or are shipping cards in something larger than a large envelope), USPS Ground Advantage handles packages and includes $100 in insurance per label. If you own a printer, you can print labels and prepare the envelope or box at home. This saves you from standing in line at the post office. Simply place your package in the mailbox or a USPS drop-off location. Going the FedEx or UPS routes means you can schedule a pickup time online. Finally, for more on selling Pokémon cards—or pretty much anything else—check out our guide on how to sell on eBay. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: See ChatGPT, Claude, and Other AIs Handle the Same Prompt With a $55 Tool
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.00
TL;DR: ChatPlayground AI puts multiple AI models in one place, so you can compare their responses to the same prompt. A lifetime subscription is currently on sale for $54.97. Getting a useful AI answer often means checking it against another model. Instead of opening several different AI tools and copying the same prompt back and forth, ChatPlayground AI lets you run multiple models side by side and compare the results in one place. A lifetime subscription is currently $54.97 (MSRP $619). ChatPlayground AI sends any prompt to several models at once and lines up the responses in one window, so you can see how they differ and pick what works best. The platform supports more than 25 models, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Llama, and Perplexity. That means you can use the same workflow for chat, coding help, content drafts, or image ideas and compare model output without copying and pasting everywhere. You can tweak a prompt, run it again, and see how each model changes the answer. Prompt engineering tools help you refine and reuse effective prompts. ChatPlayground AI also lets you upload images and PDFs, then ask questions about them, so you can check how different models handle the same document or screenshot. Saved chat history keeps longer projects and useful prompts easy to revisit. The Unlimited Plan is a lifetime subscription with unlimited messages each month. It’s aimed at prompt engineers, startups, and teams that test or use AI heavily and need room to experiment. You can use it on any desktop that runs a recent version of Chrome, Edge, or Firefox, with no set limit on how many devices you sign in from. Until September 20, get a ChatPlayground AI lifetime subscription on sale for $54.97. Prices subject to change. PCMag editors select and review products independently. If you buy through StackSocial affiliate links, we may earn commissions, which help support our testing. About Our Expert Products featured in these stories are selected by our partners at StackCommerce. If you buy something through links on our site, PCMag may earn an affiliate commission.

item.title: Show Your ID to Unlock Windows? Microsoft's Next Upgrade Gets Terrifyingly Personal
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.79
Windows 11 will soon ask for and remember your age so apps and sites know whether you’re an adult. That's scary enough, but Microsoft is already on to the next step of making you prove your age, either by submitting a government ID or a selfie. To date, three US states have already passed laws forcing Windows and other operating systems to implement age checks of various forms. In other news, Microsoft is taking a strong public stance against AI rights, publishing a code of conduct that's sharply critical of how Anthropic is developing Claude. Additionally, Frank Shaw, Microsoft’s legendary head of communications, is leaving the company. Read on for a look at what we know about Windows 11’s age verification scheme, how Microsoft is campaigning against legal personhood for AI, and my thoughts about the end of an era for Microsoft PR. The Era of Age Verification Is Here (and Still Very Confusing) OS-level age verification laws are having a moment. A California law will require most operating systems to collect users' ages starting in 2027, with similar legislation in Colorado and Illinois to follow. Congress is also considering laws that would extend such requirements nationally. In response, Microsoft announced two levels of age checks for Windows 11 PCs: unverified and verified. Apps will be able to request your age from the OS via the Windows Age API, which returns a range such as under 10, 10-12, 13-15, 16-17, or 18+. You can enter an age without proof, but it's unverified. To verify your age, you have to provide more personal information. Microsoft explains that it's “expanding age assurance through the Microsoft account” for situations where high confidence is necessary, such as meeting local legal requirements.
